**File:** `codex-rs/secrets/src/local.rs`
**Anchor:** `LocalSecretsBackend::set`
**Severity:** high

`set` and `delete` both follow the same read-modify-write shape with no lock spanning the sequence:

```rust
pub fn set(&self, scope: &SecretScope, name: &SecretName, value: &str) -> Result<()> {
    ...
    let mut file = self.load_file()?;
    file.secrets.insert(canonical_key, value.to_string());
    self.save_file(&file)
}
```

`load_file` decrypts and parses the whole `local.age`/`codex_auth.age`/`mcp_oauth.age` file into a
`SecretsFile { secrets: BTreeMap<String,String> }`, and `save_file` re-encrypts and atomically
replaces the entire file. There is no cross-process or cross-thread lock guarding this
load-mutate-save cycle: the only synchronization primitive in the file, `MCP_OAUTH_CACHE`
(`static Mutex<Option<CachedMcpSecrets>>`), is a decrypt-result cache keyed by content hash and is
released well before `save_file` runs; it does nothing to serialize writers.

The doc comment on `LocalSecretsNamespace::CodexAuth` itself describes the expected usage pattern
that makes this an "ordinary condition," not an edge case: "Codex authentication credentials used
by the CLI, TUI, app server, and other clients." If two of those clients (or two tasks in the same
process, since `SecretsManager` is `Clone` and backed by an `Arc<dyn SecretsBackend>`) call `set`
or `delete` concurrently — e.g. two OAuth token refreshes racing, or a `set` racing a `delete` — the
second writer's `load_file()` observes a snapshot that predates the first writer's `save_file()`,
and the second `save_file()` overwrites the whole file, silently discarding the first writer's
change. There is no error, retry, or merge; the loser's secret (or deletion) simply disappears.

I did not execute a live race (reproducing it deterministically would require injecting a delay
between `load_file` and `save_file`, which needs a source change outside this review's scope), but
the absence of any lock across the read-modify-write cycle is unambiguous from the code itself, and
the rest of this codebase treats this exact hazard as worth guarding against elsewhere (see
`codex-rs/rollout/src/session_index.rs`'s `SESSION_INDEX_LOCK` and
`codex-rs/rollout/src/writer_lock.rs`'s cross-process `WriterLockCoordinator`), which is why this
gap in the secrets store stands out.

Fix: serialize `load_file`+mutate+`save_file` with an OS file lock on the secrets file (or a
lock file alongside it), mirroring the coordination already used by the rollout writer lock.

### CR-031: `env -C`/`-u` and other value-taking flags bypass the dangerous-command classifier
**File:** `codex-rs/shell-command/src/command_safety/is_dangerous_command.rs`
**Anchor:** `dangerous_command_match_for_env`
**Severity:** high

`dangerous_command_match_for_env` walks `env`'s leading arguments to find the wrapped command it should recurse into. It only recognizes `-i` / `--ignore-environment` and `NAME=VALUE` assignments as "skip and continue"; any other flag (including ordinary GNU coreutils flags that consume a following argument, such as `-C DIR` / `--chdir DIR`, `-u NAME` / `--unset NAME`, `-S STRING`) causes the loop to `break` without advancing `command_index`. The remainder of the command (starting at that unrecognized flag) is then treated as the program to recurse into, so the flag itself (e.g. `-C`) becomes `cmd0`, matches nothing, and the classifier returns `None` — the wrapped `rm -rf` (or other dangerous command) is never inspected.

I confirmed this by adding a temporary unit test in-tree and running it:

```rust
let command = ["env", "-C", "/tmp", "rm", "-rf", "."].map(str::to_owned);
dangerous_command_match(&command) // returns None
```

`cargo test -p codex-shell-command` shows this returns `None`, whereas `env TARGET=/tmp rm -rf /tmp` (an assignment-only prefix, already covered by an existing test) correctly returns `Some(ForcedRm)`. `env -C /tmp rm -rf .` is not an obscure adversarial trick — `-C`/`--chdir` is a documented, commonly used `env` option — so this is a real gap in a security-relevant classifier under ordinary usage, not just a contrived jailbreak. The fix should special-case (or generically handle) `env` flags that consume a following value (`-C`/`--chdir`, `-u`/`--unset`, `-S`/`--split-string`, etc.) the same way `-i` is handled, rather than assuming any non-`NAME=VALUE`, non-`-i` token starts the wrapped command.

**Disposition:** fixed
**Commit:** `acb2ef1a15`
**Resolved:** 2026-09-11
**Note:** —
### CR-032: Batch job validation failures abort the entire concurrent batch, bypassing `--fail-fast`
**File:** `codex-rs/skills/src/assets/samples/imagegen/scripts/image_gen.py`
**Anchor:** `async def run_job(i: int, job: Dict[str, Any])`
**Severity:** high

Inside `_run_generate_batch`'s `run_job` closure, per-job payload construction and validation
(`n = int(payload.get("n", 1))`, `_validate_generate_payload(payload)`,
`_validate_transparency(...)`, `_job_output_paths(...)`) all run **before** the `try:` block that
wraps the actual `client.images.generate/edit` call. That `try` is the only place that converts a
failure into `(i, str(exc))` and respects `args.fail_fast`.

`_validate_generate_payload` (and friends) call `_die()` on invalid input, which raises
`SystemExit`, not a normal `Exception`. `SystemExit` derives from `BaseException`, so it is never
caught by the job's `except Exception as exc:`, nor by the batch-level
`except Exception:` around `await asyncio.gather(*tasks)` in `_run_generate_batch`. The result: a
single malformed job anywhere in a large JSONL batch (e.g. `"n": 11`, an unsupported `size` for
`gpt-image-2`, or `background: transparent` with `gpt-image-2`) raises `SystemExit` inside one
`asyncio.create_task`. That exception propagates straight out of `asyncio.gather`, past the
batch's own cancellation/cleanup code (which also only catches `Exception`), and terminates the
whole process — aborting every other job in the batch, including ones already mid-flight against
the paid Images API.

This directly contradicts the documented behavior of `--fail-fast` (which is supposed to be the
thing that makes one bad job kill the batch; without it, jobs are meant to be reported via
`any_failed` and the batch continues). Move the per-job validation (size/model/quality/background/
n) inside the same `try` that wraps the API call, and catch `SystemExit`/`InstallError`-style
"expected" failures alongside `Exception` so a single bad job degrades to "job failed" instead of
"batch aborted."

**Disposition:** fixed
**Commit:** `3466de89b5`
**Resolved:** 2026-09-11
**Note:** —
### CR-033: Recursive spawn-descendant queries hang forever on a cyclic thread-spawn graph
**File:** `codex-rs/state/src/runtime/threads.rs`
**Anchor:** `list_thread_spawn_descendants_matching`
**Severity:** high

`list_thread_spawn_descendants_matching` (backing the public `list_thread_spawn_descendants` and
`list_thread_spawn_descendants_with_status`) and `find_thread_spawn_descendant_by_path` both build
a `WITH RECURSIVE subtree(...) AS (... UNION ALL ...)` query over `thread_spawn_edges` with no
cycle guard: each recursive step only extends `depth`, so a cycle in the edge graph produces
infinitely many distinct rows and the query never terminates.

This is not a hypothetical: `upsert_thread_spawn_edge` is a public `StateRuntime` method with
`ON CONFLICT(child_thread_id) DO UPDATE SET parent_thread_id = excluded.parent_thread_id`, i.e. it
happily reparents a child to any parent, including a descendant of that child, which closes a
cycle. The sibling code path used by `list_threads`/`list_threads_by_relation`
(`push_list_threads_query`'s `DescendantsOf` branch) uses plain `UNION` (not `UNION ALL`) in its
recursive CTE specifically so a cycle terminates once no new `(child, parent)` pairs are produced —
and the test suite exercises exactly this by inserting a "cycle-closing spawn edge" and asserting
`list_threads_by_relation` still returns
(`list_threads_by_relation_filters_spawn_graph_with_keyset_pagination`). No equivalent test exists
for `list_thread_spawn_descendants*` or `find_thread_spawn_descendant_by_path`, and their `UNION
ALL` variant does not share that protection.

I verified the underlying SQLite behavior directly: running the equivalent recursive CTE
(`UNION ALL` over a 3-node cycle A→B→C→A) via `sqlite3 :memory:` under `timeout 5` does not
complete — the process has to be killed (exit code 124) — confirming the query hangs rather than
erroring out or looping quickly.

`list_thread_spawn_descendants` is called from production code
(`codex-rs/core/src/thread_manager.rs`, `codex-rs/core/src/agent/control/spawn.rs`), and
`upsert_thread_spawn_edge` is called from `codex-rs/core/src/agent/control.rs` when persisting a
spawned thread's parent edge. All state-runtime SQL for a given `StateRuntime` shares one
`SqlitePool` capped at `max_connections(5)` (`codex-rs/state/src/sqlite.rs`), so a single hung
descendant query can pin one of only five connections indefinitely; a few concurrent callers
hitting the same cyclic subtree would exhaust the pool and stall all other state-DB access for the
process, not just the caller that triggered the cycle.

Fix: change both recursive CTEs (`list_thread_spawn_descendants_matching`'s query and
`find_thread_spawn_descendant_by_path`'s query) to use `UNION` instead of `UNION ALL` (matching
`push_list_threads_query`'s `DescendantsOf` branch), or explicitly track visited nodes / cap
recursion depth. Also worth adding a test that inserts a cycle via `upsert_thread_spawn_edge` and
asserts `list_thread_spawn_descendants`/`find_thread_spawn_descendant_by_path` still terminate, the
way `list_threads_by_relation_filters_spawn_graph_with_keyset_pagination` already does for the
other code path.

### CR-034: App-server request resolution is consumed before the RPC that delivers it succeeds, silently dropping the user's decision

**File:** `codex-rs/tui/src/app/thread_routing.rs`
**Anchor:** `try_resolve_app_server_request`
**Severity:** high

`submit_thread_op` first calls `try_resolve_app_server_request`, which calls
`PendingAppServerRequests::take_resolution(...)`. In
`codex-rs/tui/src/app/app_server_requests.rs::take_resolution`, the pending
entry is removed from the internal maps (`exec_approvals.remove`,
`file_change_approvals.remove`, `permissions_approvals.remove`,
`pop_user_input_request_for_turn`, `mcp_requests.remove`) *before* the actual
RPC (`app_server.resolve_server_request(resolution.request_id,
resolution.result)`) is attempted:

```rust
let Some(resolution) = self
    .pending_app_server_requests
    .take_resolution(&thread_id.to_string(), op)
    .map_err(|err| color_eyre::eyre::eyre!(err))?
else {
    return Ok(false);
};

match app_server
    .resolve_server_request(resolution.request_id, resolution.result)
    .await
{
    Ok(()) => { ... Ok(true) }
    Err(err) => {
        self.chat_widget.add_error_message(format!(
            "Failed to resolve app-server request for thread {thread_id}: {err}"
        ));
        Ok(false)
    }
}
```

If `resolve_server_request` fails (a realistic outcome for a remote
`ThreadParamsMode::Remote` app-server over a flaky WebSocket connection, or a
transient IPC hiccup for an embedded server), the function returns `Ok(false)`.
Because the pending entry was already removed, the user's exec/file-change/
permissions/MCP-elicitation/user-verification decision cannot be resubmitted
— there is nothing left to resolve.

Worse, `submit_thread_op` cannot distinguish "there was no pending resolution
for this op" from "the resolution failed to deliver," and falls through to
`try_submit_active_thread_op_via_app_server`, whose match arms do not cover
`ExecApproval`/`PatchApproval`/`ResolveElicitation`/`ResolveUserVerification`/
`UserInputAnswer`/`RequestPermissionsResponse` (`_ => Ok(false)`). The caller
then shows a second, misleading message: `"Not available in TUI yet for
thread {thread_id}."` on top of the first "Failed to resolve..." message,
even though the feature obviously is available — it just failed once. The
outstanding server-side request (e.g. a command execution approval) is left
unresolved with no way for the TUI to retry it, which can hang the turn
indefinitely from the server's perspective.

Fix: only remove the pending entry after `resolve_server_request` succeeds
(e.g. peek/clone the resolution, or re-insert it on failure so a retry is
possible), and drop the generic "Not available in TUI yet" fallback message
for this failure path so the user isn't shown a confusing, unrelated error.

### CR-035: `/usage` command output can silently vanish when re-invoked before the previous card is inserted into history
**File:** `codex-rs/tui/src/chatwidget/tokens.rs`
**Anchor:** `add_token_activity_output`
**Severity:** high

`add_token_activity_output` unconditionally clears any card waiting to be committed to
transcript history before installing the new one:

```rust
pub(crate) fn add_token_activity_output(&mut self, view: TokenActivityView) {
    let request_id = self.next_token_activity_request_id;
    ...
    let (cell, handle) = new_token_activity_output(view);
    self.completed_token_activity_output = None;
    self.refreshing_token_activity_output = Some(PendingTokenActivityOutput { request_id, cell, handle });
    ...
}
```

`completed_token_activity_output` holds a fully-resolved `/usage` card (which bundles the
echoed `/usage <view>` command line together with the rendered chart) that is waiting for
`usage_history_insertion_blocked()` to clear before it is spliced into permanent transcript
history. That helper reports "blocked" whenever a stream, plan stream, queued stream
consolidation, or active transcript cell is present — i.e. routinely true for the entire
duration of an active agent turn.

Sequence that loses data: user runs `/usage` while the agent's answer is still streaming;
the background `GetAccountTokenUsageResponse` comes back quickly and lands in
`completed_token_activity_output`, but insertion is deferred because the stream is still
active. Before the stream ends, the user runs `/usage` again (e.g. picks "Show usage" from
the menu a second time, or just re-issues the command). `add_token_activity_output` resets
`completed_token_activity_output` to `None`, discarding the first card — including its
echoed command line — with no error, log message, or user-visible indication that a
transcript entry was dropped. The first `/usage` invocation never appears anywhere in
history.

Fix: either queue completed-but-uninserted cards (flush the previous one via
`take_completed_token_activity_output` before installing the new pending request) or make
the drop explicit/visible instead of silent.

### CR-036: OSC 9 desktop notifications forward unsanitized text into a raw terminal escape sequence

**File:** `codex-rs/tui/src/notifications/osc9.rs`
**Anchor:** `PostNotification::write_ansi`, `fn escape_tmux_dcs_passthrough_payload`
**Severity:** high

`Osc9Backend::notify` builds `PostNotification { message, dcs_passthrough }` from whatever
string the caller passes and `write_ansi` embeds it directly into a raw control sequence:

```rust
write!(f, "\x1b]9;{}\x07", self.message)
```

(and, for the tmux DCS-passthrough branch, only escape bytes `\x1b` are doubled via
`escape_tmux_dcs_passthrough_payload` — no other control bytes, including the `\x07` (BEL)
terminator itself, are stripped or escaped).

The `message` reaching this code is not operator input: `Tui::notify` (`tui.rs`) is fed
`Notification::display()` from `codex-rs/tui/src/chatwidget/notifications.rs`, and for
`Notification::AgentTurnComplete { response }` the displayed text is the (whitespace-normalized,
length-truncated, but **not control-character-stripped**) text of the agent's final turn —
i.e. attacker/model-controlled text that can originate from untrusted tool output or web content
relayed through the model. `Notification::ExecApprovalRequested { command }` is similarly built
from the literal shell command string the agent wants to run.

If that text contains a literal BEL (`\x07`) the OSC 9 sequence is terminated early and the
remaining bytes are written to the terminal verbatim; if it contains further ESC sequences they
are also passed straight through. Depending on the terminal emulator this allows title-bar
spoofing, clipboard writes (OSC 52), or other escape-sequence side effects triggered purely by
receiving a desktop notification while the pane is unfocused — normal, expected conditions for
this code path (notifications are only emitted when `should_emit_notification` decides the
terminal is unfocused, in `tui.rs`).

This is a real gap, not a stylistic one: the codebase already has an established fix for exactly
this class of bug next to a different escape-sequence sink. `terminal_hyperlinks.rs`
(`sanitized_destination`) filters `!ch.is_control()` before embedding a URL into an OSC 8
hyperlink, and `codex-rs/tui/src/onboarding/auth.rs` has a dedicated regression test
(`mark_url_hyperlink_sanitizes_control_chars`) asserting ESC/BEL are stripped from hyperlink
destinations. No equivalent stripping exists for the OSC 9 notification message in this file.

Fix: strip (or percent/caret-escape) control characters — at minimum `\x1b` and `\x07` — from
`message` before formatting the OSC 9 command, mirroring `sanitized_destination`'s
`!ch.is_control()` filter, both in the plain and tmux-DCS-passthrough branches.

### CR-037: BlockingLruCache panics instead of no-op inside a current-thread Tokio runtime

**File:** `codex-rs/utils/cache/src/lib.rs`
**Anchor:** `lock_if_runtime`
**Severity:** high

The doc comment on `BlockingLruCache` promises: "Calls outside a Tokio runtime are no-ops." The implementation of `lock_if_runtime` is:

```rust
fn lock_if_runtime<K, V>(m: &Mutex<LruCache<K, V>>) -> Option<MutexGuard<'_, LruCache<K, V>>>
where
    K: Eq + Hash,
{
    tokio::runtime::Handle::try_current().ok()?;
    Some(tokio::task::block_in_place(|| m.blocking_lock()))
}
```

`tokio::task::block_in_place` panics ("can call blocking only when running on the multi-threaded runtime") when called from inside a `current_thread` Tokio runtime — this is documented behavior of Tokio itself (`tokio-1.53.1/src/task/blocking.rs`: "This function panics if called from a current_thread runtime"). `Handle::try_current()` succeeds for *any* runtime flavor, current-thread included, so `lock_if_runtime` doesn't fall into the "no runtime" no-op branch in that case — it instead panics.

I reproduced this directly with a minimal crate mirroring the exact logic, run under the default (current-thread) `#[tokio::test]` flavor:

```
thread 'tests::default_flavor_current_thread' panicked at src/lib.rs:3:10:
can call blocking only when running on the multi-threaded runtime
```

This is not a hypothetical edge case: the crate's own tests explicitly opt into `#[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread")]` for the two tests that exercise `BlockingLruCache` (`stores_and_retrieves_values`, `evicts_least_recently_used`), which only works around the bug for those two tests — any other caller using the default `#[tokio::test]` flavor, or any binary built with `#[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")]`, will panic the first time it touches this cache instead of getting the documented "no-op" fallback. `codex-rs/code-mode-host/src/main.rs` in this repo is itself built with `#[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")]`, demonstrating that current-thread runtimes are a real, present configuration in this codebase, not just a theoretical one.

`BlockingLruCache` is used by `codex_utils_audio::estimate_audio_token_count` (this shard, `codex-rs/utils/audio/src/lib.rs`), by `codex_utils_image`, and by `codex-rs/core/src/context_manager/history.rs`'s `ORIGINAL_IMAGE_ESTIMATE_CACHE`. Any of those call sites reached from a current-thread runtime will crash the whole process instead of degrading gracefully as documented.

Fix: either detect the runtime flavor and skip locking (falling through to the "outside a runtime" behavior) when running on a current-thread runtime, or use a non-blocking lock primitive (e.g. `std::sync::Mutex` / `parking_lot::Mutex`) instead of `tokio::sync::Mutex` + `block_in_place`, since nothing here actually needs to be `.await`-compatible — `blocking_lock` is used specifically to avoid that.

**Disposition:** fixed
**Commit:** `302910b5cf`
**Resolved:** 2026-09-11
**Note:** —
### CR-038: Malformed NUL-device path breaks `allow_null_device` on every sandbox spawn path
**File:** `codex-rs/windows-sandbox-rs/src/acl.rs`
**Anchor:** `allow_null_device`, `to_wide(r"\\\\.\\NUL")`
**Severity:** high

`allow_null_device` opens the Windows NUL device with:

```rust
let h = CreateFileW(
    to_wide(r"\\\\.\\NUL").as_ptr(),
    ...
```

`r"\\\\.\\NUL"` is a **raw** string literal, so none of its backslashes are
escape-processed. I compiled a small Rust program to check the actual bytes
produced:

```
s (as written)      len=10 bytes=[92,92,92,92,46,92,92,78,85,76]   -> \\\\.\\NUL
correct \\.\NUL      len=7  bytes=[92,92,46,92,78,85,76]           -> \\.\NUL
equal = false
```

The canonical Win32 device-namespace path for the null device is `\\.\NUL`
(two backslashes, a dot, one backslash, `NUL` — 3 backslashes total). The
literal actually used has 4 backslashes before the dot and 2 after it (6
total), i.e. it is not the string the author intended. The correct pattern is
demonstrated elsewhere in this exact function's sibling file
(`sandbox_smoketests.py` line 745 uses `Path(r"\\?\C:\sbx_longpath_test.txt")`,
which is correctly single-backslash raw-string syntax), confirming this is a
copy/paste or escaping mistake rather than intentional formatting — the
author most likely intended the non-raw-string escaping convention
(`"\\\\.\\NUL"`, which *would* decode to `\\.\NUL`) and mistakenly prefixed it
with `r`.

If `CreateFileW` does not tolerate the extra separators (I do not have a
Windows machine in this environment to confirm the live syscall behavior),
the call returns `INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE`/0 and the function silently returns
without granting the RX ACE:

```rust
if h == 0 || h == INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE {
    return;
}
```

This function is called from every sandbox process-spawn path in this
codebase: `spawn_prep.rs` (`allow_null_device_for_workspace_write`, and two
more direct call sites), `elevated_impl.rs`, and
`bin/command_runner/win.rs::spawn_ipc_process` (called for every capability
SID on every spawned child, including the common case). If the ACE grant
silently no-ops, any sandboxed command that legitimately redirects output to
`NUL` (a very common Windows idiom, e.g. `cmd /c foo > NUL 2>&1`, or
PowerShell `Out-Null`) under the restricted/capability token could start
failing with access-denied once the null-device ACE is missing, since the
function fails closed with no diagnostic. This would surface as ordinary
sandboxed commands failing unpredictably rather than as an obvious crash.

Fix: change the literal to `r"\\.\NUL"` (or drop the `r` prefix and use
`"\\\\.\\NUL"`), matching the correct convention already used in this file's
own sibling test file.

**Disposition:** fixed
**Commit:** `cf3ebed805`
**Resolved:** 2026-09-11
**Note:** Raw-string literal corrected to r"\\.\NUL" (canonical 7-byte \.\NUL). Defect and fix verified cross-platform with rustc (byte comparison against the canonical path). The CreateFileW/ACL path is #[cfg(target_os = "windows")] and cannot be compiled/run on this macOS host, so the syscall behavior was not exercised.
### CR-039: USERPROFILE_ROOT_EXCLUSIONS omits common top-level credential files, exposing them to sandboxed reads
**File:** `codex-rs/windows-sandbox-rs/src/setup.rs`
**Anchor:** `USERPROFILE_ROOT_EXCLUSIONS`, `profile_read_roots`
**Severity:** high

`USERPROFILE_ROOT_EXCLUSIONS` is a curated list of top-level `%USERPROFILE%` entries that must never be handed to the sandboxed process even when the permission profile grants broad/full-disk read access:

```rust
const USERPROFILE_ROOT_EXCLUSIONS: &[&str] = &[
    ".ssh", ".tsh", ".brev", ".gnupg", ".aws", ".azure", ".kube",
    ".docker", ".config", ".npm", ".pki", ".terraform.d",
];
```

`profile_read_roots` walks the top-level entries of `%USERPROFILE%` and excludes any entry whose *name* exactly (case-insensitively) matches one of these strings, then the result is used directly as read roots whenever `has_symbolic_root_read_access` is true (`gather_full_read_roots_for_permissions`) — which is also the codepath the **legacy** Windows sandbox backend requires (`lib.rs`'s `run_windows_sandbox_capture_with_filesystem_overrides` bails unless `permissions.has_full_disk_read_access()`, i.e. this is the default/only mode the legacy backend supports, not a rare opt-in).

The exclusion list protects credential *directories* (`.aws`, `.docker`, `.npm`, …) but misses extremely common credential *files* that live directly at `%USERPROFILE%`, notably `~/.npmrc` (npm registry auth tokens), `~/.netrc` (host/login/password for curl, ftp, etc.), `~/.pypirc` (PyPI upload credentials), and `~/.git-credentials` (plaintext git `credential.helper=store` output). None of these filenames appear in the exclusion list, and a grep of the crate confirms they are not filtered anywhere else (`grep -rn "\.npmrc\|\.netrc\|\.pypirc\|git-credentials" codex-rs/windows-sandbox-rs/` returns no matches). Because `profile_read_roots` matches on exact top-level entry name, a file such as `.npmrc` is never excluded by the `.npm` directory entry.

Any sandboxed command run through the legacy backend can therefore read these files (e.g. via `type %USERPROFILE%\.npmrc`), leaking registry/API tokens or stored passwords to the very untrusted command the sandbox exists to contain. The same exclusion list (and the same gap) is reused for write-root expansion (`filter_user_profile_root_exclusions` / `is_user_profile_root_exclusion`), so the files could also become writable if a write root ever equals the profile root exactly.

Fix: extend `USERPROFILE_ROOT_EXCLUSIONS` (or add a parallel file-name list) to cover known top-level credential dotfiles, not just credential directories.

**Disposition:** fixed
**Commit:** `18b8810892`
**Resolved:** 2026-09-11
**Note:** Added .npmrc/.netrc/_netrc/.pypirc/.git-credentials to USERPROFILE_ROOT_EXCLUSIONS (matched by exact top-level name, so the .npm dir entry did not cover .npmrc). setup module is #[cfg(target_os = "windows")]; exclusion behavior and the module tests could not be executed on this macOS host — change verified by inspection as an additive extension of the filtered constant.
### CR-040: Deny-write ACL failures are silently swallowed in the legacy sandbox
**File:** `codex-rs/windows-sandbox-rs/src/spawn_prep.rs`
**Anchor:** `apply_legacy_session_acl_rules`
**Severity:** high

Inside `apply_legacy_session_acl_rules`, every deny-write ACE application discards its `Result`:

```rust
for p in &deny {
    for root_sid in deny_root_capabilities_for_path(p, acl_sids.write_root_sids) {
        let _ = add_deny_write_ace(p, root_sid.sid.as_ptr());
    }
}
```

`deny` is the set of paths that must stay unwritable to the sandboxed process even though a broader ancestor root is writable (e.g. `.git`, `.codex`, explicit deny-write overrides created just above this loop via `std::fs::create_dir_all`). If `add_deny_write_ace` fails for any reason (transient `SetSecurityInfo` failure, AV/EDR hook, path removed concurrently, ACL already at capacity, a network-backed path that rejects ACL edits, etc.), the function proceeds as if the deny succeeded: it returns `Ok(())`, no error is surfaced to the caller, and nothing is logged. The sandboxed process then runs with write access to a path the caller explicitly asked to protect, with no diagnostic indicating the negative-permission guarantee was not applied.

This is inconsistent with the neighboring deny-read path a few lines below in the same function, which does propagate failures via `?`:

```rust
sync_persistent_deny_read_acls(codex_home, readonly_sid_str, additional_deny_read_paths, readonly_sid.as_ptr())?;
```

The asymmetry (allow-ACE failures failing closed vs. deny-ACE failures failing open) suggests this is an oversight rather than an intentional best-effort design. Fix: propagate (or at minimum log at `log_note`/error level and abort the spawn on) failures from `add_deny_write_ace`, matching the deny-read path's error handling.

**Disposition:** deferred
**Commit:** —
**Resolved:** 2026-09-11
**Note:** Premise confirmed: spawn_prep.rs:303 does 'let _ = add_deny_write_ace(p, root_sid.sid.as_ptr());', swallowing deny-write ACL failures (fails open) while the deny-read path uses '?'. Note the crate uses 'let _ =' for several other ACE ops too (allow/workspace-protect at 291/298/340/341), so it is a broader best-effort pattern, not solely deny-write — a maintainer should decide propagate-vs-log per op. Environment-blocked: windows-sandbox-rs is #[cfg(target_os = "windows")] and cannot be compiled/tested here. Recommended fix (Windows follow-up): propagate (or log-and-abort) add_deny_write_ace failures, matching sync_persistent_deny_read_acls.
### CR-041: Provisioning pipe authorization silently accepts unpackaged clients when the service itself is packaged
**File:** `codex-rs/windows-sandbox-service/src/package_identity.rs`
**Anchor:** `authorize_client_process`, arm `None if service_family.is_some() => {}`
**Severity:** high

`authorize_client_process` is the gate that is supposed to guarantee "provisioning clients must run with an installed Codex package identity" (that is literally the bail message in the sibling arm). The match is:

```rust
match client_family {
    Some(client_family) => match service_family.as_deref() { /* ... */ },
    None if service_family.is_some() => {}
    #[cfg(debug_assertions)]
    None if FOREGROUND_MODE.load(Ordering::Acquire) => {}
    None => bail!("provisioning clients must run with an installed Codex package identity"),
}
```

`client_family` is computed from `GetPackageFamilyName` on the connecting client process; it is `None` only when that process has no package identity at all (`APPMODEL_ERROR_NO_PACKAGE`), i.e. an ordinary unpackaged EXE. The second arm authorizes exactly that case — an unpackaged client — whenever `service_family` (the identity of the currently-running service process itself) is `Some`, which is precisely the normal production configuration (the service ships and runs from the installed MSIX package). In other words, in the expected, correctly-installed deployment, any local process with no Codex package identity is treated as authorized as long as the service is packaged, which inverts the intended invariant stated by the final `None` arm.

Downstream, the only remaining checks are (1) `authorize_client`, which merely confirms the impersonated pipe-client token's SID equals the opened process's own token SID — trivially true for any process run by the connecting user against their own pipe handle — and (2) machine-policy/settings validation, which is administrator-controlled but not an identity check. The named pipe DACL (`ipc.rs::pipe_security_descriptor`) grants `IU` (any interactively logged-on user) access, so any local standard user can run an arbitrary unpackaged program that opens the pipe, sends a well-formed `ProvisionSandboxRequest`, and have it processed by the LocalSystem-privileged service (creating/enabling sandbox accounts, installing WFP/firewall filters, adjusting directory ACLs, etc.) without ever being the packaged Codex client the check is meant to require.

The existing test `unpackaged_pipe_clients_are_rejected_before_sending_a_request` (`codex-rs/windows-sandbox-service/src/ipc_tests.rs`) does not exercise this branch: it early-returns unless the *test binary itself* is unpackaged, in which case `service_family` is also `None`, landing on the final `bail!` arm instead of the buggy `Some(service_family)` branch. So the packaged-service/unpackaged-client combination — the actual production case this arm covers — is untested.

Fix: the `None if service_family.is_some() => {}` arm should be removed (or inverted to require `client_family.is_some()` unconditionally outside of the debug foreground escape hatch), so an unpackaged client is only ever accepted under the existing `#[cfg(debug_assertions)] FOREGROUND_MODE` escape hatch, never in a normal packaged deployment.

**Disposition:** deferred
**Commit:** —
**Resolved:** 2026-09-11
**Note:** Premise confirmed still present (not stale): package_identity.rs:85 'None if service_family.is_some() => {}' authorizes an unpackaged client (client_family == None) whenever the service itself is packaged — the normal production config — inverting the invariant asserted by the final arm's bail! (line 88). The inner service_family match was refactored since the review snapshot, but the buggy outer arm is verbatim. Environment-blocked: windows-sandbox-service is Windows-only and cannot be compiled/tested here, and this is a LocalSystem-privileged security gate, so an untested edit is unsafe to ship blind. Recommended fix (Windows follow-up, with a maintainer decision): remove/​invert the line-85 arm so an unpackaged client is accepted only under the existing #[cfg(debug_assertions)] FOREGROUND_MODE hatch; add a test for the packaged-service/unpackaged-client case.
### CR-042: Public Codex/AsyncCodex API has no way to supply a custom approval handler, and the default silently accepts every escalated command/file-change
**File:** `sdk/python/src/openai_codex/client.py`
**Anchor:** `_default_approval_handler`
**Severity:** high

`CodexClient.__init__` accepts an optional `approval_handler`, but falls back to `self._default_approval_handler` when none is supplied:

```python
def _default_approval_handler(self, method: str, params: JsonObject | None) -> JsonObject:
    """Accept approval requests when the caller did not provide a handler."""
    if method == "item/commandExecution/requestApproval":
        return {"decision": "accept"}
    if method == "item/fileChange/requestApproval":
        return {"decision": "accept"}
    return {}
```

This handler is invoked from `_handle_server_request`, which answers any server->client JSON-RPC request the reader thread receives — i.e. whenever the app-server actually asks the client whether to allow a command execution or file change.

The public entry points `Codex.__init__` (`sdk/python/src/openai_codex/api.py`) and `AsyncCodex.__init__` construct `CodexClient(config=config)` / `AsyncCodexClient(config=config)` and never pass `approval_handler`. I grepped the whole SDK (`grep -rn "approval_handler" sdk/python`) and the only occurrences are the parameter definition, the `or self._default_approval_handler` fallback, and the two dispatch sites in `client.py` — there is no path from `Codex`/`AsyncCodex`/`Thread`/`AsyncThread`/`TurnHandle` to ever install a caller-supplied handler, and `CodexClient` itself is not re-exported from `openai_codex/__init__.py` (only `CodexConfig` is).

`ApprovalMode` (`_approval_mode.py`) is documented as "High-level approval behavior for escalated permission requests," and its default is `ApprovalMode.auto_review`, which maps to `AskForApproval.on_request` plus `ApprovalsReviewer.auto_review`. If the runtime ever exercises the on-request escalation path back to the client (rather than resolving it entirely through the server-side auto reviewer), the SDK will unconditionally answer "accept" for command execution and file changes, with no way for an embedder using only the public `Codex`/`AsyncCodex` surface to observe, log, or deny the request. A caller who read the `ApprovalMode` docstring and expects it to gate dangerous actions has no way, through the documented API, to get a real prompt/callback.

Fix: thread an optional `approval_handler` parameter through `Codex.__init__`/`AsyncCodex.__init__` (or otherwise expose a supported hook), and consider making the default handler fail closed (or clearly documented as accept-all) rather than silently accepting destructive actions.

**Disposition:** fixed
**Commit:** `73db41fc1b`
**Resolved:** 2026-09-11
**Note:** Core defect fixed: approval_handler now threads through Codex/AsyncCodex/AsyncCodexClient (additive, default None -> behavior unchanged) and ApprovalHandler is re-exported. Default handler left accept-all with an explicit docstring warning (finding's 'clearly documented as accept-all' option); flipping the default to fail-closed is a breaking product decision left to maintainers. All touched files pass py_compile; SDK approval tests are integration tests needing network deps + the app-server binary, so red/green was not executed offline.
### CR-043: `CommandExecutionStatus` union is missing the real `"declined"` value emitted by `codex exec`
**File:** `sdk/typescript/src/items.ts`
**Anchor:** `export type CommandExecutionStatus = "in_progress" | "completed" | "failed";`
**Severity:** high

`items.ts` states it is "based on item types from codex-rs/exec/src/exec_events.rs". In that file, `CommandExecutionStatus` has four variants: `InProgress`, `Completed`, `Failed`, and `Declined` (`codex-rs/exec/src/exec_events.rs`). The `Declined` variant is not a theoretical/unused case: `codex-rs/exec/src/event_processor_with_jsonl_output.rs` (the event processor behind `codex exec --experimental-json`, the exact CLI invocation this SDK spawns per `exec.test.ts`) explicitly maps `CommandExecutionStatus::Declined => ExecCommandExecutionStatus::Declined` when building the JSON item for an `ItemCompleted` notification, and `codex-rs/app-server/tests/suite/v2/turn_start_zsh_fork.rs` asserts this status is delivered on the `item/completed` stream for a declined command (i.e. one blocked by approval policy).

Since `Thread.run()` (`sdk/typescript/src/thread.ts`) collects every `item.completed` event's `item` verbatim into `Turn.items`, and `Thread.runStreamed()` forwards the raw event, any turn where the approval policy declines a command (a completely ordinary occurrence under `on-request`/`untrusted`/`on-failure` approval modes) will yield a `CommandExecutionItem` whose `status` is the string `"declined"` — a value the published TypeScript type says is impossible. Consumers doing an exhaustive `switch` over `CommandExecutionStatus` (a natural pattern encouraged by a closed union type) will silently mishandle or default-case this status with no compile-time warning, because the cast in `thread.ts` (`JSON.parse(item) as ThreadEvent`) is unchecked.

Fix: add `"declined"` to `CommandExecutionStatus` in `items.ts` to match `codex-rs/exec/src/exec_events.rs`.

**Disposition:** fixed
**Commit:** `c17a12c51d`
**Resolved:** 2026-09-11
**Note:** Union widened to include "declined"; verified against exec_events.rs (variant + snake_case serde rename) and the jsonl event-processor mapping. Pure widening (runtime already emits this value), so it cannot break existing consumers. SDK jest/ts-jest toolchain not installable offline here, so red/green was not executed locally.
## Medium

### CR-044: `--json` CLI flag has no effect anywhere in the program
**File:** `.codex/skills/babysit-pr/scripts/gh_pr_watch.py`
**Anchor:** `"--json", action="store_true", help="Emit machine-readable output (default behavior for --once and --retry-failed-now)"`
**Severity:** medium

`parse_args()` defines `--json` and its help text implies there is a non-default (i.e. non-JSON) output mode that `--json` overrides for `--watch`. In fact `args.json` is never read anywhere in the file (confirmed by grepping the whole module for `args.json`/`.json` usage — the only other match is the unrelated `.json` file-extension literal in `default_state_file_for`). `main()` always calls `print_json(...)` for every mode (`--once`, `--retry-failed-now`, and `run_watch`'s `print_event`, which itself calls `print_json`). So passing or omitting `--json` is a no-op in every code path, and the help text's claim of a "default behavior" that could be different is misleading. Either wire the flag to a real non-JSON rendering path, or remove the flag/rewrite the help text so callers (including any automation built against this CLI) don't believe `--json` changes anything.

### CR-045: `WineProcesses::shutdown` silently discards secondary cleanup errors
**File:** `bazel/rules/testing/wine/src/lib.rs`
**Anchor:** `kill_result?;\n        wait_result?;\n        wineserver_result`
**Severity:** medium

`WineProcesses::shutdown` computes three independent results before returning —
`kill_result`, `wait_result`, and `wineserver_result` (the last from stopping the
isolated `wineserver`). The comment above the return sequence explains why all
three actions are attempted unconditionally ("Every cleanup action has been
attempted, so an individual error should not cause the blocking fallback to
repeat them"), but the return statement itself only ever surfaces the *first*
non-`Ok` result in the fixed order `kill_result`, then `wait_result`, then
`wineserver_result`. If, say, the child process is later found to have exited
with a failure (`wait_result` becomes an `Err` via the `anyhow::ensure!` in the
`.and_then`) *and* stopping the isolated `wineserver` also fails, only the
"Windows process exited with …" error is ever returned or logged; the
`wineserver` failure is computed, then thrown away.

This is asymmetric with the careful error-aggregation in
`WineTestProcess::scope`, a few dozen lines above, which explicitly merges a
body error and a teardown error into one message via `.context(...)` so
neither is lost. Here, the equivalent aggregation was not done one layer down,
so a caller (or a CI log) investigating a failed Wine test can be told "the
process exited badly" while never learning that its `wineserver` was also
left dangling — exactly the kind of intermittent-failure diagnostic loss that
makes flaky Bazel/CI wine suites hard to debug. Fix by folding all non-`Ok`
results into a single combined error (e.g. via repeated `.context()` chaining
similar to `scope`'s pattern) instead of returning only the first.

I traced this by hand (I could not compile or run the crate here: it declares
`#[cfg(not(target_os = "linux"))] compile_error!(...)` and this review was done
on macOS with no `wine`/`wineserver` binaries installed), but the control flow
is unambiguous from the source: all three `_result` bindings are fully awaited
above the three-line tail, so the swallowing is in the return, not in whether
the work happened.

### CR-046: Panic-cleanup fallback can block a thread forever if `start_kill` fails
**File:** `bazel/rules/testing/wine/src/lib.rs`
**Anchor:** `fn shutdown_blocking`
**Severity:** medium

`WineProcesses::shutdown_blocking` (invoked from `Drop for WineProcesses` when
a `WineTestProcess` is dropped while panicking without having gone through
`scope`/`shutdown`) calls `self.child.start_kill()`, and if that call returns
an `Err`, it only logs the error via `log_panic_cleanup` and falls through into
the following loop:

```rust
loop {
    match self.child.try_wait() {
        Ok(Some(status)) => { ...; break; }
        Ok(None) => std::thread::sleep(Duration::from_millis(10)),
        Err(error) => { ...; break; }
    }
}
```

If `start_kill()` failed to actually deliver a kill signal (e.g. a permission
error, or any other reason the OS declines the request) and the child process
does not exit on its own, `try_wait()` will keep returning `Ok(None)`
indefinitely and this loop never breaks — it busy-waits forever on the thread
that is unwinding a panic. This is not a purely theoretical path: the fixture
used throughout this same test suite (`windows_smoke.rs`, invoked with
`--wait`) is deliberately built to `loop { std::thread::park(); }` forever
unless it is killed, so any test that panics while holding an unshut-down
`--wait` process and whose `start_kill()` fails for any reason will hang the
whole test process rather than fail fast. Since this code runs specifically on
the panic/unwind path, a hang here is worse than the panic it was trying to
report — the original failure is masked by an indefinite stall. Consider
bounding the wait loop with a deadline and forcing a `panic!`/abort log after
it elapses rather than looping unconditionally on `Ok(None)`.

I was not able to execute this against a real Wine process (no `wine`/
`wineserver` present in this environment, and the crate is Linux-only), so this
is a static trace of the control flow rather than an observed hang; the code
path and the specific interacting fixture (`--wait`) are quoted above so the
claim can be checked directly.

### CR-047: `copy_native_binaries` copies the whole target directory, not just the requested component, when staging "codex-package"
**File:** `codex-cli/scripts/build_npm_package.py`
**Anchor:** `if CODEX_PACKAGE_COMPONENT in components_set:\n    ...\n    shutil.copytree(target_dir, dest_target_dir)`
**Severity:** medium

`PACKAGE_NATIVE_COMPONENTS` models each native artifact as a named subdirectory under a
per-target-triple directory (e.g. `<target>/codex-responses-api-proxy/...`), and the loop
below the flagged line copies non-`codex-package` components exactly that way
(`target_dir / component`, copied individually). But for `CODEX_PACKAGE_COMPONENT`
("codex-package") the function does not select a `target_dir / "codex-package"`
subdirectory — it copies the *entire* `target_dir` wholesale via
`shutil.copytree(target_dir, dest_target_dir)`. If a `--vendor-src` tree ever contains more
than one component's artifacts under the same target-triple directory (a layout the
component-subdirectory convention used elsewhere in this same function explicitly
anticipates, e.g. `codex-responses-api-proxy` binaries built for the same
`x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` target placed alongside the main codex binary), building a
platform package that only requested `["codex-package"]` (every `codex-linux-x64`,
`codex-darwin-arm64`, etc. package) will silently bundle those unrelated component's files
into `vendor/<target>/` of the published single-purpose platform npm package.

I confirmed the one caller currently in the repo, `scripts/stage_npm_packages.py`
(`collect_native_component_sets` / `vendor_src_by_components`), happens to avoid triggering
this because it allocates a distinct temporary vendor root per distinct component tuple
before invoking this script, so today's `codex-linux-x64` vendor root never actually contains
`codex-responses-api-proxy` files. But `--vendor-src` is a public, documented flag of this
script (`"Directory containing pre-installed native binaries to bundle (vendor root)."`) with
no stated restriction that it must be scoped to a single component, and the function itself
enforces no such invariant. Any direct/manual invocation, or a future refactor of the
orchestrator that consolidates vendor roots to save download/build time, will start shipping
extra unreviewed binaries inside otherwise single-architecture-only npm packages.

Fix: when `CODEX_PACKAGE_COMPONENT` is requested, copy `target_dir` contents while explicitly
excluding known sibling component subdirectories (mirroring how the other components are
selected), or require/verify that `target_dir` contains no other component subdirectories
before doing the wholesale copy.

### CR-048: `decode_agent_identity_jwt` silently skips signature verification when no JWKS is supplied

**File:** `codex-rs/agent-identity/src/lib.rs`
**Anchor:** `pub fn decode_agent_identity_jwt(jwt: &str, jwks: Option<&JwkSet>) -> Result<AgentIdentityJwtClaims>`
**Severity:** medium

```rust
pub fn decode_agent_identity_jwt(
    jwt: &str,
    jwks: Option<&JwkSet>,
) -> Result<AgentIdentityJwtClaims> {
    let Some(jwks) = jwks else {
        return decode_agent_identity_jwt_payload(jwt);
    };
    ...
```

When `jwks` is `None`, the function base64url-decodes the JWT payload and deserializes it directly (`decode_agent_identity_jwt_payload`) with **no signature verification at all** — not even an "alg=none" check, just a raw payload parse. The claims returned (`agent_runtime_id`, `agent_private_key`, `account_id`, `chatgpt_user_id`, `plan_type`, `chatgpt_account_is_fedramp`, …) are exactly the fields used elsewhere for account/workspace trust decisions. The function has no doc comment at all, so nothing at the call site signals that passing `None` means "trust these claims unconditionally."

I traced the two existing call sites in `codex-rs/login/src/auth/manager.rs` (`login_with_access_token`) and `codex-rs/login/src/auth/storage.rs` (`AgentIdentityAuthRecord::from_agent_identity_jwt`): in the login path, the unverified decode is only used for an early, redundant workspace-allowlist pre-check before a *second*, fully-verified decode (`verified_record_from_jwt`, which does pass `Some(&jwks)`) gates whether anything gets persisted, so a tampered JWT is caught before `save_auth` runs. That makes today's usage effectively safe by accident of call-site discipline, not because the API says so. Because the crate is `pub`, and the `None` branch is the *only* branch that requires no network dependency (no JWKS fetch), it is the path of least resistance for any future caller (in this codebase or a downstream consumer of this crate) who wants a "quick" claims read and may not realize it disables all cryptographic verification. Add a doc comment on the function stating explicitly that `jwks: None` performs no signature verification and must only be used when the claims are already trusted through another channel, or rename the unverified path (e.g. `decode_agent_identity_jwt_unverified`) so the security property is visible at every call site.

### CR-049: `ansi_escape` panics on parser errors for subprocess-derived content

**File:** `codex-rs/ansi-escape/src/lib.rs`
**Anchor:** `pub fn ansi_escape(s: &str) -> Text<'static>`
**Severity:** medium

`ansi_escape` calls `s.into_text()` and, on any `Error::NomError` or `Error::Utf8Error` from the `ansi-to-tui` crate, logs and then calls `panic!()` unconditionally. The function's own comment concedes the assumption is inherited from upstream docs ("NomError docs claim should never happen"), i.e. the panic path is not something this crate has independently proven unreachable.

`ansi_escape_line` (built on top of this) is used by `codex-rs/tui/src/exec_cell/render.rs` to render live, streamed output from executed shell commands (`raw.as_ref()` lines coming straight from process stdout/stderr). That text is attacker/environment-controlled in the sense that any command the agent or user runs — including third-party tools, curses/progress-bar programs, or commands that emit partial/unusual escape sequences — can feed arbitrary byte content into this path. Because the input has already been converted to a Rust `&str` (valid UTF‑8) before reaching `ansi_escape`, the `Utf8Error` arm is likely dead, but the `NomError` arm is reachable for any escape sequence the vendored parser cannot handle, and turns a rendering hiccup into a full process abort of the TUI.

I have not reproduced an actual crashing payload against the pinned `ansi-to-tui = "8.0.1"` (no Rust build was run in this pass), so I can't name a concrete byte sequence that triggers `NomError` today. The defect being flagged is the error-handling design itself: a third-party parser's error variant for content that originates from arbitrary executed commands is treated as an unconditional `panic!()` instead of degrading gracefully (e.g., falling back to a plain, unstyled `Text` of the raw string). Fix: on `Error::NomError`, return the input as plain text (or strip escape bytes) instead of panicking, matching the "best effort" spirit already used for tab expansion in this same file.

### CR-050: `request_shutdown` accepts the first WebSocket frame as the shutdown ack instead of skipping control frames
**File:** `codex-rs/app-server-daemon/src/client.rs`
**Anchor:** `pub(crate) async fn request_shutdown`
**Severity:** medium

`request_shutdown` reads exactly one frame from the socket and treats it as the acknowledgment:

```rust
let reply = websocket
    .next()
    .await
    .context("shutdown socket closed without acknowledgment")??;
anyhow::ensure!(
    matches!(reply, Message::Text(ack) if ack == pid.to_string()),
    "shutdown acknowledgment did not match the managed process {pid}"
);
```

Every other reader in this same file goes through `read_message`, which explicitly loops past
any non-`Message::Text` frame (`let Message::Text(payload) = frame else { continue; };`) before
returning — this is exactly the pattern `initialize()` and the code in
`remote_control_client.rs` rely on to tolerate WebSocket-level `Ping`/`Pong`/`Close` frames that
tokio-tungstenite surfaces to `.next()` alongside data frames. `request_shutdown` bypasses that
helper and reads raw off the stream, so if the peer emits any control frame before sending the
text acknowledgment, `matches!` fails and the function returns
`Err("shutdown acknowledgment did not match the managed process {pid}")` even though the target
process did in fact acknowledge (in a frame that never gets read).

This is not purely theoretical: the sole caller, `backend::pid.rs`'s stop path, treats a
`request_shutdown` error as non-fatal but skips the cooperative shutdown entirely —
`tracing::warn!(...); waiting for force deadline` — meaning a spurious control frame turns a
graceful app-server shutdown into "wait out the full grace period and then force-kill." There is
no test exercising `request_shutdown` against a peer that sends anything other than the exact
expected text reply, so this gap is untested as well as fragile compared to the rest of the file.
Fix: reuse `read_message` (or an equivalent loop that skips non-`Text` frames) here instead of a
bare `.next()` call.

### CR-051: Inconsistent field casing in FuzzyFileSearchResult breaks the camelCase convention of its own API family
**File:** `codex-rs/app-server-protocol/schema/typescript/FuzzyFileSearchResult.ts`
**Anchor:** `match_type: FuzzyFileSearchMatchType, file_name: string`
**Severity:** medium

`FuzzyFileSearchResult` serializes two of its six fields, `match_type` and `file_name`, in snake_case, while every other member of the same fuzzy-file-search request/response/notification family is camelCase: `FuzzyFileSearchParams` (`cancellationToken`), `FuzzyFileSearchSessionCompletedNotification` (`sessionId`), and `FuzzyFileSearchSessionUpdatedNotification` (`sessionId`, `query`) all render camelCase, and this very `FuzzyFileSearchResult` type is nested inside both `FuzzyFileSearchResponse.files` and `FuzzyFileSearchSessionUpdatedNotification.files`.

I traced this to the Rust source (`codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/common.rs`): `FuzzyFileSearchParams` and `FuzzyFileSearchSessionUpdatedNotification` both carry `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]` / `#[ts(rename_all = "camelCase")]`, but the `FuzzyFileSearchResult` struct sandwiched between them (line ~1837) has neither attribute, so its multi-word fields fall back to the Rust field names verbatim. This reads as an oversight (the struct was likely added/edited without copying the sibling attribute) rather than a deliberate choice — nothing about `FuzzyFileSearchResult` mirrors an external wire format the way, for example, `FunctionCallOutputContentItem`'s snake_case fields intentionally mirror the OpenAI Responses API.

Impact: any consumer of this schema who has internalized "this API is camelCase" (reasonable, since 3 of its 4 sibling types are) will get `undefined` for `matchType`/`fileName` unless they specifically special-case this one result type. TypeScript consumers of these `.ts` files directly get compile-time protection, but any other consumer (JS without types, generated bindings in other languages driven by this schema, hand-written docs/examples) will not. Fix is on the Rust side: add `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]` / `#[ts(rename_all = "camelCase")]` to `FuzzyFileSearchResult` in `common.rs` and regenerate; this generated `.ts` file should not be hand-edited.

### CR-052: `ConfigLayer.ts` declares `disabledReason` as always-present, but the wire format omits it whenever a layer is enabled

**File:** `codex-rs/app-server-protocol/schema/typescript/v2/ConfigLayer.ts`
**Anchor:** `disabledReason: string | null`
**Severity:** medium

`ConfigLayer` is generated from `codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/config.rs`:

```rust
pub struct ConfigLayer {
    pub name: ConfigLayerSource,
    pub version: String,
    pub config: JsonValue,
    #[serde(skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]
    pub disabled_reason: Option<String>,
}
```

`disabled_reason` has `skip_serializing_if` but no `#[serde(default)]`, and no `#[ts(optional = nullable)]`. I checked the vendored `ts-rs-macros` 11.1.0 source (`ts-rs-macros-11.1.0/src/optional.rs`): a field is only auto-inferred as TS-optional when `attr.maybe_omitted && attr.has_default` — i.e. it requires *both* `skip_serializing_if` and `serde(default)`. Since this field only has the former, ts-rs emits the field as required (`disabledReason: string | null`, no `?`), which is exactly what is checked into this file.

I confirmed with a standalone `serde`/`serde_json` repro (equivalent struct/attribute) that `skip_serializing_if` alone — without `serde(default)` — still fully omits the key from the serialized JSON when `None`:

```
$ cargo run -q
{"name":"user"}
```

(the `disabled_reason` key is entirely absent, not `null`).

So any `ConfigLayer` returned by `config/read` for an enabled layer (the common case — most layers have no disabled reason) will be serialized without a `disabledReason` key at all, while the checked-in TS type promises the key is always present with value `string | null`. TypeScript/JS consumers that destructure `layer.disabledReason` and compare with `=== null` will get `undefined !== null`, silently taking the "has a reason" branch, or code that assumes the key exists when spreading/serializing the object round-trip will diverge from the real wire shape. Fix by adding `#[serde(default)]` (or `#[ts(optional = nullable)]`) to `disabled_reason` in `config.rs` and regenerating the schema so it reads `disabledReason?: string | null,`.

### CR-053: `fs/watch` response claims a canonicalized path but returns the raw request path

**File:** `codex-rs/app-server-protocol/schema/typescript/v2/FsWatchResponse.ts`
**Anchor:** `Canonicalized path associated with the watch.`
**Severity:** medium

`FsWatchResponse.path` is documented as "Canonicalized path associated with the watch," which is a specific contract promise (symlinks resolved, path in canonical on-disk form) that a client can reasonably build logic on — e.g. de-duplicating watches by resolved identity, or comparing the returned `path` against `realpath` output to detect that a symlink was followed.

I traced the implementation in `codex-rs/app-server/src/fs_watch.rs::FsWatchManager::watch`: it never calls any canonicalization routine on the input. It ends with:

```rust
Ok(FsWatchResponse { path: params.path })
```

`params.path` is simply the caller-supplied `AbsolutePathBuf` passed straight through. I also checked `codex-rs/utils/absolute-path/src/lib.rs`: `AbsolutePathBuf`'s `TryFrom<PathBuf>`/`TryFrom<&Path>` impls only make the path absolute — they do not canonicalize — and the type's own doc comment states it is "not guaranteed to be canonicalized or exist on the filesystem." A separate, never-called `.canonicalize()` method exists on the type but `watch()` does not use it.

So calling `fs/watch` with a path that traverses a symlink (e.g. `/tmp/project/HEAD` on macOS, where `/tmp` is itself a symlink to `/private/tmp`) returns `path: "/tmp/project/HEAD"` verbatim, not the canonical `/private/tmp/project/HEAD` the doc promises. The existing unit tests in `fs_watch.rs` (`watch_uses_client_id_and_tracks_the_owner_scoped_entry`, `connection_closed_removes_only_that_connections_watches`) only assert `response.path == path` for inputs that happen to contain no symlink component, so they pass without exercising the documented canonicalization behavior at all.

Fix: either call `AbsolutePathBuf::canonicalize()` (or the sandbox-aware equivalent) on `params.path` before constructing the response, and add a test that watches through a symlink to confirm the returned path is resolved, or correct the doc comment to say the path is echoed back unmodified.

### CR-054: `minItems`/`maxItems` typed as `bigint` but JSON payloads deserialize to `number`
**File:** `codex-rs/app-server-protocol/schema/typescript/v2/McpElicitationTitledMultiSelectEnumSchema.ts`
**Anchor:** `minItems?: bigint, maxItems?: bigint`
**Severity:** medium

`McpElicitationTitledMultiSelectEnumSchema` (and its sibling `McpElicitationUntitledMultiSelectEnumSchema`, same field) declares `minItems?: bigint` and `maxItems?: bigint`. This comes from the underlying Rust fields being `u64` (`min_items: Option<u64>` / `max_items: Option<u64>` in `codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/mcp.rs`), which ts-rs maps to TypeScript `bigint`.

The problem: `serde_json` serializes a `u64` as an ordinary JSON number literal (e.g. `"minItems":3`), not as a string or any bigint-aware encoding, and `JSON.parse` in JS/TS never produces a `bigint` — it always produces a `number`. I confirmed this directly:

```
$ node -e '
const parsed = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify({ minItems: 5 }));
console.log("typeof minItems:", typeof parsed.minItems);
try { console.log(parsed.minItems + 1n); } catch (e) { console.log("error:", e.message); }
'
typeof minItems: number
error: Cannot mix BigInt and other types, use explicit conversions
```

Any TypeScript consumer that trusts this generated type — e.g. does bigint-specific handling (`typeof v.minItems === "bigint"`, arithmetic with a `n` literal, or passing the value somewhere that expects an actual `BigInt`) — will get incorrect results or a thrown `TypeError` on perfectly ordinary wire data, because the runtime value is always a plain `number`. This is not just theoretical: `minLength`/`maxLength` on the sibling `McpElicitationStringSchema` are `u32` in Rust and correctly generate as `number`, so the two "similar count constraint" fields in the same schema family have inconsistent, and in the `u64` case misleading, TypeScript types. The same `u64`→`bigint` mapping recurs in ~14 other generated files in this schema tree (e.g. `ThreadUsage.ts`, `RateLimitResetCreditsSummary.ts`), so this is a systemic characteristic of the code-generation pipeline rather than a one-off typo, but it is still a real type/runtime mismatch for any current or future TypeScript consumer of `minItems`/`maxItems`. The fix (upstream, in `mcp.rs`) is either to keep these fields as a narrower integer type (e.g. `u32`) so ts-rs emits `number`, or to add a ts-rs override so the field is exported as `number` for fields whose realistic range (item counts in a UI form) never approaches `u64`'s range.

### CR-055: `PatchChangeKind::Update.move_path` breaks the camelCase wire-format contract used everywhere else in v2

**File:** `codex-rs/app-server-protocol/schema/typescript/v2/PatchChangeKind.ts`
**Anchor:** `move_path: string | null`
**Severity:** medium

Every other field in every other type in this schema directory is camelCase
(`threadId`, `fromModel`, `showBufferingUi`, `startedAtMs`, `nextCursor`, etc.),
which matches the app-server v2 protocol's documented convention. `PatchChangeKind`
is the sole exception: the generated binding shows
`{ "type": "update", move_path: string | null }` — a raw snake_case field name
leaking into the client-facing schema.

Root cause, in the Rust source
(`codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/item.rs`):

```rust
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, ...)]
#[serde(tag = "type", rename_all = "camelCase")]
#[ts(tag = "type")]
#[ts(export_to = "v2/")]
pub enum PatchChangeKind {
    Add,
    Delete,
    Update { move_path: Option<PathBuf> },
}
```

`#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]` on an enum only renames the *variant*
names (which is why the tag values correctly come out as `"add"`, `"delete"`,
`"update"`); it does not cascade into the fields of struct-like variants. I
verified this empirically by compiling the exact enum shape with `serde` +
`serde_json` in isolation: `PatchChangeKind::Update { move_path: Some("x") }`
serializes to `{"type":"update","move_path":"x"}` — the field stays
snake_case on the wire, not just in the generated `.ts` binding.

This is a real, fixable inconsistency rather than a stylistic quibble: the
same crate already has the correct fix pattern in use for this exact class of
bug (tagged enum with per-variant fields) via `rename_all_fields = "camelCase"`
in `codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/thread.rs`,
`codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/realtime.rs`, and
`codex-rs/code-mode-protocol/src/host/message.rs`. `PatchChangeKind` was
simply missed. Any TypeScript/JS consumer that (reasonably, given every
sibling type) writes `patch.kind.movePath` will silently read `undefined`
instead of the actual move-destination path, because the real JSON key is
`move_path`.

Fix: add `rename_all_fields = "camelCase"` (or an explicit
`#[serde(rename = "movePath")]` on the field) to `PatchChangeKind` so the wire
format and generated TS binding read `movePath`, consistent with the rest of
the v2 schema. Note this is a wire-format change, so downstream Rust code that
pattern-matches `PatchChangeKind::Update { move_path }` is unaffected (field
name is a Rust-side identifier, not exposed to serde renaming), but any
already-shipped external client depending on the current `move_path` JSON key
would need a coordinated migration.

### CR-056: Generated TS schema for `thread/list` is missing the `projectId` filter field
**File:** `codex-rs/app-server-protocol/schema/typescript/v2/ThreadListParams.ts`
**Anchor:** `export type ThreadListParams = {`
**Severity:** medium

The checked-in ts-rs binding is stale relative to its Rust source. `ThreadListParams` in `codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/thread.rs` has a `project_id: Option<Option<String>>` field (added in commit `3b4569a920`, "Add experimental app-server project APIs (#38940)", annotated `#[experimental("thread/list.projectId")]` and `#[ts(optional = nullable, type = "string | null")]`), which serializes to camelCase `projectId` per the struct's `#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]`. That commit's description explicitly says it "export[s] the new protocol schemas and TypeScript types," but the regeneration was not actually run (or its output was not committed) for this file — `grep -n projectId ThreadListParams.ts` returns nothing, and `git show 3b4569a920 -- .../ThreadListParams.ts` shows no diff to the file at all.

Any consumer that treats this generated file as the authoritative TypeScript contract for the `thread/list` request (SDKs, the app's own TS client code, docs tooling) has no way to know the field exists: passing `{ projectId: "..." }` as a `ThreadListParams` object literal is a TypeScript excess-property error, and nothing in the type surface documents the filter that the server actually accepts. Fix by regenerating the ts-rs bindings (or manually adding `projectId?: string | null,` with the corresponding doc comment) so the schema matches the current Rust struct.

**File:** `codex-rs/app-server-protocol/schema/typescript/v2/ThreadMetadataUpdateParams.ts`

Same root cause and same source commit (`3b4569a920`) as the `ThreadListParams` finding, affecting a second struct in this shard. The Rust struct `ThreadMetadataUpdateParams` has:

with the doc comment "Omit to leave the project unchanged, use an empty string to clear it, or provide an existing project ID to assign it." ### CR-058: `bigint` type declared for usage/token fields that serialize as plain JSON numbers

**File:** `codex-rs/app-server-protocol/schema/typescript/v2/ThreadUsageBreakdownGroup.ts`
**Anchor:** `estimatedUsageCreditsMicros: bigint, netNewInputTokens: bigint | null, cachedInputTokens: bigint | null, inputTokens: bigint | null, outputTokens: bigint | null, totalTokens: bigint | null`
**Severity:** medium

`ThreadUsageBreakdownGroup` and `ThreadUsage` (`estimatedUsageCreditsMicros: bigint, estimatedUsageUsdMicros: bigint | null` in `ThreadUsageBreakdownGroup.ts`/`ThreadUsage.ts`) declare their numeric usage fields as `bigint`. The underlying Rust fields are plain `i64` with no custom serializer (`codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/thread_usage.rs`, `pub estimated_usage_credits_micros: i64`, etc.) — no `#[serde(serialize_with = ...)]` that stringifies the value, and no `#[ts(type = "number")]` override. `serde_json` therefore emits these fields as ordinary JSON number literals, and `JSON.parse` in any TS/JS consumer produces a `number`, never a `bigint`. I confirmed this with `node -e`:

```
node -e '
const r = JSON.parse("{\"estimatedUsageCreditsMicros\": 123456789012345}");
console.log(typeof r.estimatedUsageCreditsMicros, r.estimatedUsageCreditsMicros);
console.log(r.estimatedUsageCreditsMicros + 10n);
'
# -> number 123456789012345
# -> ERROR: Cannot mix BigInt and other types, use explicit conversions
```

A consumer that trusts the generated type and writes normal `bigint` arithmetic (or passes the value to an API expecting `bigint`) will throw at runtime, because the real value is a `number`.

This is a real inconsistency, not an inherent property of the schema toolchain: the very same generated directory shows the correct pattern elsewhere for identically-typed `i64` fields — `TokenUsageBreakdown` (`codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/thread.rs`, `#[ts(type = "number")] pub total_tokens: i64`, etc.), `Turn.startedAt`/`completedAt`/`durationMs` (`#[ts(type = "number | null")] pub started_at: Option<i64>`), and `ToolRequestUserInputParams.autoResolutionMs` (`#[ts(type = "number | null")] pub auto_resolution_ms: Option<u64>`) all explicitly override the ts-rs default so the emitted type matches the actual wire value. `ThreadUsageBreakdownGroup`/`ThreadUsage` simply omit that override.

Fix: add `#[ts(type = "number")]` (or `"number | null"` for the `Option<i64>` fields) to the affected fields in `codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/thread_usage.rs` and regenerate the schema, consistent with the convention already used for `TokenUsageBreakdown` and `Turn` in the same module.

### CR-059: Thread-resume serialization scope can diverge from the resource actually mutated

**File:** `codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/common.rs`
**Anchor:** `($actual_params:ident, thread_or_path($params:ident . $thread_field:ident, $params2:ident . $path_field:ident))`
**Severity:** medium

The `thread_or_path` arm of `serialization_scope_expr!` (used by `ThreadResume` and `ThreadFork`) computes the per-request mutual-exclusion key as follows: if `thread_id` is non-empty, it *always* returns `ClientRequestSerializationScope::Thread { thread_id }`, regardless of whether `path` is also set; it only falls back to `ClientRequestSerializationScope::ThreadPath { path }` when `thread_id` is empty.

`ThreadResumeParams::path`'s own doc comment (`codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/thread.rs`) states: "If specified for a non-running thread, the thread_id param will be ignored." That means the resource actually resumed/mutated by the request is determined by `path`, not `thread_id`, precisely in the case where `thread_id` refers to a thread that is not currently running — yet the serialization scope still keys exclusively on `thread_id` in that case.

This scope is consumed by `RequestSerializationQueueKey::from_scope` in `codex-rs/app-server/src/request_serialization.rs` to build the exclusive-access lock key used to serialize concurrent requests against the same thread/rollout resource (`ClientRequestSerializationScope::Thread{..}` and `::ThreadPath{..}` map to distinct, unrelated queue keys). Consequently, two concurrent `thread/resume` (or `thread/fork`) requests that ultimately operate on the same on-disk rollout file — one carrying a (possibly stale/incorrect) non-empty `thread_id` plus the shared `path`, another carrying the same `path` with an empty or different `thread_id` — are not mutually excluded, because they hash to different `RequestSerializationQueueKey` values (`Thread{id}` vs `ThreadPath{path}`), defeating the very mechanism this scope machinery exists to provide.

This requires the experimental `#[experimental("thread/resume.path")]` field to be exercised with a `thread_id`/`path` pair that doesn't already correspond 1:1 (which is somewhat unusual client behavior), so likelihood is lower than the first finding, but the divergence is a direct, documented consequence of the field semantics versus the scope macro's logic, not a hypothetical.

Fix: when `path` is present, key the scope on `path` (or on a scope that folds both `thread_id` and `path` together) whenever there is any possibility the server will resolve by path — i.e., mirror the "non-running thread" fallback semantics in the scope computation rather than assuming `thread_id` alone is authoritative.

### CR-060: Per-chunk UTF-8 decoding corrupts multi-byte characters split across exec output reads

**File:** `codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/event_mapping.rs`
**Anchor:** `EventMsg::ExecCommandOutputDelta(exec_command_output_delta_event) => { ... String::from_utf8_lossy(&exec_command_output_delta_event.chunk).to_string() ... }`
**Severity:** medium

`item_event_to_server_notification` converts each raw `ExecCommandOutputDeltaEvent.chunk` into the `item/commandExecution/outputDelta` notification's `delta: String` field via `String::from_utf8_lossy(&chunk).to_string()`, run independently per chunk with no carry-over state.

The chunk itself is produced in `codex-rs/core/src/exec.rs` as `let chunk = tmp[..n].to_vec();` — the raw bytes returned by a single `read()` call into a fixed-size buffer, with no awareness of UTF-8 character boundaries. Whenever a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence (e.g. any non-ASCII text, box-drawing characters, emoji, accented Latin letters) straddles the boundary between two reads, each half is decoded independently. `String::from_utf8_lossy` has no way to recover a split sequence between calls, so both the truncated leading bytes and the orphaned continuation byte(s) are each replaced with the U+FFFD replacement character — the original character is permanently lost from that delta, even though the bytes were received correctly.

This is a real, reachable defect for any command executed during a turn (`item/commandExecution/outputDelta`, used for normal in-turn tool calls) that streams non-ASCII output long enough for a chunk boundary to land mid-character — an ordinary occurrence, not a contrived edge case. Contrast this with the newer, connection-scoped `command/exec` API's `CommandExecOutputDeltaNotification`, which deliberately uses `delta_base64: String` ("Base64-encoded output bytes") to avoid exactly this class of bug — confirming the project is aware of the hazard for one code path but not the other.

Impact is bounded to the live-streaming view: `build_command_execution_end_item` decodes the fully aggregated buffer once at completion (`ExecCommandEndEvent.aggregated_output: String`), so the final persisted/displayed output is correct. The bug only corrupts characters shown to clients while the command is still running.

Fix: buffer any incomplete trailing UTF-8 sequence across deltas (e.g. via `String::from_utf8` and carrying over the undecodable tail to prefix the next chunk, as `std::io::BufRead`/`encoding_rs` style incremental decoders do), or switch this notification to a byte-safe (base64) encoding like the newer `command/exec` API.

### CR-061: `LoginAccountParams` derives plain `Debug`, leaking raw credentials if ever formatted or logged
**File:** `codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/protocol/v2/account.rs`
**Anchor:** `pub enum LoginAccountParams`
**Severity:** medium

`LoginAccountParams` carries several long-lived, highly sensitive secrets verbatim as plain
`String` fields: `ApiKey.api_key`, `ChatgptAuthTokens.access_token` (a JWT, per its own doc
comment: "used for backend API requests and email extraction"), `AmazonBedrock.api_key`, and
`AmazonBedrockAccessKeys.{access_key_id, secret_access_key, session_token}`. The enum is declared
with `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, Debug, Clone, PartialEq, JsonSchema, TS, ExperimentalApi)]`
with no custom `Debug` impl, so `format!("{:?}", params)` or any `tracing::debug!("{:?}", ...)` /
`error!("... {:?}", ...)` / panic message that includes the value will print every secret in the
clear.

This is a real inconsistency within the same file: `ChatgptAuthTokensRefreshResponse`, defined
later in this exact file, carries a comparable bearer token (`access_token`) and was given a
hand-written `Debug` impl specifically to redact it:

```rust
impl fmt::Debug for ChatgptAuthTokensRefreshResponse {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        f.debug_struct("ChatgptAuthTokensRefreshResponse")
            .field("access_token", &"<redacted>")
            ...
```

`LoginAccountParams` is the inbound counterpart carrying the *original* credentials (including a
plaintext AWS `secret_access_key`, which is arguably more sensitive than the derived
`ChatgptAuthTokensRefreshResponse.access_token`), yet it still derives `Debug` unmodified. I did
not find an active call site in this shard or in the sampled `app-server`/`tui` call sites
(`account_processor.rs`, `message_processor.rs`, `tui/src/onboarding/{auth.rs,bedrock.rs,
auth/headless_chatgpt_login.rs}`) that currently formats `LoginAccountParams`/`ClientRequest` with
`{:?}`, so this is not confirmed as actively exploited today. However, `{:?}`-formatting a request
enum is an extremely common Rust debugging/error-context idiom (ad-hoc `debug!`/`trace!` during
troubleshooting, `.expect()`/`.unwrap()` panic payloads, `anyhow`/`eyre` context, crash-reporter
serialization of the enclosing request), and this type is exactly the kind of struct that a future
contributor would casually log while debugging a login failure. Given the codebase already
recognizes and mitigates this exact risk for a sibling type in the same file, and separately
region-redacts secrets in command text elsewhere (see `CommandExecutionPresentation`/
`preserves_command_plugin_id_and_redacts_secrets_across_legacy_upsert` in
`thread_history.rs`), the omission here looks like a gap rather than an intentional choice.

Fix: give `LoginAccountParams` (or at minimum the `AmazonBedrockAccessKeys`, `AmazonBedrock`,
`ApiKey`, and `ChatgptAuthTokens` variants) a manual `Debug` impl that redacts `api_key`,
`access_token`, `secret_access_key`, and `session_token`, mirroring the pattern already used for
`ChatgptAuthTokensRefreshResponse`.

### CR-062: `is_secret` is ignored when prompting for `tool/requestUserInput` answers, echoing secrets to the terminal

**File:** `codex-rs/app-server-test-client/src/request_user_input.rs`
**Anchor:** `fn prompt_for_answers_with`
**Severity:** medium

`ToolRequestUserInputQuestion::is_secret` is part of the protocol and is honored by the TUI: `tui/src/bottom_pane/request_user_input/render.rs::render_notes_input` masks the composer with `'*'` whenever `question.is_secret` is true (`self.composer.render_with_mask(area, buf, Some('*'))`).

`prompt_for_answers_with` in this file — the interactive handler this test client uses whenever the app-server sends a `tool/requestUserInput` server request — never reads `question.is_secret`.
