Every question, secret or not, is answered via `write!(output, "Answer: ")` followed by a plain `input.read_line(&mut line)` against the process's controlling terminal, which echoes the typed characters in cleartext (no `termios`/no-echo handling, no password-style input crate). A plugin or MCP server that asks for a secret (API token, password, etc.) via this flow will have that secret echoed to the developer's terminal and captured in any terminal scrollback/session recording, unlike the officially supported TUI client. Fix: when `question.is_secret` is true, disable terminal echo while reading the line (e.g. via a password-input crate) the same way the TUI masks composer input.

### CR-063: Attestation request timeout (100ms) is too short for realistic attestation providers and fails open

**File:** `codex-rs/app-server/src/attestation.rs`
**Anchor:** `ATTESTATION_GENERATE_TIMEOUT`
**Severity:** medium

`ATTESTATION_GENERATE_TIMEOUT` is `Duration::from_millis(100)`, and
`request_attestation_header_value_with_timeout` uses it as the hard deadline for a full
round trip: find a subscribed connection, send a `ServerRequestPayload::AttestationGenerate`
request over the transport, have the client generate the attestation value (which is the
kind of call that typically goes through platform APIs such as Apple App Attest, Android
Play Integrity, or a TPM/secure-enclave signing operation — these routinely take several
hundred milliseconds to a few seconds), and return the response.

I traced the caller in `codex-rs/core/src/client.rs`
(`generate_attestation_header_for`, called from `create_realtime_call_with_headers`,
`realtime_sideband_headers`, and two other call sites) and confirmed the header is attached
on a fail-open basis:

```rust
if let Some(header_value) = self.generate_attestation_header_for().await {
    extra_headers.insert(X_OAI_ATTESTATION_HEADER, header_value);
}
```

When `header_for_request` times out, `request_attestation_header_value_with_timeout` returns
`app_server_attestation_header_value(AppServerAttestationStatus::Timeout, None)` (still
`Some(..)`, but with no token), and the outbound request simply proceeds without a usable
attestation value. Under ordinary conditions — i.e. any client whose attestation generation
genuinely takes more than 100ms, which is common for hardware-backed attestation — this
control silently degrades on essentially every request rather than surfacing a hard error,
defeating the purpose of sending it at all. For comparison, the sibling "ask the connected
client something and wait" facility in this same shard
(`codex-rs/app-server/src/current_time.rs`, `CURRENT_TIME_REQUEST_TIMEOUT`) uses a 10-second
deadline for the same kind of app-server → client → app-server round trip, which suggests
100ms was not sized against realistic attestation-generation latency.

Fix: either raise `ATTESTATION_GENERATE_TIMEOUT` to a value consistent with real attestation
providers (seconds, not milliseconds), or make it configurable, and consider surfacing
non-`Ok` `AppServerAttestationStatus` values (especially repeated `Timeout`) as a metric so a
silently-empty attestation header doesn't go unnoticed in production.

### CR-064: Imported session thread is left behind (not discarded) when metadata/persist/shutdown fails

**File:** `codex-rs/app-server/src/external_agent_migration/session_importer.rs`
**Anchor:** `ExternalAgentSessionImporter::persist_session`
**Severity:** medium

`persist_session` creates a new thread, appends its rollout items, then calls
`update_thread_metadata`, `persist_thread`, and `shutdown_thread` in sequence.
Only the `append_items` failure path cleans up the just-created thread:

```rust
if !rollout_items.is_empty()
    && let Err(err) = self.thread_store.append_items(...).await
{
    let _ = self.thread_store.discard_thread(thread_id).await;
    return Err(SessionImportStepFailure::new("failed_to_append_thread_items", ...));
}

self.thread_store
    .update_thread_metadata(...)
    .await
    .map_err(|err| SessionImportStepFailure::new("failed_to_update_thread_metadata", ...))?;
self.thread_store
    .persist_thread(thread_id, PersistContext::Standard)
    .await
    .map_err(|err| SessionImportStepFailure::new("failed_to_persist_thread", ...))?;
self.thread_store
    .shutdown_thread(thread_id)
    .await
    .map_err(|err| SessionImportStepFailure::new("failed_to_shutdown_thread", ...))?;
```

If `update_thread_metadata`, `persist_thread`, or `shutdown_thread` returns an
error (e.g. a transient thread-store/disk error), the `?` propagates the
failure straight to the caller without calling `discard_thread`. The caller
(`create_session_import`) records this as an import failure via
`record_import_error`/`SessionImportFailure`, so the user is told the import
failed — but the thread that was already created and had its rollout items
appended is never discarded. It is left in the thread store with default/
partial metadata (no title, no correct `cwd`/timestamps, since
`update_thread_metadata` is exactly the step that sets those) and is never
recorded in the external-agent session ledger either (that only happens for
threads that make it into `completed_imports`), so a retried import of the
same source session will not recognize it as already-imported and will create
yet another orphaned thread on each failed retry.

This is inconsistent with the sibling `append_items` error path in the same
function, which does discard the thread, and looks like an oversight rather
than an intentional choice. Fix: wrap the `update_thread_metadata` /
`persist_thread` / `shutdown_thread` calls so that any failure also discards
`thread_id` before returning the error, matching the `append_items` branch.

### CR-065: `thread/revert` leaves the thread permanently unloaded if reload fails after teardown
**File:** `codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors/thread_processor.rs`
**Anchor:** `ThreadRequestProcessor::thread_revert_response`, `ThreadRequestProcessor::reload_paginated_thread`
**Severity:** medium

`thread_revert_response` intentionally avoids a full teardown so that "Full teardown would force clients to call thread/resume after a successful revert" (see the comment right above `self.outgoing.cancel_requests_for_thread(...)`). To do this it:

1. Shuts down and removes the live thread from `thread_manager` (`self.thread_manager.remove_thread(&thread_id).await`).
2. Calls `self.thread_store.revert_thread(...)`, stashing the result in `revert_result` without checking it yet.
3. Calls `self.reload_paginated_thread(...).await?` to rebuild the in-memory runtime from the (possibly reverted) store.
4. Only then checks `revert_result?`.

Step 3 uses `?`, so if `reload_paginated_thread` itself fails — e.g. `self.thread_manager.resume_thread_with_history(...)` errors (auth failure, model/config load error, IO error reading the rollout after revert), or the subsequent `restore_thread_settings` / `checkpoint_thread_settings` / `ensure_listener_task_running` calls fail — the function returns `Err` immediately. At that point the thread has already been removed from `thread_manager` in step 1 and is never reloaded. Unlike other teardown paths in this file (e.g. `finalize_thread_teardown`, or `unload_thread_without_subscribers`), there is no `ThreadClosedNotification`, no cleanup of `thread_state_manager`/`thread_watch_manager`, and critically no indication in the returned JSON-RPC error that the client must issue a fresh `thread/resume` to make the thread usable again. The client only sees `internal_error(format!("error reloading thread after revert: {err}"))` and has no way to know the thread is now unloaded rather than merely "revert failed, thread otherwise intact."

I confirmed the *common* failure mode (invalid `beforeTurnId`) does *not* hit this: `codex-rs/app-server/tests/suite/v2/thread_revert.rs`'s `thread_revert_preserves_fork_cutoff_after_cold_resume` test sends a revert with a nonexistent turn id, gets `"turn not found: missing-turn"`, and successfully continues using the same thread afterward — because `revert_thread` fails validation before mutating the store, so `reload_paginated_thread` still succeeds against the untouched history. The gap is specifically when `reload_paginated_thread`'s own steps fail (not `revert_thread`'s validation), which is untested and, based on the code, leaves the thread stuck unloaded with a generic internal error and no recovery hint.

Fix: on failure inside `reload_paginated_thread`, either retry/fall back to reloading the pre-revert history, or explicitly run the same teardown notifications used elsewhere (`finalize_thread_teardown` + `ThreadClosedNotification`) so clients know to call `thread/resume`, and/or include that guidance in the error message.

### CR-066: Unsanitized task_id enables backend path-traversal redirection in `codex apply`
**File:** `codex-rs/chatgpt/src/get_task.rs`
**Anchor:** `let path = format!("/wham/tasks/{task_id}");`
**Severity:** medium

`get_task` builds the request path by directly interpolating the caller-supplied `task_id` (the positional argument of `codex chatgpt apply <task_id>`, see `ApplyCommand::task_id` in `apply_command.rs`) with no validation and no percent-encoding. The resulting string is then joined with `chatgpt_base_url` in `chatgpt_client::chatgpt_get_request` via plain `format!("{}/{}", base, path)` and handed to `reqwest`/`url::Url::parse`.

Because the `url` crate normalizes dot-segments during parsing (this is standard RFC 3986 / WHATWG behavior, not an `url`-crate quirk), a `task_id` containing `../` segments escapes the intended `/wham/tasks/` namespace entirely. I verified this concretely with the crate actually used here:

```
raw joined string: https://chatgpt.example.com/backend-api/wham/tasks/../../v1/other-endpoint
parsed path:        /backend-api/v1/other-endpoint
```

So `codex chatgpt apply '../../some/other/path'` sends an authenticated GET (with the user's bearer token, `chatgpt-account-id`, etc., all attached automatically by `chatgpt_get_request`) to an attacker- or input-chosen path on the same backend host, not to `/wham/tasks/<id>`. Since `task_id` is often sourced from automation (scripts extracting an ID from a PR description, webhook payload, or other semi-trusted text and passing it straight to `codex apply`), a value that isn't a well-formed opaque ID can silently redirect a credentialed request to an arbitrary same-host endpoint.

Fix: validate `task_id` against an expected opaque-identifier shape (e.g., alphanumeric/hyphen) before use, or percent-encode it as a single path segment (e.g., via `url::form_urlencoded` byte-escaping or `utf8_percent_encode` with the `NON_ALPHANUMERIC`/path-segment encode set) instead of splicing it into the format string raw.

### CR-067: `redact_detail` over-redacts diagnostic text that merely mentions "token"/"secret" as English words

**File:** `codex-rs/cli/src/doctor/output.rs`
**Anchor:** `fn redact_detail`
**Severity:** medium

`redact_detail` is applied to every `DoctorCheck` detail line (via `structured_json_details` for `--json` and via `parsed_details`/`detail_lines` for the human renderer), and also to every `DoctorIssue` field (`cause`, `measured`, `expected`, `remedy`, `fields`) via `redacted_json_issue`. Its secret-detection heuristic is a plain substring test against the whole lowercased line:

```rust
let secret_keys = [
    "openai_api_key", "codex_api_key", "codex_access_token",
    "authorization", "bearer_token", "token", "secret",
];
if secret_keys.iter().any(|key| lower.contains(key)) {
    let name = detail.split(':').next().unwrap_or(detail);
    format!("{name}: <redacted>")
}
```

Because `"token"` and `"secret"` are matched as bare substrings (not just as label names), this fires on purely descriptive sentences that never contain a secret value. `auth_check` in `codex-rs/cli/src/doctor.rs` builds exactly such sentences via `stored_auth_issues` and feeds them through `format!("stored auth issue: {issue}")`:

- `"stored auth issue: ChatGPT auth is missing an access token"` → `"stored auth issue: <redacted>"`
- `"stored auth issue: ChatGPT auth is missing a refresh token"` → `"stored auth issue: <redacted>"`
- `"stored auth issue: personal access token auth is missing a personal access token"` → `"stored auth issue: <redacted>"`
- `"stored auth issue: agent identity auth is missing an agent identity token"` → `"stored auth issue: <redacted>"`
- `"stored auth issue: Bedrock access key auth is missing a secret access key"` → `"stored auth issue: <redacted>"`

The same happens to the MCP check's `"{name}: bearer token env var {env_var} is not set"` detail line (`mcp_check_from_servers` in `doctor.rs`), which collapses to `"{name}: <redacted>"` and hides which env var is missing.

I extracted the exact `redact_detail`/`is_safe_presence_value` logic into a standalone Rust program and ran it (`rustc -O` + execute) to confirm the behavior rather than just reading it:

```
"stored auth issue: ChatGPT auth is missing an access token" => "stored auth issue: <redacted>"
"stored auth issue: ChatGPT auth is missing a refresh token" => "stored auth issue: <redacted>"
"stored auth issue: personal access token auth is missing a personal access token" => "stored auth issue: <redacted>"
"stored auth issue: Bedrock access key auth is missing a secret access key" => "stored auth issue: <redacted>"
"stored auth issue: agent identity auth is missing an agent identity token" => "stored auth issue: <redacted>"
"stored auth issue: API key auth is missing an API key" => "stored auth issue: API key auth is missing an API key"
```

This is a real functional regression in a tool whose entire purpose is to explain *why* a check failed: a user with expired/incomplete ChatGPT tokens, a missing Bedrock secret access key, or a missing agent-identity token, running `codex doctor` or `codex doctor --json` (e.g. to attach to a support ticket via `--feedback`), sees `"stored auth issue: <redacted>"` instead of the actionable message the code clearly intended to show — even though none of these strings ever contain an actual secret value. No existing test exercises `redact_detail` against the `stored_auth_issues` output or the MCP "bearer token env var" message, so the gap wasn't caught.

Fix: only redact when the *label* (text before the first `: `) indicates a secret-bearing field (as is already done for the `"env var"` case), or tighten the value-side match to require something that looks like an actual credential (e.g. skip redaction when the value contains no `=`/no long opaque token and is a normal English sentence), rather than matching `"token"`/`"secret"` anywhere in the full string.

### CR-068: `codex mcp list --json` / `codex mcp get --json` leak MCP server secrets that the human-readable output masks
**File:** `codex-rs/cli/src/mcp_cmd.rs`
**Anchor:** `"http_headers": http_headers` (in the `McpServerTransportConfig::StreamableHttp` JSON arm of `run_list` and `run_get`)
**Severity:** medium

`run_list` and `run_get` both build a JSON transport blob directly from the config struct:

```rust
McpServerTransportConfig::StreamableHttp {
    url, bearer_token_env_var, http_headers, env_http_headers, http_headers_helper,
} => serde_json::json!({
    "type": "streamable_http",
    "url": url,
    "bearer_token_env_var": bearer_token_env_var,
    "http_headers": http_headers,
    "env_http_headers": env_http_headers,
    "http_headers_helper": http_headers_helper.as_ref().map(|_| "<redacted>"),
}),
```

and, for stdio servers, the analogous arm embeds `"env": env` verbatim. `http_headers` and `env` are the two fields that hold literal secret values a user supplied directly (e.g. `codex mcp add name --env API_KEY=sk-live-...`, or a static `Authorization` header configured on a streamable-HTTP server) — as opposed to `env_vars`/`env_http_headers`, which only hold the *name* of an environment variable to read the secret from at connect time.

The non-JSON path in the same file proves this distinction is deliberate: `run_get`'s text branch explicitly masks `http_headers` values (`format!("{k}=*****")`) while printing `env_http_headers` unmasked (`format!("{k}={var}")`, since that's just a variable name). `run_list`/`run_get`'s stdio text branch calls the shared `format_env_display` helper (`codex-rs/utils/cli/src/format_env_display.rs`), which masks every `env` value with `*****` for exactly this reason.

`--json` bypasses all of this masking and prints the literal header/env values in cleartext. Anyone piping `codex mcp list --json` / `codex mcp get <name> --json` into logs, CI artifacts, support bundles, or other automation — a very ordinary use of `--json`, which exists specifically for machine consumption — gets the secrets the text UI was written to protect. Fix by masking `http_headers` and `env` the same way in the JSON serializer (e.g. reuse `format_env_display`-style masking, or emit `{"present": true}` markers instead of raw values), consistent with `http_headers_helper`'s existing `<redacted>` treatment in the same object literal.

### CR-069: Diff/patch contents and task metadata written in plaintext to a CWD-relative `error.log`
**File:** `codex-rs/cloud-tasks-client/src/http.rs`
**Anchor:** `fn append_error_log`
**Severity:** medium

`append_error_log` opens `"error.log"` as a relative path and appends to it on every
notable event, including full patch bodies on apply/preflight failures:

```rust
let _ = writeln!(
    &mut log,
    "----- PATCH BEGIN -----\n{diff}\n----- PATCH END -----"
);
...
append_error_log(&log);
```

and `fn append_error_log(message: &str) { ... std::fs::OpenOptions::new().create(true)
.append(true).open("error.log") ... }`. Because the path is relative, the file lands in
whatever directory the process's CWD happens to be — typically the user's project
working tree when running `codex cloud`/the cloud-tasks TUI. This has two concrete
consequences a caller would not expect:

1. On Unix, the file is created with the process's default `umask`-derived mode
   (commonly world- or group-readable, e.g. 0644), so on shared/multi-user hosts other
   local users can read proprietary source diffs and task prompts that get written here
   on any apply/preflight failure.
2. Because the file is created inside the user's repo working tree and is not
   `.gitignore`d by anything in this crate, it can be picked up by `git add -A`/`git add .`
   and accidentally committed, leaking patch contents and internal task ids into version
   control history.

This is a duplicate implementation of the same pattern already present in
`codex-rs/cloud-tasks/src/util.rs`, so the behavior is evidently intentional
elsewhere in the codebase, but within this file it still represents an unlogged,
undocumented, unbounded plaintext sink for potentially sensitive diff content. Suggest
writing to a path under `codex_home`/a dedicated log directory with restrictive
permissions (0600) instead of a bare relative filename, and truncating/rotating the
file so it cannot grow unbounded.

### CR-070: Closing the task-details overlay does not stop a pending load from reopening it
**File:** `codex-rs/cloud-tasks/src/lib.rs`
**Anchor:** `app::AppEvent::DetailsDiffLoaded { id, title, diff }`
**Severity:** medium

Opening a task's details (`Enter` on the list) sets `app.diff_overlay = Some(...)` and spawns background `get_task_diff`/`get_task_text` calls. Pressing `Esc`/`q` while overlay is shown clears it: `app.diff_overlay = None`. However, the handlers for `DetailsDiffLoaded`, `DetailsMessagesLoaded`, and `DetailsFailed` treat "no overlay currently open" as "open a fresh overlay for this result" rather than "the user dismissed this, drop it":

```rust
app::AppEvent::DetailsDiffLoaded { id, title, diff } => {
    if let Some(ov) = &app.diff_overlay
        && ov.task_id != id { continue; }     // only guards a DIFFERENT overlay, not "no overlay"
    ...
    } else {
        let mut overlay = app::DiffOverlay::new(id.clone(), title, None);
        ...
        app.diff_overlay = Some(overlay);      // resurrects a dismissed overlay
    }
    app.details_inflight = false;
    ...
}
```

The `if let Some(ov) = &app.diff_overlay && ov.task_id != id` guard only fires when a *different* task's overlay is currently open; when `app.diff_overlay` is `None` (because the user closed it), the condition is false and the `else` branch below constructs and re-displays a brand-new overlay for the task the user already dismissed. Repro: select a task, press `Enter` (spinner "Loading details…" appears), immediately press `Esc` to return to the list (or press `n` to start composing a new task), then wait for the in-flight `get_task_diff`/`get_task_text` call to complete — the details overlay pops back up over whatever the user is now doing (including over the New Task composer, since `ui::draw` renders the diff overlay on top of any other screen unconditionally whenever `app.diff_overlay.is_some()`).

Compare with `AttemptsLoaded`, which handles this correctly by gating on `Some(ov)` with no resurrecting `else` branch. Fix: only reopen/update an overlay when one is already present for this task id (or track a generation/cancellation token per details request, as is already done for the task list via `list_generation`).

### CR-071: Code-mode notification IDs are not deduplicated, unlike tool-invocation IDs
**File:** `codex-rs/code-mode/src/grpc_session/state.rs`
**Anchor:** `SessionState::admit_notification`
**Severity:** medium

`admit_notification` parses `notification.notification_id` only to validate that it is a well-formed UUID; it never checks the ID against a "seen" set before admitting the callback:

```rust
pub(super) fn admit_notification(&mut self, notification: &grpc::Notification) -> Result<CallbackAdmission, String> {
    self.require_open()?;
    Uuid::parse_str(&notification.notification_id).map_err(...)?;
    ...
    execution.notifications += 1;
    self.notifications += 1;
    Ok(CallbackAdmission::Active(execution.cancellation.child_token()))
}
```

Compare this with the sibling function `admit_invocation`, which explicitly guards against ID reuse using the bounded `RecentIds` cache (`seen_invocations`) before admitting a tool call:

```rust
if self.invocations.contains_key(&call.invocation_id) || self.seen_invocations.contains(&invocation_id) {
    return Err("code-mode tool invocation ID was reused".to_string());
}
```

`state_tests.rs` even has a dedicated regression test for this on the invocation side (`duplicate_invocation_ids_are_rejected`), but there is no equivalent test or check for notifications. Because `SessionState` is explicitly written to defend the client against a misbehaving/buggy code-mode host (see the identical `MAX_IDENTIFIER_BYTES`/UUID/`check_cell_ownership` validations applied uniformly to invocations, notifications, and cell closures), a host that resends the same `notification_id` twice for a cell (whether due to a host bug or a compromised host process) will have both calls admitted and delivered to `CodeModeSessionDelegate::notify`, producing duplicate notification text delivered to the user/transcript. The `RecentIds` utility already used for `seen_invocations`/`cancelled_invocations` in this same file could be reused for notifications with the same bounded-memory tradeoff.

Fix: track `notification_id` the same way `invocation_id` is tracked (a `RecentIds` set checked before admission) so a repeated notification ID is rejected/ignored instead of being delivered twice.

### CR-072: `#[experimental(...)]` on an enum variant's field is silently ignored by `#[derive(ExperimentalApi)]`
**File:** `codex-rs/codex-experimental-api-macros/src/lib.rs`
**Anchor:** `derive_for_enum`
**Severity:** medium

`derive_for_enum` builds one match arm per variant and always destructures the
variant with a wildcard (`Self::#variant_name { .. }` / `Self::#variant_name ( .. )`),
so it only ever inspects the variant-level `#[experimental("...")]` attribute
(via `experimental_reason(&variant.attrs)`). Any `#[experimental(...)]` (or
`#[experimental(nested)]`) attribute placed on a *field inside* an enum
variant — exactly the syntax the struct path supports via
`experimental_reason(&field.attrs)` / `has_nested_experimental(field)` in
`derive_for_struct` — is never read, never registered with
`inventory::submit!`, and never contributes to `experimental_reason()`. There
is no compile error or warning; the annotation simply becomes dead weight.

I reproduced this by temporarily adding to
`codex-rs/app-server-protocol/src/experimental_api.rs`'s test module:

```rust
#[derive(ExperimentalApi)]
enum EnumFieldLevelShape {
    Tuple(#[experimental("enum/field/tuple")] u8),
    Named { #[experimental("enum/field/named")] value: u8 },
}
```

and asserting `ExperimentalApiTrait::experimental_reason(&EnumFieldLevelShape::Tuple(1))
== Some("enum/field/tuple")`. Running
`cargo test -p codex-app-server-protocol --lib experimental_api::tests::scratch_probe_field_level_experimental_inside_enum_variant`
fails with `left: None, right: Some("enum/field/tuple")` — the macro compiles
the type fine but silently drops the gate. (The temporary test was reverted
after confirming the failure; it is not part of this diff.)

The crate's own doc comment for `ExperimentalField` states the convention is
"`<method>` for method-level gates or `<method>.<field>` for field-level
gates," and the macro's test suite (`experimental_api.rs::tests`) exercises
field-level struct annotations and variant-level enum annotations side by
side, but never a field-level annotation on an enum variant — so nothing
catches a contributor reasonably assuming the two compose the way they do for
structs. Grepping the current `app-server-protocol` usages, every existing
`#[experimental(...)]` inside an `enum` is attached to the variant itself, so
this is not yet firing in shipped protocol types, but it is a live trap for
the next contributor who tries to gate a single field of a multi-field enum
variant (e.g. an `AmazonBedrockAccessKeys { access_key_id, secret_access_key,
session_token, region }`-shaped variant where only one field should require
the experimental capability): the field would silently ship ungated instead
of being flagged as requiring `experimentalApi` capability.

Fix: either thread field-level presence checks through `derive_for_enum` the
same way `derive_for_struct` does (matching on the variant's actual fields
instead of `..`), or make `experimental_reason_attr`/`has_nested_experimental`
detection on enum-variant fields a hard compile error so misuse fails loudly
instead of silently.

### CR-073: NUL-byte field-separator ambiguity lets one MCP tool displace another during dedup

**File:** `codex-rs/codex-mcp/src/tools.rs`
**Anchor:** `normalize_tools_for_model_with_prefix`, `raw_tool_identity`
**Severity:** medium

`normalize_tools_for_model_with_prefix` is called once per turn with the *aggregate* tool list gathered from every configured/connected MCP server (see the caller in `connection_manager/tool_catalog.rs`, which does `tools.extend(server_tools)` across all servers before calling this function). To detect exact duplicates and to decide which tools need a disambiguating hash suffix, it builds an identity string by joining several attacker/server-controlled fields with a raw `\0` byte and no escaping:

```rust
let raw_namespace_identity = format!(
    "{}\0{}\0{}",
    tool.server_name, tool.callable_namespace, tool.connector_id.as_deref().unwrap_or_default()
);
let raw_tool_identity = format!(
    "{}\0{}\0{}",
    raw_namespace_identity, tool.callable_name, tool.tool.name
);
if !seen_raw_names.insert(raw_tool_identity.clone()) {
    warn!("skipping duplicated tool {}", tool.tool.name);
    continue;
}
```

`tool.callable_namespace`, `tool.callable_name`, `tool.tool.name`, and `tool.connector_id` are all plain JSON strings supplied by the remote MCP server (or, for Codex Apps, derived from connector metadata reported by a connector), so they can legally contain an embedded `U+0000` byte. Because the separator itself is a literal `\0` with no escaping of `\0` occurring inside a field, two semantically different field tuples can produce byte-identical joined strings — the classic delimiter-injection ambiguity. Minimal proof (the concatenation semantics are the same as Rust's `format!`, verified independently with a short script):

```
ns1, name1 = "a", "b\0c"   ->  "a" + "\0" + "b\0c" == "a\0b\0c"
ns2, name2 = "a\0b", "c"   ->  "a\0b" + "\0" + "c"  == "a\0b\0c"
```

`(ns1, name1) != (ns2, name2)` yet their `\0`-joined byte strings are identical. Applied to `raw_tool_identity`, a malicious or compromised MCP server (or a connector funneled through the shared `codex_apps` server) can craft its own `callable_namespace`/`callable_name`/`tool.tool.name` values containing embedded NUL bytes so that its own tool's `raw_tool_identity` collides byte-for-byte with a different, legitimate tool from a different server or connector. Whichever tool is inserted into `seen_raw_names` first wins; the second is silently dropped from the model-visible tool catalog (only a `warn!` is logged, nothing is surfaced to the user). Iteration order is not attacker-controlled per attempt, but a malicious server can retry across reconnects/sessions, or target its own duplicate handling to reliably suppress a specific competing tool.

This is a real defect in a dedup/identity mechanism that the module's own doc comment says exists precisely "so every model-visible name is unique": an untrusted or semi-trusted MCP server should not be able to make an unrelated, legitimate tool disappear from the model's tool list. Fix by hashing/escaping the individual fields before joining (e.g., length-prefix each field, or hash each field independently and join the hashes) rather than concatenating raw attacker-controlled strings with an unescaped separator.

### CR-074: Injected network-request header secrets are protected in `Debug` but not in `Serialize`

**File:** `codex-rs/config/src/config_requirements.rs`
**Anchor:** `NetworkHeaderInjectionToml`, `impl std::fmt::Debug for NetworkHeaderInjectionToml`
**Severity:** medium

`NetworkHeaderInjectionToml` carries literal header values for admin-configured
"requirements-only header injections" (`pub headers: BTreeMap<String, String>`),
which the doc comment says "annotate matching requests" — i.e. this is exactly
the shape used to inject things like `Authorization: Bearer <token>` into
proxied requests. The type derives `Serialize`:

```rust
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub struct NetworkHeaderInjectionToml {
    pub host: String,
    pub methods: Vec<String>,
    pub path_prefixes: Vec<String>,
    pub headers: BTreeMap<String, String>,
}
```

but its `Debug` impl is hand-written specifically to redact the header values,
exposing only the header *names*:

```rust
impl std::fmt::Debug for NetworkHeaderInjectionToml {
    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
        f.debug_struct("NetworkHeaderInjectionToml")
            .field("host", &self.host)
            .field("methods", &self.methods)
            .field("path_prefixes", &self.path_prefixes)
            .field("header_names", &self.headers.keys().collect::<Vec<_>>())
            .finish()
    }
}
```

This custom `Debug` impl is direct evidence the author considered these values
secret and wanted them kept out of logs/`{:?}` output. `Serialize` receives no
equivalent treatment, so any code path that serializes this value directly
(`serde_json::to_value`, `toml::to_string`, or embedding it in another
`Serialize` response type) will include the raw header values verbatim. The
sibling runtime type `NetworkConstraints` (`pub struct NetworkConstraints { ...
pub header_injections: Option<Vec<NetworkHeaderInjectionToml>>, ... }`, in the
same file) also derives `Serialize`, and it is consumed outside this crate
(e.g. `codex-rs/tui/src/debug_config.rs` imports `codex_config::NetworkConstraints`).
I checked that specific consumer and it hand-formats the struct field-by-field
(`format_network_constraints`) without ever calling `Serialize` on it, so today's
known call site does not leak — but that safety exists only because each caller
remembers to avoid the derived `Serialize`, not because the type itself protects
the secret the way `Debug` does. A future "dump effective config" JSON export,
app-server response, or diagnostics bundle that serializes `NetworkConstraints`
(or `ConfigRequirementsWithSources`, which nests `NetworkRequirementsToml`,
also `Serialize`) would leak injected header secrets even though the adjacent
`Debug` impl makes clear that was never intended.

Fix: give `NetworkHeaderInjectionToml` a custom `Serialize` impl (or a
`#[serde(skip_serializing)]`/redacting wrapper for `headers`) that matches the
redaction already applied to `Debug`, and add a test asserting that
`serde_json::to_value`/`toml::to_string` of a `NetworkConstraints` containing
`header_injections` never contains the configured secret value.

### CR-075: Additional-context marker key has no length bound, bypassing the value token budget
**File:** `codex-rs/context-fragments/src/additional_context.rs`
**Anchor:** `MAX_ADDITIONAL_CONTEXT_VALUE_TOKENS`

**Severity:** medium

In both `additional_context_body` and `additional_context_developer_body`, only `value` is passed through `truncate_middle_with_token_budget(value, MAX_ADDITIONAL_CONTEXT_VALUE_TOKENS)`; `key` is used at full length, unbounded, in both the rendered marker text (`format!("{key}>{value}</external_{key}")` / `format!("<{key}>{value}</{key}>")`) and in `content_kind()` (`ContentItemKind(format!("additional_content.{}", self.key))`, persisted in `internal_chat_message_metadata_passthrough.content_item_kinds`).

Since `key` comes straight from the caller-supplied `HashMap<String, AdditionalContextEntry>` (see the previous finding for the call path) with no length cap, a caller can submit an arbitrarily large key string (megabytes) and it will be injected into the model context and persisted verbatim, completely bypassing the 1,000-token budget that this module is otherwise careful to enforce on `value`. This lets a single `additional_context` entry blow far past the intended per-entry context/token budget.

Fix: apply the same `truncate_middle_with_token_budget` (or a strict length/charset cap suited to an identifier) to `key` before it is used to build the marker or the `ContentItemKind`.

### CR-076: Plugin enable/disable analytics silently dropped for plugin names containing dots
**File:** `codex-rs/core-plugins/src/toggles.rs`
**Anchor:** `collect_plugin_enabled_candidates`
**Severity:** medium

`collect_plugin_enabled_candidates` detects a plugin-enablement write by splitting the config `key_path` on `.` and matching on the resulting segment count (`[plugins, plugin_id, enabled]`, `[plugins, plugin_id]`, or `[plugins]`). This assumes the `plugin_id` segment never itself contains a `.`.

That assumption is false: `codex_plugin::PluginId`/`validate_plugin_segment` (`codex-rs/plugin/src/plugin_id.rs`) explicitly allows dots in the *plugin name* portion of an id (`allow_dots = kind == "plugin name"`), and `PluginId::as_key()` renders as `{plugin_name}@{marketplace_name}`. Real callers build the write path directly from this key, e.g. `codex-rs/tui/src/app/background_requests.rs`: `key_path: format!("plugins.{plugin_id}")`.

For a plugin named e.g. `vendor.tool` installed from marketplace `npm-registry`, the resulting key path is `plugins.vendor.tool@npm-registry`, which splits into exactly 3 segments (`["plugins", "vendor", "tool@npm-registry"]`). None of the three match arms fire (the 3-segment arm requires the last segment to be the literal string `"enabled"`, and the 2-segment arm requires exactly two segments), so the toggle falls through to `_ => {}` and is silently dropped from `pending_changes`.

I verified this with a standalone repro of the exact match logic:
```
segments = ["plugins", "vendor", "tool@npm-registry"]
=> NO MATCH - toggle silently dropped
```
(compiled and run separately; matches the arms in `toggles.rs` verbatim).

The actual config write (`config_manager.write_value`/`batch_write` in `codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors/config_processor.rs`) is unaffected since it uses structured params rather than this string-splitting heuristic, so plugin enablement itself still works. But `emit_plugin_toggle_events` — which fires `analytics_events_client.track_plugin_enabled/disabled` — never runs for these plugins, so enable/disable telemetry silently under-reports for any plugin whose name contains a dot, a value the plugin id validator explicitly permits.

Fix: parse the key path structurally (e.g. strip the `"plugins."` prefix, then use `PluginId::parse` on the next component using a marketplace-aware split such as `rsplit_once('@')`/matching how `PluginId::parse` already handles the `@`) instead of naively splitting the whole path on `.`.

### CR-077: Blocking synchronous filesystem read on the per-turn tool-spec hot path, bypassing sandboxed I/O
**File:** `codex-rs/core/src/agent/role.rs`
**Anchor:** `spawn_tool_spec::format_role`
**Severity:** medium

`format_role` (used by `spawn_tool_spec::build`, which is called every turn from `agent_type_description` in `codex-rs/core/src/tools/spec_plan.rs` while assembling the `spawn_agent` tool description) computes a "locked settings" note for custom agent roles:

```rust
let locked_settings_note = declaration
    .config_file
    .as_ref()
    .and_then(|config_file| {
        built_in::config_file_contents(config_file)
            .map(str::to_owned)
            .or_else(|| std::fs::read_to_string(config_file).ok())
    })
    ...
```

For any non-built-in (user-defined) role with a `config_file`, `built_in::config_file_contents` returns `None`, so `std::fs::read_to_string(config_file)` executes: a synchronous, blocking local-disk read performed directly on the tokio task building the turn's tool specs, once per configured custom role, on every single turn.

This is inconsistent with how the same role file is actually loaded for execution a few lines away in `load_role_layer_toml`, which uses the async, sandbox-aware `codex_exec_server::read_sensitive_file_to_string`. Two consequences:

1. Performance: a blocking syscall inside (what is, given the call site, effectively) an async turn-construction path can stall the executing tokio worker thread on slow/network-backed home directories, once per turn per custom role — with no caching.
2. Correctness under sandboxing: `std::fs::read_to_string` always reads from the codex-core process's own local filesystem, never through the executor/sandbox abstraction used elsewhere in this file. In any configuration where role config files are expected to be resolved through that abstraction (e.g., non-local exec/environment setups), the note is silently omitted even when the role's model/reasoning effort really are locked, producing tool documentation that understates the role's actual constraints.

Fix: reuse the async `read_sensitive_file_to_string` path (already used by `load_role_layer_toml`) and cache the parsed note per role/config-file so it isn't reread every turn.

### CR-078: Approval-cache canonicalization does not deliver the wrapper-path stability its own doc comment promises
**File:** `codex-rs/core/src/command_canonicalization.rs`
**Anchor:** `canonicalize_command_for_approval`, "This keeps approval decisions stable across wrapper-path differences (for example `/bin/bash -lc` vs `bash -lc`)"
**Severity:** medium

`canonicalize_command_for_approval` normalizes an exec command's argv into a
canonical form so that, per its doc comment, approval decisions are "stable
across wrapper-path differences (for example `/bin/bash -lc` vs `bash -lc`)
and across shell wrapper tools." Its sole caller,
`PermissionRequest::cache_keys` in `codex-rs/core/src/tools/approvals.rs`,
builds the actual lookup/storage key as:

```rust
ApprovalCacheKey::ExecCommand(UnifiedExecApprovalKey {
    environment_id: environment_id.clone(),
    executable: command.first().cloned(),
    command: canonicalize_command_for_approval(command),
    ...
})
```

`UnifiedExecApprovalKey` (`codex-rs/core/src/tools/runtimes/unified_exec.rs`)
derives `PartialEq`/`Hash` over every field, including `executable`, which is
populated straight from the raw, uncanonicalized `command.first()` — the
literal first argv token (e.g. `"/bin/bash"` vs `"bash"`, or `"bash"` vs
`"zsh"`), not the shell-agnostic value that `canonicalize_command_for_approval`
computes.

Concretely: approving `/bin/bash -lc "cargo test -p codex-core"` and then
running `bash -lc "cargo test -p codex-core"` produces two `command` values
that are identical after canonicalization (confirmed by the existing test
`canonicalizes_word_only_shell_scripts_to_inner_command`, which only asserts
equality of `canonicalize_command_for_approval`'s return value, not of the
full cache key) — but the two `UnifiedExecApprovalKey`s still differ because
`executable` is `"/bin/bash"` in one case and `"bash"` in the other. The
overall cache lookup therefore misses, and the user is re-prompted for a
command that the canonicalization layer, and its documentation, say should be
recognized as already approved. The same gap applies to the heredoc/complex
script canonical form (`__codex_shell_script__` prefix) and to the
PowerShell canonical form.

This does not weaken approval enforcement (it fails toward *more* prompts,
not fewer), but it means the documented behavior of this function is not
actually achieved by its only caller, and any future caller who trusts the
doc comment (or extends the canonical form) is likely to be surprised that
wrapper-path/tool differences still bust the cache. Fix by either dropping
`executable` from the cache key (the canonicalized `command` already encodes
the relevant identity) or by deriving `executable` from the same canonical
representation instead of the raw argv.

### CR-079: Environment shell name becoming known is silently dropped from the model-visible diff

**File:** `codex-rs/core/src/context/world_state/environment.rs`
**Anchor:** `EnvironmentSnapshot::has_same_diff_value`
**Severity:** medium

`has_same_diff_value` intentionally treats a `shell: None` vs `shell: Some(_)` mismatch as "no difference":

```rust
&& self
    .shell
    .as_ref()
    .zip(other.shell.as_ref())
    .is_none_or(|(current, previous)| current == previous)
```

`Option::zip` returns `None` whenever either side is `None`, and `None.is_none_or(_)` is vacuously `true`, so this clause contributes "unchanged" whenever the shell field goes from unknown to known (or vice versa), as long as `cwd`/`status`/`error`/`is_primary` stay the same. The caller (`EnvironmentsState::render_diff`) only forces a re-render for this case through a narrower, PowerShell-specific condition (`shell_version_added && previous.shell.is_none()`), which does not fire for ordinary shells (bash/zsh/cmd) or for non-single-local environments.

This is not hypothetical: the module's own test `snapshots()` exercises exactly this transition — an `EnvironmentStatus::Available` environment whose `shell` goes from `None` to `Some("zsh")` with nothing else changing — and the checked-in snapshot (`codex_core__context__world_state__environment__tests__snapshots.snap`, case `{"environments":{"local":{"cwd":"/repo","status":"available"}}} -> {"environments":{"local":{"cwd":"/repo","shell":"zsh","status":"available"}}}`) records the result as `None`: no fragment is produced at all. Once an environment's shell resolves after it has already been reported `Available` (e.g. async shell detection on a remote/secondary environment), the model is never told what shell it is running, and will not learn this for the rest of the conversation unless some unrelated field on that same environment changes at the same time. Since shell identity directly affects what command syntax the model should generate, this is a real, user-visible correctness gap, not merely a design nicety.

Fix: drop the `Option::zip`/`is_none_or` short-circuit (or otherwise special-case a `None -> Some` or `Some -> None` transition as "different") so a newly-resolved or newly-lost shell name always forces the environment block to re-render.

### CR-080: Custom multi-agent mode instructions are never retracted when the mode is later cleared

**File:** `codex-rs/core/src/context/world_state/multi_agent_mode.rs`
**Anchor:** `MultiAgentModeState::render_diff`
**Severity:** medium

`render_diff` matches on `(&self.mode, previous)`:

```rust
(None, PreviousSectionState::Known(previous))
    if previous.mode == Some(MultiAgentMode::Proactive) =>
{
    MultiAgentMode::ExplicitRequestOnly
}
(None, PreviousSectionState::Unknown) => MultiAgentMode::ExplicitRequestOnly,
(None, PreviousSectionState::Absent | PreviousSectionState::Known(_)) => return None,
```

When the mode transitions from `Some(Proactive)` to `None`, the code deliberately re-asserts `ExplicitRequestOnly` so the model is told to stop behaving proactively. But when the previous mode was `Some(MultiAgentMode::Custom(hint_text))` and the current mode becomes `None` (the override is removed/unset), the guard on the first arm only matches `Proactive`, so control falls through to the catch-all `(None, PreviousSectionState::Known(_)) => return None`. No fragment is emitted, and no removal/replacement notice is ever sent (unlike sibling sections such as `agents_md.rs`, `context_window_guidance.rs`, and `managed_developer_instructions.rs`, which all emit an explicit "no longer applies" notice on an analogous Some -> None transition).

Because the previously-sent `MultiAgentModeInstructions` fragment (containing the custom hint text) remains, uncontradicted, in the retained conversation history, the model will continue to follow the stale custom multi-agent policy indefinitely after it has been disabled or replaced with the default. This is a real behavioral regression path (e.g. an admin/user turns off a custom `multi_agent_mode` override mid-session), and the test suite's own `snapshots()` case list confirms the gap: it covers `(Known(&custom), Known(&empty))` where `empty` is `Some(Custom(""))` — not the actual `None`/disabled state — and never exercises `(Known(&custom), Known(&inactive))` at all, whereas the analogous `(Known(&proactive), Known(&inactive))` and `(Known(&explicit), Known(&inactive))` cases are both tested.

Fix: extend the `previous.mode == Some(MultiAgentMode::Proactive)` guard to also match `Some(MultiAgentMode::Custom(_))` (or otherwise emit a removal notice for any previously-known non-default mode when the current mode becomes `None`).

### CR-081: Guardian fast-approval path can approve an action after the request was cancelled
**File:** `codex-rs/core/src/guardian/decision.rs`
**Anchor:** `Some(ApprovalDecision::Allow) if !require_fresh_review => { ... Some(ReviewDecision::Approved) }`
**Severity:** medium

`decide_approval` computes `require_fresh_review` once, near the top of the function:

```rust
let require_fresh_review = options.require_synchronous_review
    || model_requires_review && !turn.config.features.enabled(codex_features::Feature::GuardianV2)
    || options.external_cancel.as_ref().is_some_and(CancellationToken::is_cancelled)
    || reasons.retry.is_some()
    || matches!(&request.request, Ok(GuardianApprovalRequest::ExecCommand { sandbox_permissions, .. })
        if sandbox_permissions.requires_escalated_permissions());
```

This snapshots `external_cancel.is_cancelled()` at that instant. The function then awaits
`session.services.extensions.decide_approval(&input).await`, which can take an arbitrary amount of
time (it is exactly the kind of pluggable/possibly-networked call that the synchronous Guardian
review exists to back up). If the caller's cancellation token is cancelled *during* that await
(e.g. the user hits interrupt while the fast-decision extension is still working), and the
extension subsequently returns `ApprovalDecision::Allow`, the code takes this branch:

```rust
Some(ApprovalDecision::Allow) if !require_fresh_review => {
    let request = match request.validate(&context) { Ok(request) => request, Err(decision) => return Some(decision) };
    ...
    Some(ReviewDecision::Approved)
}
```

`require_fresh_review` is still `false` here because it was computed before the cancellation
happened, and this branch never re-reads `options.external_cancel`. The function returns
`ReviewDecision::Approved` even though the request has since been cancelled.

Contrast this with the two other places in the same function that make an approval decision: the
`full_access` early-return explicitly re-checks `external_cancel.is_some_and(CancellationToken::is_cancelled)`
right before returning `Approved`, and the `runtime.review(...)` path (used when `require_fresh_review`
is true or the decision is `AskUser`/`None`) goes through `ReviewRuntime::prepare`
(`guardian/review_request.rs`), which explicitly checks cancellation and returns
`ReviewDecision::Abort` when it fires. Only the "extension already said Allow, no fresh review
needed" fast path skips this check, so a reader who sees the other two branches guard against
cancellation would not expect this third branch to skip it silently. The result is a race window
in which an approval already superseded by an interrupt/cancel can still come back `Approved` to
the caller in `tools/approvals.rs`, which awaits this decision directly with no separate
cancellation race of its own (`spawn_approval_decision(...).await` is not raced against the token
at the call site).

Fix: re-check `options.external_cancel` immediately before returning `Some(ReviewDecision::Approved)`
in this branch (mirroring what the `full_access` branch already does), or recompute the
cancellation flag after the `decide_approval` await instead of relying on the value captured
before it.

### CR-082: Model-reroute warning hardcodes a specific model pair and cause for any server-reported model mismatch
**File:** `codex-rs/core/src/session/mod.rs`
**Anchor:** `maybe_warn_on_server_model_mismatch`
**Severity:** medium

`maybe_warn_on_server_model_mismatch` is invoked from `codex-rs/core/src/session/turn.rs` for every `ResponseEvent::ServerModel(server_model)` event, i.e. whenever the `openai-model` response header (set unconditionally by the server, see `codex-rs/codex-api/src/sse/responses.rs` and `codex-rs/codex-api/src/endpoint/responses_websocket.rs`) names a model different from the one that was requested. The function itself is written generically — it compares `requested_model` and `server_model` case-insensitively and only proceeds when they actually differ — and it correctly threads the real `requested_model`/`server_model` values into the structured `ModelRerouteEvent { from_model, to_model, .. }`.

However, the free-text warning it also emits is a hardcoded literal that ignores both variables:

```rust
let warning_message = format!(
    "Your account was flagged for potentially high-risk cyber activity and this request was routed to gpt-5.2 as a fallback. To regain access to gpt-5.3-codex, apply for trusted access: {CYBER_VERIFY_URL} or learn more: {CYBER_SAFETY_URL}"
);
```

and the reason attached to the structured event is likewise fixed:

```rust
reason: ModelRerouteReason::HighRiskCyberActivity,
```

`ModelRerouteReason` currently has only this one variant (`codex-rs/protocol/src/protocol.rs`), and nothing in `maybe_warn_on_server_model_mismatch` checks that the requested model is actually a `MODEL_SPECIALTY_CYBER` model, or that `server_model` is actually `"gpt-5.2"`, before choosing this message — unlike other similar-purpose code in the same file (e.g. `unsupported_service_tier_warning`, a few lines below) which interpolates the real values into its message. Because the `openai-model` header is a generic "which model actually served this request" signal (used for other purposes such as etag/rate-limit propagation in the same response), any future or incidental server-side model substitution unrelated to the cyber-safety fallback (deprecation routing, load shedding, A/B testing, etc.) will still produce this exact, specific, and in that case false statement to the end user: that their account was flagged for high-risk cyber activity and that they were rerouted from `gpt-5.3-codex` to `gpt-5.2`, even if the actual `requested_model`/`server_model` are a completely different pair. This path has no test coverage anywhere in the crate (`grep -rn "maybe_warn_on_server_model_mismatch"` only matches the definition and its single call site), so nothing currently guards against the message drifting out of sync with the models actually involved.

Fix: interpolate `requested_model`/`server_model` into the warning text (or gate the whole cyber-specific message behind an explicit check that the model pair matches the known cyber-fallback case), and/or extend `ModelRerouteReason` with an `Other`/`Unknown` variant used when the mismatch is not attributable to that specific policy.

### CR-083: Execve program path is lossily re-encoded before Guardian review, decoupling the reviewed identity from the executed bytes

**File:** `codex-rs/core/src/tools/approvals.rs`
**Anchor:** `program: program.to_string_lossy().into_owned(),` in `ApprovalAction::into_guardian_request`
**Severity:** medium

`ApprovalAction::Execve` carries `program: AbsolutePathBuf`, which preserves the exact byte sequence of the executable path that will be passed to `execve()` (this variant backs the ptrace/execve interception path used to gate unsandboxed process escalation in `core/src/tools/runtimes/zsh_fork/unix_escalation.rs`). When this action is converted into a `GuardianApprovalRequest` for the automated reviewer:

```rust
#[cfg(unix)]
Self::Execve { id, source, program, argv, cwd, additional_permissions, .. } =>
    crate::guardian::GuardianApprovalRequest::Execve {
        id, source,
        program: program.to_string_lossy().into_owned(),
        argv, cwd, additional_permissions,
    },
```

`to_string_lossy()` replaces any invalid-UTF-8 bytes in the path with U+FFFD before the value is used both for the human/automated-reviewer-facing display and, in `core/src/guardian/review.rs::plugin_attribution_for_command`, as the actual command string matched against plugin/exec-policy attribution rules. Unix paths are arbitrary byte sequences and are not guaranteed to be valid UTF-8, so a program path containing invalid UTF-8 will be reviewed/attributed under a different string than the bytes the kernel will actually execute. This is inconsistent with the sibling `ExecCommand` path in the same function, which explicitly preserves the raw cwd via `LegacyAppPathString::from_path_uri` specifically to avoid this kind of lossy re-encoding (see the `non_utf8_cwd_preserves_approval_routing` test in `approvals_tests.rs`, which only covers `cwd`, not `Execve.program`). Because this feeds the same-session Guardian automated reviewer and its exec-policy/plugin-attribution matching for a privilege-escalation-relevant syscall interception path, two different real-world executables with different non-UTF-8 byte sequences can render to the same lossy display/attribution string, or a program's true byte identity may simply not match what a deny/allow rule expects.

Fix: represent `GuardianApprovalRequest::Execve::program` with a byte-preserving type (e.g. the same `LegacyAppPathString`/`PathUri` treatment used for `cwd`), or otherwise ensure attribution/policy matching operates on the original `AbsolutePathBuf` rather than a lossily-converted `String`.

### CR-084: Dynamic tool call can hang instead of failing over when the active turn is already cleared
**File:** `codex-rs/core/src/tools/handlers/dynamic.rs`
**Anchor:** `request_dynamic_tool`
**Severity:** medium

`request_dynamic_tool` creates a oneshot channel and only moves the sender into
turn state on the `Some(at)` arm of the match:

```rust
let (tx_response, rx_response) = oneshot::channel();
let prev_entry = {
    let mut active = session.active_turn.lock().await;
    match active.as_mut() {
        Some(at) => {
            let mut ts = at.turn_state.lock().await;
            ts.insert_pending_dynamic_tool(call_id.clone(), tx_response)
        }
        None => None,
    }
};
...
let response = rx_response.await.ok();
```

When `active.as_mut()` is `None`, `tx_response` is *not* moved, so it is not
dropped early — Rust drops it only at the end of the enclosing function scope,
which is after the `rx_response.await` statement. Since nothing else holds the
sender, `rx_response.await` never resolves on its own: the sender is being
kept alive specifically by the code path that is supposed to represent "there
is nowhere to deliver this response." I confirmed this drop-timing behavior
with a standalone reproduction (`tokio::sync::oneshot`, a `match` that only
moves the sender in one arm): the receiver times out/hangs on the arm that
doesn't move the sender, and resolves immediately on the arm that does.

This is reachable: `codex-rs/core/src/session/turn_suspension.rs`
(`suspend_turn_and_shutdown`) clears `session.active_turn` via `active.take()`
*before* calling `task.cancellation_token.cancel()` a few lines later, so
there is a window where a concurrently-running dynamic tool dispatch can
observe `active_turn == None`. In current call paths this is masked because
`codex-rs/core/src/tools/parallel.rs` always dispatches tool handlers inside a
`tokio::spawn` wrapped by `AbortOnDropHandle`, racing the dispatch against the
same `cancellation_token`; once that token is cancelled the spawned task is
aborted, which forcibly drops the whole future (including the leaked
`tx_response`). So today the practical impact is bounded to the tiny window
between the `take()` and the `cancel()` call, and is fully cleaned up shortly
after — but the intended fallback ("fail the call cleanly because there is no
active turn to answer it") does not actually work: it silently depends on an
unrelated abort happening to arrive later. If this handler is ever invoked
outside that specific dispatch wrapper (e.g. a future refactor, a test, or a
different caller that awaits the handler directly without a paired
cancellation-token abort), the call will hang forever instead of returning
`None`.

Fix: explicitly drop the sender in the `None` arm (e.g. `None => { drop(tx_response); None }`), or restructure so the value is always consumed in the match (`Some(at) => Some(...), None => { drop(tx_response); None }`), so the "no active turn" path fails over immediately rather than relying on an external cancellation to eventually abort the future.

### CR-085: `exec_command` leaks a reserved process ID when `get_command` rejects the request

**File:** `codex-rs/core/src/tools/handlers/unified_exec/exec_command.rs`
**Anchor:** `ExecCommandHandler::handle_call`
**Severity:** medium

In `handle_call`, a process ID is allocated from the shared pool before the command is
resolved:

```rust
let process_id = manager.allocate_process_id().await;
let resolved_command = get_command(
    &args,
    shell,
    &shell_mode,
    turn_environment.config().allow_login_shell,
)
.map_err(FunctionCallError::RespondToModel)?;
```

`get_command` (in `unified_exec.rs`) returns `Err` in two ordinary, model-reachable
situations: the model sets `login: true` while the environment's config disallows login
shells, or the model sets `shell` while the turn is running in `UnifiedExecShellMode::ZshFork`.
Both are exercised directly by existing tests (`test_get_command_rejects_explicit_login_when_disallowed`,
`exec_command_rejects_login_when_selected_environment_disallows_it`, and
`test_get_command_rejects_explicit_shell_in_zsh_fork_mode` in `unified_exec_tests.rs`), so this
is not a corner case — it is the normal rejection path for a disallowed argument combination.

When `get_command` returns `Err`, the `?` propagates immediately and `handle_call` returns
without ever calling `manager.release_process_id(process_id)`. Every other early-return path in
this function (missing sandbox cwd, permission normalization failure, `intercepted_patch` error)
explicitly releases the reserved ID first; this one does not. I confirmed by reading
`UnifiedExecProcessManager::allocate_process_id`/`release_process_id`
(`core/src/unified_exec/process_manager.rs`) that in production (non-deterministic) mode a
process ID is only returned to the pool via `release_process_id`, which removes it from
`reserved_process_ids`; an ID that is never released stays reserved for the lifetime of the
`UnifiedExecProcessManager` (i.e., the session), so `allocate_process_id`'s retry loop can never
reuse it.

The pool is large (`rand::rng().random_range(1_000..100_000)`), so a single leak is harmless, but
a model that repeatedly retries `exec_command` with a disallowed `login`/`shell` combination (for
example, retrying after seeing the rejection message, or a client that always sets
`login: true`) leaks one reserved ID per attempt with no cap other than the ~99,000-entry space.
Fix by releasing `process_id` before returning the `get_command` error, e.g.:

```rust
let resolved_command = match get_command(&args, shell, &shell_mode, turn_environment.config().allow_login_shell) {
    Ok(resolved) => resolved,
    Err(err) => {
        manager.release_process_id(process_id).await;
        return Err(FunctionCallError::RespondToModel(err));
    }
};
```

### CR-086: Two independent tests share the same hardcoded global temp-dir marker path

**File:** `codex-rs/core/tests/suite/hooks.rs`
**Anchor:** `permission_request_hook_allows_exec_command_without_user_approval`, `permission_request_hook_sees_raw_exec_command_input`
**Severity:** medium

Both `permission_request_hook_allows_exec_command_without_user_approval` (around line 2994) and
`permission_request_hook_sees_raw_exec_command_input` (around line 3287) compute:

```rust
let marker = std::env::temp_dir().join("permissionrequest-exec-command-marker");
```

This is the literal same path in both tests — verified with `grep -n
"std::env::temp_dir()" codex-rs/core/tests/suite/hooks.rs`, which shows the identical
string `"permissionrequest-exec-command-marker"` used twice, whereas every other test in
the same file that needs a temp marker (`pretooluse-exec-command-marker`,
`plugin-pretooluse-exec-command-marker`, `pretooluse-config-toml-marker`,
`pretooluse-exec-command-blocked-context-marker`) uses a distinct literal name. Unlike
those other tests, and unlike the majority of this file's fixtures, neither of these two
tests uses a per-test `TempDir` for the marker — they both reach into the process-wide,
machine-wide OS temp directory (`std::env::temp_dir()`), which is shared not just across
threads in one test binary but across concurrently-running test processes on the same
host (e.g. under `cargo nextest`, which runs test cases in separate processes in
parallel by default).

Each test does: write `"seed"` to the marker, submit a turn whose shell command is
`rm -f {marker}`, then `assert!(!marker.exists(), ...)`. Because both tests target the
exact same path, when they run concurrently (the default execution mode for Rust's test
harness — `#[tokio::test]` functions in the same binary run on independent OS threads
unless `--test-threads=1` is passed, and separate test binaries/processes still share
the OS temp directory), one test's `fs::write(&marker, "seed")` can race with the
other's `rm -f`/existence check. Concretely: Test A completes its turn and is about to
assert `!marker.exists()`; at that exact moment Test B (running concurrently) executes
its own `fs::write(&marker, "seed")` as part of its own setup. Test A's assertion then
observes a marker that exists — not because Test A's own approved command failed to
remove it, but because an unrelated, concurrently-running test recreated the file. This
produces a spurious, hard-to-reproduce CI failure in `permission_request_hook_allows_exec_command_without_user_approval`
or `permission_request_hook_sees_raw_exec_command_input` (or, in the tighter direction, a
false-positive pass by Test B if it inherits a leftover deletion). The other marker-based
tests avoid this correctly by giving each test a distinct literal filename in the shared
temp dir.

Fix: give one of the two tests a distinct marker filename (or better, put both under a
per-test `TempDir` as `pre_tool_use_json_deny_blocks_exec_command_before_execution` and
others in the same file already do), so the two tests no longer contend for the same
global path.

### CR-087: `ExecServerTransportParams` Debug impl redacts WebSocket headers but not stdio command env vars
**File:** `codex-rs/exec-server/src/client_api.rs`
**Anchor:** `impl std::fmt::Debug for ExecServerTransportParams`
**Severity:** medium

The manual `Debug` impl for `ExecServerTransportParams` explicitly redacts the `WebSocketUrl`
variant's headers:

```rust
Self::WebSocketUrl { websocket_url, connect_timeout, initialize_timeout, .. } => f
    .debug_struct("WebSocketUrl")
    ...
    .field("http_headers", &"<redacted>")
    .finish(),
```

but the `StdioCommand` variant prints its `command` field verbatim:

```rust
Self::StdioCommand { command, initialize_timeout } => f
    .debug_struct("StdioCommand")
    .field("command", command)
    .field("initialize_timeout", initialize_timeout)
    .finish(),
```

`command` is a `StdioExecServerCommand` with a derived `#[derive(Debug)]` that includes
`env: HashMap<String, String>`. `environments.toml` (see `environment_toml.rs`) lets a user attach
arbitrary environment variables to a stdio-launched environment (the test fixtures use
`CODEX_LOG=debug`, but nothing prevents a user from putting a real credential there, e.g. an SSH
`sshpass`-style token or an API key consumed by the remote `codex exec-server` invocation). The
codebase clearly treats this struct as something that must not leak secrets through `{:?}` — see
the parallel, explicitly-redacted `WebSocketUrl.http_headers`, `EnvironmentRegistryConnectResponse`
(`environment_registry.rs`), and `RemoteEnvironmentOptions` (`environment/connect_options.rs`), all
three of which have dedicated tests asserting the secret does not appear in `{:?}` output. No
equivalent test exists for `StdioCommand`, and this asymmetry means a future (or already-existing
elsewhere in the workspace) `tracing::debug!(?transport_params)` / error-context call would leak a
configured stdio environment's secrets in cleartext while a reader of this file would reasonably
assume all variants are covered, given the established pattern. Redact `command.env` (and
`command.args`, which can also carry secrets passed as CLI flags) the same way `http_headers` is
redacted.

### CR-088: Gap-closing exec-server process events can be rejected purely for exceeding the per-event byte cap
**File:** `codex-rs/exec-server/src/client.rs`
**Anchor:** `OrderedSessionEvents::insert_pending`
**Severity:** medium

`insert_pending` has three size/count guards that exist to bound the client's
out-of-order reorder buffer for `process/output`, `process/exited`, and
`process/closed` notifications. Two of the three guards are explicitly
exempted when the incoming event is the next expected sequence number
(`closes_gap`), because — per the comment directly above the call site —
"the next expected event is synchronously published by every caller, so it
can drain a full buffer without becoming retained state":

```rust
let closes_gap = seq == next_seq;
if !closes_gap && self.pending.len() >= MAX_PENDING_PROCESS_EVENTS { return Err(...); }

let event_bytes = pending_process_event_bytes(&event);
if event_bytes > MAX_PENDING_PROCESS_EVENT_BYTES { return Err(...); }   // <-- not exempted
let pending_bytes = self.pending_bytes.saturating_add(event_bytes);
if !closes_gap && pending_bytes > MAX_PENDING_PROCESS_EVENT_BYTES { return Err(...); }
```

The middle check (`event_bytes > MAX_PENDING_PROCESS_EVENT_BYTES`, 1 MiB) is
missing the same `!closes_gap &&` guard that both its neighbors have. So a
single legitimate, in-order `ExecOutputDeltaNotification` chunk larger than
1 MiB is rejected even though — being gap-closing — it would never actually
sit in the reorder buffer: `publish_ready` drains it in the same call,
immediately after `insert_pending` returns.

The `Err` return propagates out of `publish_ordered_event` through
`finish_process_event`, which calls `session.set_failure(message)` and
`inner.remove_session_if(...)` — i.e. the entire exec-server session is torn
down and marked failed because of one oversized-but-perfectly-ordinary output
chunk, not because the client was actually at risk of buffering unbounded
data.

I copied the exact logic (verbatim, only trimming unrelated imports) into a
standalone Rust program and confirmed the behavior:

```
result for gap-closing 1MiB+1 byte event: Err("process event exceeds 1048576 bytes")
```

i.e. a `seq == 1` event (the very first, always gap-closing) with a
1 MiB+1-byte payload is rejected outright, with no exemption, despite it
never being retained.

I could not confirm from the files in this shard whether the current local
reader (`codex_sandboxing::spawn_process`, feeding `stream_output` in
`local_process.rs`, which is outside this shard) ever forwards a single chunk
above 1 MiB in one notification — typical pipe/PTY read buffers are well
under that, so this may not be reachable today. But the check is inconsistent
with its own documented intent and neighboring guards, and would surface as
a spurious session failure the moment any executor (including a future or
remote one) forwards a larger single output chunk. Fix: exempt the per-event
byte check with `!closes_gap &&`, matching the other two guards.

### CR-089: Synthetic HTTP body-stream failure notification masks the real disconnect reason
**File:** `codex-rs/exec-server/src/client/http_response_body_stream.rs`
**Anchor:** `fail_all_http_body_streams`
**Severity:** medium

`fail_all_http_body_streams` builds a synthetic terminal delta for every open stream when the
connection is failing:

```rust
HttpRequestBodyDeltaNotification {
    request_id: request_id.clone(),
    seq: 1,
    delta: Vec::new().into(),
    done: true,
    error: Some(message.clone()),
}
```

`seq` is hardcoded to `1` regardless of how far that stream has actually progressed. On the
consumer side, `HttpResponseBodyStream::recv()` checks the sequence number *before* it looks at
`delta.error`:

```rust
if delta.seq != *next_seq {
    finish_remote_stream(inner, request_id, closed).await;
    return Err(ExecServerError::Protocol(format!(
        "http response stream `{request_id}` received seq {}, expected {}",
        delta.seq, *next_seq
    )));
}
...
if let Some(error) = delta.error { ... }
```

`next_seq` starts at `1` and is incremented for every real chunk already delivered. As soon as a
streamed response has produced at least one chunk (the ordinary case for anything actually worth
streaming) and the underlying exec-server connection then drops, `client_recovery.rs::recover()`
calls `fail_all_http_body_streams(disconnect_message)` for every open stream. The synthetic
`seq: 1` no longer matches `next_seq` (which is now `>= 2`), so the consumer takes the
sequence-mismatch branch and reports a confusing
`"http response stream `http-N` received seq 1, expected 2"` instead of the real
`"... failed: {disconnect_message}"`. I traced this by hand: `next_seq` is only reset by
constructing a new stream, and every successfully-processed delta (real or synthetic) increments
it, so any stream that has consumed ≥1 chunk before the disconnect will hit this path
deterministically. The failure path that *does* report the correct message only fires when
`tx.try_send` returns `Full` (channel backpressure), which is the uncommon case.

Both paths still return an `Err` of the same enum variant, so retry/recovery classification is
unaffected — the impact is limited to misleading diagnostics/telemetry for the common mid-stream
disconnect case. Fix by tracking (or accepting) the stream's current sequence number when
synthesizing the failure delta, or by checking `delta.error`/`delta.done` before enforcing the
sequence invariant for terminal deltas.

### CR-090: `HTTP_HEADER_ENV_DENYLIST` is an incomplete blocklist for header-injected environment variables
**File:** `codex-rs/exec-server/src/client/route_aware_http_client.rs`
**Anchor:** `HTTP_HEADER_ENV_DENYLIST`
**Severity:** medium

`RouteAwareHttpRequestRunner::build_headers` lets an `HttpRequestParams` header specify
`value_env_var`, in which case the value is read from `std::env::var(&env_var)` **in the process
that actually performs the request** (the executor/remote runtime for remote environments, per the
module doc comment) and appended to the header value, then sent to the request's `url`, which is
otherwise only constrained to be `http`/`https` (any host). This is a deliberate mechanism (see
`codex-mcp/src/executor_environment_http_client.rs`, which uses it to attach
`Authorization: Bearer <env value>` for executor-owned MCP servers using a config-supplied
`bearer_token_env_var`) so that secrets never have to leave the process that holds them.

The only guard against this being used to exfiltrate a *different*, unrelated secret from that same
process is a hardcoded blocklist:

```rust
const HTTP_HEADER_ENV_DENYLIST: &[&str] = &[
    CODEX_EXEC_SERVER_NOISE_AUTH_TOKEN_ENV_VAR,
    OPENAI_FEDERATION_RULE_ID_ENV_VAR,
    ...
    "OPENAI_API_KEY", "CODEX_API_KEY", "CODEX_ACCESS_TOKEN", "CODEX_CONNECTORS_TOKEN",
    "AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID", "AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY", "AWS_SESSION_TOKEN",
    "AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET", "AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE", "GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS",
];
```

This is a blocklist, not an allowlist: any environment variable present in the executor process
that is *not* on this list (a newly-added cloud credential, a `GITHUB_TOKEN`, a database URL, an
internal service token, etc.) can be read and forwarded verbatim to any header/URL a caller
supplies via `value_env_var`, and nothing in this file will catch it. The list already shows signs
of having been extended reactively (`CODEX_CONNECTORS_TOKEN`, `AZURE_FEDERATED_TOKEN_FILE`), which
is the pattern that makes blocklists unreliable over time — every new secret-bearing env var
introduced anywhere else in the codebase has to be remembered and added here, and there is no
compile-time or test-time enforcement tying the two together. I did not find a way to invoke this
with a fully untrusted/attacker-chosen header+URL from this shard alone (the current caller,
`ExecutorEnvironmentHttpClient`, sets a fixed header name and a config-supplied env var name), but
the guard exists precisely because the codebase anticipates less-trusted callers, and a blocklist
is a weaker version of the allowlist this comment's own threat model calls for. Prefer inverting
this to an explicit allowlist of header/env-var names that legitimate callers are permitted to use.

### CR-091: `RemoteExecProcess::drop` calls `tokio::spawn` without checking for a runtime
**File:** `codex-rs/exec-server/src/remote_process.rs`
**Anchor:** `impl Drop for RemoteExecProcess`
**Severity:** medium

```rust
impl Drop for RemoteExecProcess {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        self.session.cancel_network_policy_decisions();
        let session = self.session.clone();
        tokio::spawn(async move {
            session.unregister().await;
        });
    }
}
```

`tokio::spawn` panics if called outside a Tokio runtime context ("there is no reactor
running... must be called from the context of a Tokio 1.x runtime"). This crate is aware of
that hazard and defends against it elsewhere: `FileReadRegistration::drop` in
`remote_file_stream.rs` captures a `tokio::runtime::Handle` at creation time and only spawns
via `if let Some(runtime) = runtime { runtime.spawn(...) }`, falling back to doing nothing if
no handle is available. `RemoteExecProcess::drop` has no such guard, and it is the only
`Drop` impl in this crate (`rg "impl Drop for" src`) that unconditionally calls
`tokio::spawn`.

If an `Arc<RemoteExecProcess>` is ever dropped from a context without an active Tokio
runtime — e.g. during process/runtime teardown, a synchronous `Drop` chain triggered while a
runtime is shutting down, or a unit test that constructs one outside `#[tokio::test]` — this
panics. Given the sibling type in the same file already had to be written defensively for
exactly this failure mode, this asymmetry looks like an oversight rather than an intentional
design choice. Fix by capturing `tokio::runtime::Handle::try_current()` (or otherwise
guarding the spawn) the same way `FileReadRegistration` does.

### CR-092: Fabricated JSON-RPC error ID for malformed messages can collide with a real pending request
**File:** `codex-rs/exec-server/src/server/request_dispatcher.rs`
**Anchor:** `handle_malformed_message`
**Severity:** medium

`handle_malformed_message` reports a malformed inbound frame back to the client using a
hard-coded sentinel ID:

```rust
if self
    .outgoing_tx
    .send(RpcServerOutboundMessage::Error {
        request_id: RequestId::Integer(-1),
        error: invalid_request(reason),
    })
    .await
```

JSON-RPC 2.0 places no restriction on the sign or range of a numeric `id`; a client is free to
issue a request with `id: -1` (the spec only reserves `null` and requires the ID to be echoed
back verbatim). Because the exec-server connection multiplexes many pipelined requests on one
transport (see `JsonRpcConnectionEvent`/`incoming_rx.recv()` in `processor.rs`), a malformed line
can arrive on the wire interleaved with an unrelated, well-formed request that happens to use
`id: -1`. When that happens, the client's own request/response correlation table will resolve
the real pending call with this unrelated "malformed message" error instead of its actual
result, silently corrupting an otherwise valid request. The existing test suite only exercises
IDs starting at 1 (`RequestId::Integer(1)`, harnesses using `next_request_id` starting at 1), so
this collision path is untested.

Fix: use an ID space that cannot collide with client-chosen request IDs (e.g. `RequestId::Null`,
which JSON-RPC reserves for exactly this "the ID could not be determined" case), or track and
reject truly out-of-band malformed-message IDs distinctly from response dispatch.

### CR-093: `codex exec --json` cannot distinguish a declined patch from a failed one

**File:** `codex-rs/exec/src/event_processor_with_jsonl_output.rs`
**Anchor:** `map_item_with_id`
**Severity:** medium

In `EventProcessorWithJsonOutput::map_item_with_id`, the `ThreadItem::FileChange` arm maps the
source status with:

```rust
status: match status {
    PatchApplyStatus::InProgress => ExecPatchApplyStatus::InProgress,
    PatchApplyStatus::Completed => ExecPatchApplyStatus::Completed,
    PatchApplyStatus::Failed | PatchApplyStatus::Declined => {
        ExecPatchApplyStatus::Failed
    }
},
```

`PatchApplyStatus::Declined` (the source/domain status, e.g. the user rejected an approval
prompt for the patch) is folded into `ExecPatchApplyStatus::Failed`. The exported/public
`PatchApplyStatus` enum in `codex-rs/exec/src/exec_events.rs` only has three variants
(`InProgress`, `Completed`, `Failed`) — there is no `Declined` variant to map to.

This is inconsistent with the sibling `CommandExecutionStatus` handling one function up in the
same file, which *does* preserve the distinction:

```rust
status: match status {
    CommandExecutionStatus::InProgress => ExecCommandExecutionStatus::InProgress,
```
