```rust
    CommandExecutionStatus::Completed => ExecCommandExecutionStatus::Completed,
    CommandExecutionStatus::Failed => ExecCommandExecutionStatus::Failed,
    CommandExecutionStatus::Declined => ExecCommandExecutionStatus::Declined,
},
```

and with `exec_events.rs`'s own `CommandExecutionStatus`, which has a `Declined` variant, and
with the human-readable renderer in `codex-rs/exec/src/event_processor_with_human_output.rs`
(`render_item_completed`), which maps `PatchApplyStatus::Declined` to the distinct text
`"declined"` (separate from `"failed"`).

The practical effect: a script parsing `codex exec --json` output sees
`item.completed` with `type: "file_change"` and `status: "failed"` both when patch application
genuinely errored and when the user/approval policy declined to apply the patch — two states
that call for very different automated responses (retry/backoff vs. surface for
approval) — while the human-facing `codex exec` output for the exact same underlying event
correctly prints `declined`. The fix is to add a `Declined` variant to the public
`PatchApplyStatus` in `exec_events.rs` (mirroring `CommandExecutionStatus`) and map it through
instead of collapsing it into `Failed`.

### CR-094: `--add-dir` relative paths resolve against the wrong cwd when combined with `--worktree`

**File:** `codex-rs/exec/src/lib.rs`
**Anchor:** `for path in &mut add_dir { if path.is_relative() { *path = std::env::current_dir()?.join(&*path); } }`
**Severity:** medium

Inside `run_main`'s `--worktree` branch, relative `--add-dir` paths are rewritten to absolute paths by joining them against `std::env::current_dir()` (the raw OS process working directory) before the worktree checkout is created and before the final `Config` is built. That result is stored back into `add_dir`, which later becomes `ConfigOverrides.additional_writable_roots` and is threaded verbatim into the final config build.

This is inconsistent with the non-worktree code path: `codex-rs/core/src/config/mod.rs` resolves `additional_writable_roots` with `AbsolutePathBuf::resolve_path_against_base(path, resolved_cwd.as_path())`, i.e. relative to the *effective* cwd (`--cwd`/`-C`, or process cwd if unset) — not necessarily the raw process cwd. By the time the `--worktree` loop runs, `config_cwd` has already been computed from `--cwd`/`-C` (or process cwd if none was given) and is in scope a few lines above the loop, but the loop ignores it and re-derives a base from `std::env::current_dir()` instead.

Concretely: `codex exec --cwd ../other-repo --worktree --add-dir logs "do work"` run from `/home/user` will resolve `logs` to `/home/user/logs` (the shell's cwd) instead of `../other-repo/logs` relative to the requested `--cwd`, silently granting/denying write access to the wrong directory once the worktree checkout is created and the sandbox's writable-root list is built from the (already-absolutized, now-wrong) path. Because `additional_writable_roots` feeds directly into the sandbox's writable-root list, this is a sandbox-boundary correctness issue, not just a cosmetic one. No existing test exercises `--cwd`/`-C` together with a relative `--add-dir` under `--worktree` (the only worktree test that uses `--add-dir` with a relative path never diverges the actual process cwd from the effective `--cwd`, since it never passes `-C`/`--cwd` at all), so the divergence goes unnoticed.

Fix: resolve relative `add_dir` entries against `config_cwd.as_path()` (already computed at that point) instead of `std::env::current_dir()`.

### CR-095: Host-executable basename fallback silently breaks on Windows when a rule's program token is not lowercase
**File:** `codex-rs/execpolicy/src/policy.rs`
**Anchor:** `match_host_executable_rules`
**Severity:** medium

`match_host_executable_rules` computes a `basename` from the resolved absolute
path with `executable_path_lookup_key`, which (per
`codex-rs/execpolicy/src/executable_name.rs`) lowercases the filename and
strips known executable suffixes only `#[cfg(windows)]`. It then looks that
basename up directly in `self.rules_by_program`:

```rust
let Some(basename) = executable_path_lookup_key(program.as_path()) else { return Vec::new(); };
let Some(rules) = self.rules_by_program.get_vec(&basename) else { return Vec::new(); };
```

`rules_by_program` is keyed by `PolicyBuilder::add_rule` using
`rule.program().to_string()`, i.e. the literal, un-normalized first pattern
token exactly as written in the `.rules` file (see `parser.rs`'s
`prefix_rule` builtin, which does `Arc::from(head.as_str())` with no case
folding). On Windows, if a policy author writes `prefix_rule(pattern =
["Git", "status"])` (or any other non-lowercase program name) and later
resolves an absolute path like `C:\Program Files\Git\bin\Git.exe`, the
computed basename is the lowercase `"git"`, which will never match the
stored key `"Git"`. The host-executable resolution path (`--resolve-host-
executables` / `MatchOptions.resolve_host_executables = true`, which
`codex-rs/core/src/exec_policy.rs` sets unconditionally for exec approval)
silently returns no match instead of the intended basename-fallback rule,
even though the rule for the bare command name does exist.

None of the tests in `execpolicy/tests/basic.rs` exercise this because every
host-executable test hardcodes the pattern's first token and the
`host_executable(name = ...)` value as the same lowercase literal `"git"`
(e.g. `host_executable_resolution_uses_basename_rule_when_allowed`), so the
case-normalization asymmetry between the rule key (raw, case-preserved) and
the lookup key (lowercased on Windows) is never exercised. Fix by normalizing
the pattern's first token through the same `executable_lookup_key` used for
`host_executable` names before inserting into `rules_by_program` (or by
normalizing at lookup time using the un-lowered basename first, then falling
back), so program-name matching is consistent across the exact-match and
basename-fallback code paths on Windows.

### CR-096: Non-atomic write in `clean_rules_file` can corrupt the policy file on a mid-write failure
**File:** `codex-rs/execpolicy/src/sandbox_migration.rs`
**Anchor:** `clean_rules_file`
**Severity:** medium

`clean_rules_file` rewrites the policy file in place by writing the new
(shorter) content before truncating:

```rust
file.seek(SeekFrom::Start(0)).await?;
file.write_all(retained.as_bytes()).await?;
file.set_len(retained.len() as u64).await?;
```

Because `retained` is always a strict prefix-preserving subsequence of the
original lines (lines are only removed, never rewritten in place), `retained.len()
<= contents.len()` whenever a change is needed. If `write_all` returns an
error after a partial write (e.g. `ENOSPC`, an interrupted write, or any I/O
error), the `?` returns immediately and `set_len` is never reached. The file
is left containing the new `retained` bytes followed by whatever tail of the
*old* content was not overwritten — a byte-for-byte splice that is not a
valid sequence of the original lines and will generally not be parseable
Starlark. The same intermediate, un-truncated state is observable by any
process reading the file if the OS process is killed between the `write_all`
and `set_len` calls (e.g. OOM kill, `SIGKILL`, power loss), since no fsync or
temp-file-plus-rename technique is used, unlike the atomic
`persist_noclobber`-based approach already used a few lines away in
`write_migration_marker` for the marker file itself.

Because `prefix_rule_migration` only writes the migration marker after
`clean_rules_file` returns `Ok`, a later run will retry and can self-heal
once the same call succeeds cleanly, but any process that reads/parses the
policy file in the corrupted window (or before the next successful retry)
will see a broken policy file. Fix by truncating the file to zero length
before writing the new content, or better, writing `retained` to a temp file
in the same directory and renaming it over `policy_path` atomically, the same
pattern already used for `MIGRATION_MARKER_FILENAME`.

### CR-097: `GoalService::set_thread_goal` silently skips runtime effects and event emission unless the caller remembers two extra opt-in calls
**File:** `codex-rs/ext/goal/src/api.rs`
**Anchor:** `GoalSetOutcome::apply_runtime_effects`, `GoalSetOutcome::thread_goal_updated_item`
**Severity:** medium

`set_thread_goal` persists the goal change to the database and returns a `GoalSetOutcome`, but it does *not* itself apply the change to the live runtime or emit a `ThreadGoalUpdated` event. Both effects are exposed as separate methods on the returned struct (`outcome.apply_runtime_effects(&goal_service)` and `outcome.thread_goal_updated_item()`) that the caller must remember to invoke; `codex-rs/ext/goal/tests/goal_extension_backend.rs`'s `goal_service_external_set_active_preserves_concurrent_usage` test only passes because it explicitly calls `outcome.apply_runtime_effects(...)`.

This is inconsistent with the sibling mutator `clear_thread_goal`, which calls `runtime.apply_external_goal_clear(goal).await` internally with no action required from the caller. A caller who follows the pattern established by `clear_thread_goal` (or who just does `let outcome = service.set_thread_goal(...).await?;` and uses `outcome.goal`) will get a goal that is `Active` in the database but where:
- an idle thread is never kicked via `continue_if_idle()` to actually resume work on the newly active goal,
- objective-change steering is never injected into a running turn, and
- no `ThreadGoalUpdated` event/rollout item is produced, so any UI or rollout log watching for goal updates never sees the change until the next turn boundary happens to re-read state from the database.

Nothing in the type signature signals that these two follow-up calls are mandatory for correctness. Either fold `apply_runtime_effects`/event emission into `set_thread_goal` itself (matching `clear_thread_goal`'s behavior), or make `GoalSetOutcome` a must-use type that cannot be safely discarded without applying its effects (e.g. document it loudly and add a `#[must_use]`/debug-assert on drop), so a future caller cannot accidentally reintroduce this exact bug that the existing test happens to avoid.

### CR-098: Discarded reviewer session is dropped without calling `shutdown()`, unlike every other retirement path
**File:** `codex-rs/ext/guardian-reviewer/src/pool.rs`
**Anchor:** `ReviewerPool::prewarm`
**Severity:** medium

`prewarm()` spawns a session *before* taking the pool's `state` lock:

```rust
let cancellation = self.cancellation.child_token();
let guard = cancellation.clone().drop_guard();
let session = factory.spawn(factory.context(None), TrunkNew, None, cancellation.clone()).await?;
let mut state = self.state.lock().await;
if !cancellation.is_cancelled() && state.trunk.is_none() {
    state.trunk = Some(Arc::new(Trunk { session: Arc::new(session), .. }));
    drop(guard.disarm());
}
Ok(())
```

If another `prewarm()` (or a concurrent `review()`, which spawns the trunk while holding the lock for the whole spawn) wins the race and `state.trunk` is already `Some` by the time this call re-acquires the lock, the `if` body is skipped, `guard` is never disarmed, and the function returns. The `session` local is simply dropped; `guard`'s `Drop` impl cancels the child `CancellationToken`, but `ReviewerSession::shutdown()` — the method the trait doc requires callers to await ("Shutdown must cancel the runtime and await its termination") — is never called, and no background task is spawned to call it.

Every other place this file retires a session goes through an explicit, awaited (or backgrounded) `shutdown()` call: `invalidate()` calls `session.cancel()` + `shutdown_in_background(session)`; `review()`'s `SessionDisposition::Discard` branch calls `shutdown_in_background`; `EphemeralCleanup::drop` calls `shutdown_in_background`. `prewarm()`'s losing branch is the only path that relies solely on cancelling a token and hoping the session cleans itself up. Depending on what a concrete `ReviewerSession` implementation actually holds (subprocess handles, network connections, a live thread/session in `ThreadManager`), this can leak that resource whenever two prewarm attempts (or a prewarm racing a review) contend for the trunk slot. There is no test file for `pool.rs` in this crate, so this path is currently unexercised by any test.

Fix: on the losing branch, explicitly call (or background) `session.shutdown()` the same way `invalidate()`/`review()`/`EphemeralCleanup` do, rather than relying on cancellation alone.

### CR-099: Discarded trunk session can be reused by a concurrent review before it is removed and shut down
**File:** `codex-rs/ext/guardian-reviewer/src/pool.rs`
**Anchor:** `ReviewerPool::review`
**Severity:** medium

At the end of `review()`, the trunk's single-permit semaphore guard is released *before* the code checks whether the just-run review wants the session discarded:

```rust
drop(guard);
if disposition == SessionDisposition::Discard {
    let mut state = self.state.lock().await;
    if state.trunk.as_ref().is_some_and(|current| Arc::ptr_eq(current, &trunk))
        && let Some(removed) = state.trunk.take()
    {
        shutdown_in_background(Arc::clone(&removed.session));
    }
}
```

Between `drop(guard)` and the `state.lock().await` a few lines later, another concurrent `review()` call for the same parent (same context) can acquire the now-free `review_lock` permit and start running a brand-new review against the very session that this call is about to remove from `state.trunk` and pass to `shutdown_in_background`. The second caller's in-flight turn can then be cancelled/torn down mid-review by the shutdown triggered from underneath it, rather than ever being isolated onto an ephemeral fork the way a genuinely busy trunk would route it.

This is a real ordering bug, not a deliberate deadlock-avoidance choice: every other acquisition of `review_lock` in this file uses non-blocking `try_acquire()`, so holding the permit while taking `state.lock()` (i.e., performing the discard/removal before `drop(guard)`) cannot deadlock against the earlier "state lock then try_acquire" ordering used during trunk selection. The consequence is bounded by the codebase's fail-closed posture (a disrupted review surfaces as a session error/timeout, which existing code maps to a denial), so this is not a security bypass, but it is a genuine availability/correctness bug under concurrent reviews of the same parent thread — a condition the pool's own doc comments say it is designed to handle ("concurrent reviews fork committed context").

Fix: perform the discard check and `state.trunk` removal (and start of `shutdown_in_background`) while still holding `guard`, then drop it afterward — or re-acquire the permit before deciding to touch `state.trunk`.

### CR-100: Local image-generation save path skips the hardlink/symlink protections applied in the sandboxed path
**File:** `codex-rs/ext/image-generation/src/tool.rs`
**Anchor:** `save_image_generation_result`
**Severity:** medium

When `save_root` is `Some(..)` (the non-executor/local save path), the function decodes the base64 result and calls `LOCAL_FS.create_directory(...)` followed directly by `LOCAL_FS.write_file(...)` at a deterministic path built from `session_id`/`call_id`. It performs none of the checks that the `None` branch (executor/sandboxed environment path) performs a few lines later on the same kind of write: no check that the parent directory isn't a symlink, and no check that the destination doesn't already exist before writing.

The sandboxed branch documents exactly why these checks matter: `// Existing destination hardlinks could otherwise overwrite files outside the workspace.` and `// Full-access executor contexts do not prevent symlinked output directories.` `WriteFileOptions::default()` (see `codex-rs/file-system/src/lib.rs`, `follow_symlinks: true`) confirms `write_file` follows symlinks/hardlinks at the destination rather than refusing to write through them, so the same risk applies to `LOCAL_FS.write_file` in the `save_root` branch: if something (an earlier step in the same turn, another process, or a leftover artifact from a previous run) has planted a symlink/hardlink at the computed artifact path, the save silently overwrites whatever that link points to instead of failing.

Fix: apply the same "parent is not a symlink" and "destination must not already exist" checks to the `save_root` branch that are already applied to the executor-environment branch, so the two code paths enforce the same invariant the comments describe.

### CR-101: Ad-hoc note directory creation races when the notes tree does not yet exist
**File:** `codex-rs/ext/memories/src/local/ad_hoc_note.rs`
**Anchor:** `ensure_directory`
**Severity:** medium

`ensure_directory` checks for an existing directory with `metadata_or_none`, and if it returns `None`, calls `tokio::fs::create_dir(path).await?`, propagating any error (including `io::ErrorKind::AlreadyExists`) straight out via `?`. `ensure_notes_dir` calls this once per path segment (`extensions`, `extensions/ad_hoc`, `extensions/ad_hoc/notes`).

If two `add_ad_hoc_note` calls run concurrently against a fresh memory root (e.g. two parallel tool calls both writing the first-ever ad-hoc note in a thread), both can observe `metadata_or_none` returning `None` for `extensions` before either has created it. Both then call `create_dir`; the loser gets `AlreadyExists`, which is returned as `MemoriesBackendError::Io` even though the directory now legitimately exists and the operation could otherwise have succeeded. This is a genuine race under a condition (parallel tool calls) that this framework explicitly supports elsewhere (e.g. `supports_parallel_tool_calls`), so a reader would not expect it to fail spuriously here.

Fix: treat `AlreadyExists` from `create_dir` as success (fall through to the post-creation metadata/symlink check) instead of propagating it as an error.

### CR-102: Queue-service integration test overflows the default thread stack and aborts the whole test binary

**File:** `codex-rs/ext/queue/tests/queue_service.rs`
**Anchor:** `externally_changed_queues_dispatch_independently_and_retry_failed_wakes`
**Severity:** medium

Running this test with the toolchain's default stack size crashes the process instead of
failing the individual test. Reproduced directly:

```
cd codex-rs
env -u RUST_MIN_STACK cargo test -p codex-queue-extension --test queue_service \
  externally_changed_queues_dispatch_independently_and_retry_failed_wakes -- --exact
```

Output:

```
thread 'externally_changed_queues_dispatch_independently_and_retry_failed_wakes' (...) has overflowed its stack
fatal runtime error: stack overflow, aborting
error: test failed, to rerun pass `-p codex-queue-extension --test queue_service`
Caused by:
  process didn't exit successfully: ... (signal: 6, SIGABRT: process abort signal)
```

This is deterministic (reproduced twice) and also occurs when running the full
`cargo test -p codex-queue-extension` suite: the six tests that sort before it alphabetically
pass, then the process aborts on this test, and none of the ten tests that would have run after
it are executed at all — a single test's stack requirement takes down the entire binary rather
than being reported as one failure.

Setting `RUST_MIN_STACK=8388608` (8 MiB) makes the test (and the rest of the suite) pass
reliably, which is exactly the workaround this repository's own CI workflows already export
globally (`.github/workflows/rust-ci.yml`, `rust-ci-full.yml`, `rust-ci-full-nextest-platform.yml`
all set `RUST_MIN_STACK: "8388608"`), so CI does not see this crash. The test itself is
functionally correct — with the larger stack it exercises real external-queue-mutation,
independent-thread-dispatch, and resume-from-rollout behavior successfully. The problem is purely
that this one test's generated async state (many long-lived locals held across many `.await`
points inside one `#[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)]` function, several
of which are 25-second-timeout waits) is large enough to overflow a plain default-stack run.

Anyone invoking `cargo test -p codex-queue-extension` (or `cargo test --test queue_service`)
locally without manually exporting `RUST_MIN_STACK` — the ordinary way to run a single crate's
tests while iterating — gets a confusing hard process abort with no indication of *which*
assertion, if any, was wrong, and loses coverage of every other test in the binary for that run.
Consider splitting this test into smaller independent test functions (fewer live locals per
`.await` chain), or moving the large fixture/plumbing into a boxed helper so the per-test future
stays small, or documenting the `RUST_MIN_STACK` requirement next to the test / in the crate's
README so a local run doesn't look like an unrelated crash.

### CR-103: Orchestrator skill resource reads are not bounded during transfer, unlike the executor path
**File:** `codex-rs/ext/skills/src/provider/orchestrator.rs`
**Anchor:** `OrchestratorSkillProvider::read`, `contents.len() > MAX_SKILL_RESOURCE_CONTENT_BYTES`
**Severity:** medium

`OrchestratorSkillProvider::read` fetches the whole MCP resource before checking its size:

```rust
let result = tokio::time::timeout(ORCHESTRATOR_SKILL_READ_TIMEOUT,
        client.read_resource(CODEX_APPS_MCP_SERVER_NAME, request.resource.as_str()))
    .await??;
let contents = result.contents.into_iter().find_map(|contents| match contents {
    ResourceContent::Text { uri, text, .. } if uri == request.resource.as_str() => Some(text),
    ...
});
...
if contents.len() > MAX_SKILL_RESOURCE_CONTENT_BYTES {
    return Err(SkillProviderError::new(format!(
        "orchestrator skill resource {} exceeds the {MAX_SKILL_RESOURCE_CONTENT_BYTES}-byte read limit",
        ...
    )));
}
```

`client.read_resource` (`codex-mcp/src/resource_client.rs::McpResourceClient::read_resource`)
parses the full JSON-RPC response into an owned `String` with no incremental size ceiling of its
own before returning to this caller; the `MAX_SKILL_RESOURCE_CONTENT_BYTES` (1 MiB) check here
only runs after the entire resource is already materialized in memory. Compare this to the
sibling executor path in the same crate, `provider/executor.rs::read_bounded_text`, which streams
the file with `read_file_stream` and aborts as soon as the running total exceeds
`MAX_SKILL_RESOURCE_CONTENT_BYTES`:

```rust
while let Some(chunk) = stream.next().await {
    let chunk = chunk.map_err(&read_error)?;
    if contents.len().saturating_add(chunk.len()) > MAX_SKILL_RESOURCE_CONTENT_BYTES {
        return Err(...);
    }
    contents.extend_from_slice(&chunk);
}
```

Because orchestrator resources are explicitly treated as less trusted elsewhere in this same file
(`catalog_entry_from_resource`'s output is marked `with_external_context()` in `tools/mod.rs`), a
misbehaving or compromised MCP "app"/connector attached as `CODEX_APPS_MCP_SERVER_NAME` can return
an arbitrarily large resource body and force Codex to allocate and hold the entire blob in memory
before the size check finally rejects it — the same class of resource-exhaustion vector the
executor path was explicitly written to avoid. I confirmed the absence of an intermediate cap by
reading `codex-mcp/src/resource_client.rs::read_resource` (outside this shard but directly in the
call chain); I have not checked every lower transport layer (e.g. the underlying `rmcp` client) for
an independent hard cap, so it is possible another layer mitigates this, but nothing in the
reviewed skills-extension code enforces one.

### CR-104: Executor skill catalog bypasses the thread-level cache used by every other catalog source
**File:** `codex-rs/ext/skills/src/tools/mod.rs`
**Anchor:** `SkillToolContext::catalog`, `SkillToolAuthoritySelector::Executor`
**Severity:** medium

`SkillToolContext::catalog()` handles the two tool-reachable authorities differently. For
`Orchestrator` it calls `self.thread_state.orchestrator_catalog_snapshot(&self.providers, ...)`,
which goes through `SkillsThreadState`'s `orchestrator_cache` (a cache that lives on the
`Arc<SkillsThreadState>` and is shared across every step and tool call in the thread, per
`codex-rs/ext/skills/src/state.rs`). For `Executor` it instead does:

```rust
let mut catalog = self
    .executor_catalog
    .get_or_init(|| self.providers.list_executor_for_turn(query))
    .await
    .clone();
```

`self.executor_catalog` is a brand-new `Arc<OnceCell<SkillCatalog>>` constructed fresh inside
`skill_tools()` every time tools are built (see `codex-rs/ext/skills/src/extension.rs`,
`build_skill_tools`/`tools_for_step`, which is called once per sampling step and always
constructs a new `SkillToolContext`). It never touches
`SkillsThreadState::executor_catalog_snapshot`/`executor_root_catalog`, the per-root cache that
`state.rs` documents as covering "catalogs for stable selected roots" that "remain cached until
this thread state is dropped" specifically so repeated discovery is unnecessary.

The practical effect: the world-state contribution (`CatalogContext::discover_executor_catalog`
in `world_state_catalogs.rs`) populates and reuses `SkillsThreadState`'s executor cache, but every
time the model actually calls `skills.list`/`skills.read` with `authority: executor` in a
different step, `tools_for_step` rebuilds a fresh `SkillToolContext` whose local `OnceCell` has no
relationship to that cache, so `providers.list_executor_for_turn(query)` re-runs full executor
skill discovery (a real filesystem walk or exec-server round trip when no
`executor_capability_discovery` snapshot is supplied) even though the identical roots were already
discovered and cached earlier in the same thread. Orchestrator does not have this problem because
its lookup is routed through the shared cache.

I traced this by reading `tools/mod.rs` (`SkillToolContext`/`skill_tools`), `state.rs`
(`SkillsThreadState`), and the call sites in `extension.rs` that wire `tools_for_step` per step; I
did not add a live reproduction because exercising it end-to-end requires constructing a resolved
executor environment plus multiple simulated sampling steps, which is significant scaffolding
beyond this shard's files. The fix is to route the `Executor` branch of `SkillToolContext::catalog`
through `self.thread_state`'s executor cache the same way the `Orchestrator` branch already does.

### CR-105: Case-insensitive boundary replace panics on self-overlapping needles

**File:** `codex-rs/external-agent-migration/src/rewrite.rs`
**Anchor:** `replace_case_insensitive_with_boundaries`
**Severity:** medium

`replace_case_insensitive_with_boundaries` advances `search_start = start + 1` after *every* iteration, including a successful boundary match (where `last_emitted` is set to `end`). Its sibling function `replace_with_boundaries` (the case-sensitive path used for `case_sensitive_term_variants`) instead advances `search_start = end` after a match, which is the correct, non-overlapping behavior.

When the needle has a non-trivial border (i.e. some prefix of the needle equals some suffix of the needle, e.g. `"a.a"`), two matches of the same needle can overlap in the haystack. Because the loop restarts scanning from `start + 1` instead of `end`, the second match's `start` can be smaller than the first match's `last_emitted`, and the subsequent `output.push_str(&input[last_emitted..start])` panics because `last_emitted > start` (Rust panics on slices where `start > end`).

I confirmed this by extracting the function verbatim into a standalone file and running it with `rustc`:

```rust
fn main() {
    let input = "a.a.a";
    let result = replace_case_insensitive_with_boundaries(input, "a.a", "X");
    println!("result = {result}");
}
```

This panics with:
```
thread 'main' panicked at repro_rewrite.rs:28:35:
byte range starts at 3 but ends at 2
```

None of the `RewriteProfile` needles currently wired up in the crate (`"CLAUDE.md"`, `"claude"`, `"claude code"`, `"claude-code"`, `"claude_code"`, `"claudecode"`, `.cursorrules`, `"Cursor"`, and the test profiles) happen to have a border, so this is not reachable through today's call sites. But `RewriteProfile::new`/`with_case_sensitive_term_variants` are public crate APIs with no documented or enforced restriction against border-containing needles, and `rewrite()` is invoked on arbitrary user-authored file content (AGENTS.md-equivalents, skills, subagent instructions) during migration. Adding or editing a term list in the future with a self-overlapping word (e.g. any phrase whose first letters repeat, such as `"ana"`, `"abab"`, `"a a"`) would silently turn any migration run that happens to contain that overlap in the source content into a panic, aborting the whole import. Fix by changing `search_start = start + 1` to `search_start = end` after a successful match (mirroring `replace_with_boundaries`), or at minimum `search_start = last_emitted.max(start + 1)`.

### CR-106: Retained user-message recording never deduplicates messages without a `message_id`, undermining replay idempotency and the bounded retention family
**File:** `codex-rs/history/src/retained_context.rs`
**Anchor:** `RetainedContext::record_user_message`
**Severity:** medium

`record_user_message` only attempts to recognize a re-delivered record via this guard:

```rust
if let Some(index) = self.user_messages.iter().position(|entry| {
    message.message_id.is_some() && entry.value.message_id == message.message_id
}) {
    if self.user_messages[index].value == message && self.user_messages[index].inherited == inherited {
        return;
    }
    self.user_messages.remove(index);
}
```

When `message.message_id` is `None`, `message.message_id.is_some()` is `false`, so the closure short-circuits to `false` for every existing entry — the position lookup can never match, and every call unconditionally appends a brand-new `Ordered<RetainedUserMessage>` (with `bound_family` then possibly evicting an older, unrelated entry from the 8-slot `MAX_FAMILY_RECORDS` family to make room).

`message_id: None` is not a rare/legacy corner case — it is the ordinary shape of a locally authored user message before any server-assigned response id exists. The caller in `codex-rs/core/src/context_manager/history_user_authorization.rs` builds the record as `message_id: item.id().map(|id| id.as_str().to_owned())`, and `ResponseItem::Message { id: None, .. }` is the standard construction for local/user-authored items throughout the protocol crate (e.g. `codex-rs/protocol/src/models.rs` test fixtures at line ~2617 build exactly this shape for `role: "user"`). So for a large fraction of real user instructions, the identity-based dedup path in `record_user_message` is dead code, and every invocation for the "same" logical message (e.g. replay during a resume/reconciliation path that re-processes surviving history, or any retry that re-invokes `record_user_authorization`) produces a new, distinct `RetainedContextOrder::Local` entry rather than being recognized as the same source.

This directly contradicts the idempotency the sibling method promises for the analogous family (`record()` for verified answers is explicitly documented and tested as "Same-event delivery is idempotent"), and it weakens the security-relevant guarantee this module exists to provide: `bound_family` can silently evict a still-valid, distinct restriction/instruction to make room for a duplicate of another message, and code that assumes `(turn_id, text)`/`message_id` uniquely identifies one retained record (e.g. `rollback`'s `first_removed_message_id` lookup, and `ReconciledRetainedContext::new`'s de-dup-by-identity logic in `codex-rs/history/src/reconciled_retained_context.rs`) is working against a family that can contain multiple records for what is really one delivered message.

I verified this by static reading of the guard (message_id-less entries can never satisfy `position(...)`) and by confirming `message_id: None` is the common shape for a locally authored user message in the protocol crate; I was not able to fully trace, from within this shard alone, every call site that might re-invoke `record_user_authorization`/`record_user_message` for the same logical item (that plumbing lives in `codex-rs/core/src/context_manager/history.rs`, outside this shard), so I cannot certify duplicate recording happens under every-day, non-retry conditions — hence medium rather than high. The fix is to fall back to `(turn_id, text)` (or another stable identity) for the position lookup when `message_id` is absent, mirroring what `ReconciledRetainedContext` already does for its own matching.

### CR-107: Spilled hook output is written world-readable/listable under the shared OS temp directory
**File:** `codex-rs/hooks/src/output_spill.rs`
**Anchor:** `HookOutputSpiller::maybe_spill_text_with_limit`
**Severity:** medium

When a hook's `additionalContext`, feedback message, or Stop continuation prompt exceeds its token budget, `maybe_spill_text_with_limit` writes the full text to `<std::env::temp_dir()>/hook_outputs/<thread_id>/<uuid>.txt` via `fs::create_dir_all` and `fs::write` (`HookOutputSpiller::new`, `spilled_hook_output_preview`). Neither call sets restrictive permissions, and I confirmed with `grep -rn "set_permissions\|Permissions::from_mode\|0o600\|0o700" codex-rs/hooks/src/` that no permission hardening exists anywhere in this crate.

On a typical Unix system the process umask (commonly `022`) leaves the created `hook_outputs` directory and its thread subdirectories at mode `0755` and the spilled `.txt` files at `0644`, both readable/listable by any other local account. On a shared or multi-user host (CI runners, shared dev boxes, jump hosts) this lets any co-resident user run `ls /tmp/hook_outputs/` to enumerate active/past thread IDs and then read the full spilled content of any oversized hook output — which by construction is exactly the content the token-budget truncation was trying to keep out of the model context because it was too large, and which may contain command output, file contents, or other data a `PreToolUse`/`PostToolUse`/`Stop` hook decided to surface. The UUID-named file itself is unguessable, but that provides no protection once the parent directory is listable.

Fix: create the `hook_outputs` directory (and the per-thread subdirectory) with mode `0700`/`0600` on Unix (e.g. via `std::fs::Permissions`/`std::os::unix::fs::PermissionsExt` after `create_dir_all`, or by opening the file with `OpenOptions::mode(0o600)` before writing), and consider a per-user rather than purely OS-shared temp root.

### CR-108: Bracketed IPv6 `NO_PROXY`/proxy-bypass entries with an explicit port never match

**File:** `codex-rs/http-client/src/outbound_proxy.rs`
**Anchor:** `no_proxy_entry_matches_origin`
**Severity:** medium

`no_proxy_entry_matches_origin` strips a leading `http://`/`https://` and then calls `trim_matches(['[', ']'])` before attempting to split off a trailing `:port`:

```rust
let mut entry = entry
    .strip_prefix("http://")
    .or_else(|| entry.strip_prefix("https://"))
    .unwrap_or(entry)
    .trim_matches(['[', ']'])
    .to_ascii_lowercase();
let mut port = None;
let parsed_host_port = entry.rsplit_once(':').and_then(|(host, candidate_port)| {
    if host.contains(':') { return None; }
    ...
});
```

`str::trim_matches` only strips a run of matching characters that is anchored at the very start/end of the string. For an entry such as `"[::1]:8080"`, the trailing character is `'0'`, not `']'`, so only the leading `'['` is removed and the string becomes `"::1]:8080"` (verified directly: `"[::1]:8080".trim_matches(['[', ']'])` returns `"::1]:8080"` under rustc 1.x). The subsequent `rsplit_once(':')` then produces `host = "::1]"`, which still contains `:`+`]`, so the `host.contains(':')` guard rejects the split and `parsed_host_port` is `None`. The port is never extracted, and the leftover `"::1]:8080"` (containing a stray `]`) is compared verbatim against `origin.host` (e.g. `"::1"`), which can never match.

This function is compiled for `target_os = "windows"` (via `windows.rs::proxy_bypass_matches_origin`) and is the code path that decides whether a destination should bypass the WinHTTP/IE-configured proxy. A bracketed-IPv6-with-port bypass entry — the standard, unambiguous way to write such an entry, since an unbracketed IPv6 literal cannot be combined with a port — will silently fail to match, so traffic to that destination is routed through the configured proxy instead of going direct, contrary to the administrator's `NO_PROXY`/bypass-list intent. Plain hostnames, IPv4, and bracketed-IPv6-without-port all work correctly (and are covered by `no_proxy_matches_exact_suffix_wildcard_and_port`); only the bracketed+port combination is broken, and no test exercises it.

Fix: strip a matching pair of brackets explicitly (e.g. `entry.strip_prefix('[').and_then(|e| e.strip_suffix(']'))` when locating the port, falling back to the whole string when no `]` is present) instead of using `trim_matches` on both ends independently.

### CR-109: Non-connect/non-timeout transport errors leak full request URLs (with secrets) into `TransportError::Network`

**File:** `codex-rs/http-client/src/transport.rs`
**Anchor:** `ReqwestTransport::map_error`
**Severity:** medium

`map_error` strips the URL only for the connect-error and timeout branches:

```rust
fn map_error(err: reqwest::Error) -> TransportError {
    if err.is_connect() {
        TransportError::Connection(err.without_url())
    } else if err.is_timeout() {
        TransportError::Timeout
    } else {
        TransportError::Network(err.to_string())
    }
}
```

`reqwest::Error`'s `Display` impl (`reqwest-0.12.28/src/error.rs`) appends `" for url ({url})"` whenever the error carries a URL and `without_url()` has not been called:

```rust
if let Some(url) = &self.inner.url {
    write!(f, " for url ({url})")?;
}
```

Any error that is neither a connect error nor a timeout — e.g. a body/decode error from `resp.bytes().await` when a connection drops mid-response, or a `Kind::Redirect` error from an invalid `Location` header — falls into the `else` branch and is converted with `err.to_string()`, which still contains the full request URL. Several call sites in this codebase legitimately put secrets in the query string (the sibling module explicitly acknowledges this: `RouteAwareRequestError::without_url()` in `route_aware_client_pool.rs` documents "Use this for requests whose URL can contain credentials, such as signed blob uploads."). `ReqwestTransport`/`HttpTransport` is used throughout `codex-api` (responses, images, search, session, memories, realtime_call, models endpoints), so any of those requests that fail with a decode/body/redirect error rather than a connect/timeout error will produce a `TransportError::Network(String)` containing the unredacted URL. That string is propagated by `codex-api/src/auth.rs` and `codex-api/src/api_bridge.rs` (`TransportError::Network(msg) | TransportError::Build(msg) => CodexErr::Stream(msg)`), i.e. into a user/telemetry-facing error rather than being stopped inside this crate.

This is inconsistent with the rest of the crate, which goes out of its way to keep URLs (and the credentials some of them carry) out of logs and errors — `transport_tests.rs` even has a dedicated test, `connection_failures_are_classified_without_exposing_request_urls`, that only covers the connect-error path. There is no equivalent test for decode/body/redirect errors, and none would pass today.

Fix: call `err.without_url()` before `.to_string()` (or otherwise strip/redact the URL) for every branch that does not already have dedicated handling, not just the connect-error branch.

### CR-110: Credential file permissions are not re-applied when `auth.json` already exists
**File:** `codex-rs/login/src/auth/storage.rs`
**Anchor:** `impl AuthStorageBackend for FileAuthStorage { fn save(...)`
**Severity:** medium

`FileAuthStorage::save` opens `auth.json` with `OpenOptions::new().truncate(true).write(true).create(true)` and, on Unix, `.mode(0o600)`. The `mode()` value passed to `open(2)` is only applied by the kernel when the call actually **creates** a new inode (`O_CREAT` with no pre-existing file). If the file already exists, `open()` reuses the existing inode and its existing permission bits are left untouched — the `mode(0o600)` has no effect on an existing file.

I verified this directly:
```
touch perm_test.txt && chmod 644 perm_test.txt   # rw-r--r--
# open with OpenOptions::new().truncate(true).write(true).create(true).mode(0o600), write, close
ls -l perm_test.txt   # still -rw-r--r--
```
The permissions stayed at `644` after the "0600" open+write.

`save()` is the single write path used for every login (`login_with_api_key`, `login_with_access_token`, `login_with_bedrock_api_key`, `login_with_bedrock_access_keys`) and for every OAuth token refresh (`persist_tokens` → `storage.save`) and Agent Identity task-ID persistence (`persist_agent_identity_record`). None of these call sites ever `chmod` the file explicitly; they all rely on the `mode(0o600)` passed to `open()`.

Concretely: if `auth.json` ever ends up with broader permissions than `0600` — e.g. restored from a backup, synced via a dotfiles/cloud-sync tool that doesn't preserve Unix permissions, copied by the user, or created by an older build of this binary before this mode flag existed — every subsequent save (including fully automatic background token refreshes that happen without any user action) will silently keep writing the refreshed OAuth refresh token, access token, Bedrock AWS secret key, personal access token, or Agent Identity private key into that same group/world-readable file. There is no self-healing: the loose permission persists across every refresh cycle for the life of the file.

Fix: explicitly `set_permissions`/`fchmod` the file to `0o600` after opening/before writing (or after writing), on every `save()`, rather than relying solely on the `open()` mode argument, which POSIX only honors on file creation.

### CR-111: Message history persists raw text with no secret redaction despite a known TODO
**File:** `codex-rs/message-history/src/lib.rs`
**Anchor:** `// TODO: check `text` for sensitive patterns`
**Severity:** medium

`append_entry` writes the caller-supplied `text` verbatim into `~/.codex/history.jsonl` (one JSON object per line, persisted to disk with `0o600` permissions) with no scrubbing of secrets. The comment directly above the write path acknowledges this ("TODO: check `text` for sensitive patterns") but no such check exists in this crate, and the crate does not depend on `codex_secrets`/`redact_secrets`, which is used pervasively elsewhere in this same shard (e.g. `codex-rs/memories/write/src/phase1.rs::job::serialize_filtered_rollout_response_items`, `codex-rs/memories/write/src/rollout_input.rs`) specifically to keep API keys/tokens that show up in rollout content out of persisted artifacts and out of prompts sent to the model. If a user pastes a credential into a message (e.g. an API key while asking for help debugging), and history persistence is enabled (`HistoryPersistence::SaveAll`), that credential is written to disk unredacted and will resurface any time the on-disk history is displayed, synced, or backed up. Given the rest of the codebase treats this class of data specially, callers/readers would not expect message history to be the one place where it is stored as-is. Fix: apply the same redaction pass (`codex_secrets::redact_secrets` or equivalent) to `text` before constructing `HistoryEntry`, or explicitly document/gate this limitation so it isn't a silent gap.

### CR-112: Managed Bedrock access-key sessions are not classified as recoverable on AWS's real expiry status code
**File:** `codex-rs/model-provider/src/amazon_bedrock/mod.rs`
**Anchor:** `is_recoverable_auth_error`, `uses_aws_auth_recovery`
**Severity:** medium

`AmazonBedrockModelProvider::is_recoverable_auth_error` is:

```rust
fn is_recoverable_auth_error(&self, error: &TransportError) -> bool {
    matches!(
        error,
        TransportError::Http { status, .. } if *status == http::StatusCode::UNAUTHORIZED
    ) || (self.uses_aws_auth_recovery() && error::is_refreshable_auth_error(error))
}
```

and `uses_aws_auth_recovery` is:

```rust
fn uses_aws_auth_recovery(&self) -> bool {
    let source = self.auth_source();
    source == auth::BedrockAuthSource::CredentialExport
        || (self.auth_recovery.is_some()
            && matches!(
                source,
                auth::BedrockAuthSource::ConfiguredAwsProfile | auth::BedrockAuthSource::AwsSdk
            ))
}
```

`BedrockAuthSource::ManagedAccessKeys` (real SigV4-signed requests built from Codex-vended, session-token-based AWS credentials via `AwsAuthContext::load_with_access_keys`, see `amazon_bedrock/auth.rs::resolve_auth_method`) is never included in `uses_aws_auth_recovery`'s match arms. That means for this auth source, `is_recoverable_auth_error` only recognizes a literal `401 Unauthorized`.

`error_tests.rs::classifies_only_refreshable_bedrock_auth_failures` (in this same crate) demonstrates that the standard AWS failure mode for an expired temporary session is `403 Forbidden` with body `ExpiredTokenException`/`UnrecognizedClientException`/`InvalidClientTokenId` — `is_refreshable_auth_error` explicitly classifies these as refreshable. Every other SigV4 code path that can hit this exact error shape (`CredentialExport`, `ConfiguredAwsProfile`, `AwsSdk`) is covered by `uses_aws_auth_recovery`; `ManagedAccessKeys` is signed the same way (`resolve_auth_method`'s `ManagedAccessKeys` arm also calls `AwsAuthContext::load_with_access_keys`) but is excluded.

Practical effect: when a user is on Codex-managed Bedrock access keys (`CodexAuth::BedrockAccessKeys`) and the vended session expires, Bedrock will very likely return `403 ExpiredTokenException` (matching AWS's documented behavior for SigV4 requests, not `401`). `is_recoverable_auth_error` returns `false` for that response, `recover_from_unauthorized` also short-circuits to `NotConfigured` (it starts with `if !self.uses_aws_auth_recovery() { return Ok(NotConfigured) }`), so the provider-level recovery/retry path that exists specifically for this class of error is skipped, and the request fails hard even though the same error body would be treated as transient/retryable for a profile- or SDK-sourced Bedrock session.

I ran the existing `codex-model-provider` test suite (`cargo test -p codex-model-provider --lib`, 37/37 passing) and confirmed no test exercises `is_recoverable_auth_error`/`recover_from_unauthorized` for the `ManagedAccessKeys` source with a 403 body, so this gap is not covered either way. I have not been able to verify against a live Bedrock endpoint which exact status AWS returns for an expired Codex-vended session; the fix, if the 403 behavior is confirmed, is to add `ManagedAccessKeys` (and re-check whether `ManagedBearerToken` needs it too) to `uses_aws_auth_recovery`'s match, gated appropriately so it doesn't also enable a nonexistent `self.auth_recovery`/`self.credential_export` refresh attempt for that source.

### CR-113: Unbounded read on the network-proxy attribution preface allows connection-slot exhaustion

**File:** `codex-rs/network-proxy/src/attribution.rs`
**Anchor:** `read_attribution_token`, `stream.stream.peek(&mut marker).await?`
**Severity:** medium

`read_attribution_token` is the first thing every accepted HTTP-proxy and SOCKS5 connection goes
through (`BindConnectionAttribution` wraps the whole `http_service`/`socks_acceptor` in
`http_proxy.rs` and `socks5.rs`). The very first operation is:

```rust
let mut marker = [0_u8; 1];
let read = stream.stream.peek(&mut marker).await?;
```

This `peek` has no timeout. If a client opens a TCP connection to the HTTP or SOCKS5 listener and
never writes a byte, this `await` never resolves — there is no outer accept-level or per-connection
deadline anywhere in the crate (confirmed by grepping `http_proxy.rs`/`socks5.rs`/the
`connection_lifecycle` module for `timeout`/`Duration::from`; the only timeouts that exist there are
inside `#[cfg(test)]` code). `CancelOnShutdown` only cancels connections when the whole proxy shuts
down, not on a per-connection idle timeout.

This is inconsistent with the rest of the same module and the rest of the crate: once the magic byte
does match, the remaining frame (`magic`, length, token) is read inside
`tokio::time::timeout(ATTRIBUTION_FRAME_TIMEOUT, ...)` (3s), and the analogous first-byte sniff in
`codex-rs/network-proxy/src/brokered_tunnel.rs::peek_protocol` explicitly wraps its initial read in
`timeout(PREFIX_TIMEOUT, stream.read(&mut buf))` specifically so a silent client can't stall the
connection. The equivalent guard is simply missing on the `peek()` call that runs first, before any
of that bounded logic is ever reached.

Any process able to reach the proxy's listening socket (this includes the sandboxed child processes
this proxy exists to mediate for) can hold arbitrarily many connections open by connecting and never
sending data, tying up one task/socket per connection indefinitely. Fix by wrapping the initial
`peek` in the same `ATTRIBUTION_FRAME_TIMEOUT` (or a dedicated shorter timeout) and returning a
`TimedOut` error on expiry, mirroring the pattern already used a few lines later in the same function
and in `brokered_tunnel::peek_protocol`.

### CR-114: `Timer::record` combined with `Drop` double-records the duration metric
**File:** `codex-rs/otel/src/metrics/timer.rs`
**Anchor:** `impl Drop for Timer`
**Severity:** medium

`Timer::record(&self, additional_tags)` is a public, non-consuming method (`&self`, not `self`) that records the elapsed duration via `self.client.record_duration(...)`. Separately, `impl Drop for Timer` unconditionally calls `self.record(&[])` when the `Timer` value goes out of scope. Nothing in `Timer` tracks whether `record` was already called explicitly, so any caller who does the natural thing — call `timer.record(&extra_tags)` at a meaningful point and then let the guard drop normally at the end of the scope — gets the duration histogram incremented twice: once with `extra_tags` and once more with no tags, from the same measured interval.

The `additional_tags` parameter only makes sense if `record` is meant to be called explicitly (otherwise the API would just be "drop the guard"), so this is not a theoretical misuse — it's the intended usage of the documented public method, and it silently corrupts the resulting histogram (double counts, and also emits an extra data point with a different tag set than the caller asked for). I checked all current call sites in the repo (`grep -rn "start_timer"` across `codex-rs`) and none currently call `.record()` explicitly before drop, so today's callers only hit the single Drop-triggered record — but the bug is live for the first caller who uses `record()` as designed, and it is impossible to know from the type that this will happen since `Timer` gives no consuming/"disarm" API.

Fix: make `record` consume `self` (or set an internal flag / use `Option`-wrapped state that `Drop` checks) so an explicit `record()` call suppresses the automatic Drop-time recording.

### CR-115: `format_allow_prefixes` truncates by character count, not by the byte budget its constant name promises

**File:** `codex-rs/protocol/src/models.rs`
**Anchor:** `format_allow_prefixes`, constant `MAX_ALLOW_PREFIX_TEXT_BYTES`
**Severity:** medium

`format_allow_prefixes` renders the list of allowed exec-policy command prefixes
that gets injected into the model prompt (callers: `codex-rs/prompts/src/permissions_instructions.rs`,
`codex-rs/core/src/context/world_state/permissions.rs`, and
`.../compact_permissions.rs`). It caps the rendered text with:

```rust
let byte_idx = output
    .char_indices()
    .nth(MAX_ALLOW_PREFIX_TEXT_BYTES)
    .map(|(i, _)| i);
```

`Iterator::nth(N)` on `char_indices()` skips `N` *characters*, not `N` bytes, so
`byte_idx` is the byte offset after `MAX_ALLOW_PREFIX_TEXT_BYTES` characters —
not after `MAX_ALLOW_PREFIX_TEXT_BYTES` bytes. For ASCII text these coincide,
which is why the existing test (`format_allow_prefixes_limits_output`, which
only uses ASCII tokens like `"tool-000"` and `"x".repeat(500)`) passes. Any
non-ASCII bytes in a command token (unicode file paths, non-English arguments,
emoji, etc., all plausible in real shell command prefixes recorded by the
exec-policy engine) make the actual truncated length exceed the intended
5000-byte budget, in the worst case by 4x for 4-byte UTF-8 characters.

Reproduced directly (not just read) with the project's pinned toolchain
(`rust-toolchain.toml` channel 1.95.0), isolating just the truncation logic:

```rust
let max_bytes: usize = 5000;
let full_text: String = "\u{1F600}".repeat(max_bytes + 1); // 4-byte UTF-8 char
let byte_idx = full_text.char_indices().nth(max_bytes).map(|(i, _)| i);
// byte_idx == 20000, i.e. 4x the intended 5000-byte budget
```

This defeats the purpose of `MAX_ALLOW_PREFIX_TEXT_BYTES` (bounding how much of
this rendered list is injected into the model's context/prompt) whenever
prefixes contain multi-byte UTF-8 content, and the mismatch is invisible from
the existing ASCII-only test suite. Fix by computing the byte offset directly,
e.g. via `output.floor_char_boundary(MAX_ALLOW_PREFIX_TEXT_BYTES)` (used
elsewhere in this same codebase, see
`codex-rs/protocol/src/models/executed_tool_calls.rs`) or by walking
`char_indices()` and stopping once the byte offset itself reaches the limit,
then adding a non-ASCII regression test.

### CR-116: `ToolName::Display` concatenates namespace and name with no separator, producing ambiguous/colliding output

**File:** `codex-rs/protocol/src/tool_name.rs`
**Anchor:** `impl fmt::Display for ToolName`
**Severity:** medium

`Display` for a namespaced, non-default `ToolName` is:

```rust
Some(namespace) => write!(f, "{namespace}{}", self.name),
```

This concatenates `namespace` and `name` with no delimiter at all. Two different, structurally distinct `ToolName` values can render to the identical string, e.g. `ToolName::namespaced("ab", "c")` and `ToolName::namespaced("a", "bc")` both `Display` as `"abc"`. That makes the `Display` output unsafe to use as a unique key, for deduplication, or for round-tripping back to a `(namespace, name)` pair — exactly the "legacy string boundary" use the type's own history describes (see the `Remove ToolName display helper` commit, which folded the old `ToolName::display()` helper's formula, unchanged, into this `Display` impl).

This is also inconsistent with the separator convention used elsewhere in the same tool system to flatten a `ToolName` into one string. `codex-rs/tools/src/code_mode.rs::code_mode_name_for_tool_name` explicitly joins with `"__"` (e.g. `format!("{namespace}__{}", tool_name.name)`) unless the namespace already ends in `_`/the name starts with `_`. `Display` on `ToolName` has no equivalent separator logic, so the same `ToolName` renders differently depending on which flattening path a caller uses — e.g. `ToolName::namespaced("clock", "sleep")` renders as `"clocksleep"` via `Display` but as `"clock__sleep"` via `code_mode_name_for_tool_name`.

In-tree tests that compare `ToolName::namespaced(...).to_string()` against a router's own registered/exposed name strings (e.g. `codex-rs/core/src/tools/spec_plan_tests.rs`) don't catch this because both sides of the assertion go through the same buggy `Display` impl, so the comparison is self-consistent even though the produced string is not the canonical flattened name. Any consumer that renders a `ToolName` via `Display`/`.to_string()` for a human-facing message, a log line, or a boundary that must match the `"namespace__name"` convention used elsewhere (hook payloads, telemetry tags, Responses tool names) will get the wrong or an ambiguous string.

Fix: give the namespaced branch of `Display` the same separator (or otherwise document that `Display` is intentionally distinct from the flattening convention and must never be compared/parsed as an identifier), and add a unit test in `tool_name.rs` asserting `Display` output for at least one non-default-namespace case.

### CR-117: A single oversized cancellation ID permanently disables elicitations, not just the offending one
**File:** `codex-rs/rmcp-client/src/elicitation_client_service.rs`
**Anchor:** `VerificationCancellations`, `MAX_EARLY_CANCELLATIONS`
**Severity:** medium

`handle_notification` tracks `notifications/cancelled` messages that arrive before their
matching elicitation request in a bounded `early: HashSet<RequestId>` guarded by a
`saturated` flag. The intent, per the adjacent comment ("Bound both the number and size of
retained request IDs"), is to cap memory use from an unbounded stream of bogus
cancellations. The actual trigger conflates two unrelated conditions:

```rust
if cancellations.early.len() == MAX_EARLY_CANCELLATIONS
    || matches!(request_id, RequestId::String(id) if id.len() > 1024)
{
    cancellations.saturated = true;
    cancellations.early.clear();
} else {
    cancellations.early.insert(request_id.clone());
}
```

Reaching the 1024-entry count cap is the intended saturation path. But the second disjunct
fires on the very first notification whose `request_id` is a `RequestId::String` longer than
1024 characters — regardless of how many entries are currently tracked (even zero). Once hit,
`saturated` is set permanently for the lifetime of this `ElicitationClientService` (i.e., for
the rest of that MCP server connection), and every subsequent call to `create_elicitation`
short-circuits to `ElicitationAction::Cancel` without ever invoking `send_elicitation`:

```rust
if cancellations.saturated || cancellations.early.remove(&id) {
    return Ok(ElicitationResponse { action: ElicitationAction::Cancel, content: None, meta: None });
}
```

So a single `notifications/cancelled` referencing an oversized, unmatched string ID —
whether from a misbehaving/verbose MCP server or a deliberately crafted one — silently and
permanently breaks every future elicitation on that connection, including unrelated
`elicitation/create` requests and `openai/elicitation/create` user-verification (step-up
auth) prompts that have nothing to do with the oversized ID. The failure direction is safe
(a cancelled user-verification is treated as a decline, not a grant), so this is not an
auth-bypass, but it is a correctness/availability regression that a reader would not expect:
the comment and the count-based cap imply saturation only follows from exhausting capacity,
not from a single anomalous message.

I traced this from the source directly (pure boolean/state logic, no timing dependency); I
did not additionally drive it through a live `ElicitationClientService` instance because
constructing one requires the `SendElicitation`/`ElicitationPauseState`/`ClientInfo`
scaffolding used by `rmcp_client.rs` (outside this shard). The fix is to only ever set
`saturated` from the count-based cap, and to simply skip inserting (without saturating) an
individual ID that exceeds the length bound.

### CR-118: Ordinary MCP OAuth login does not reconcile an explicit `callback_url` port with `callback_port`

**File:** `codex-rs/rmcp-client/src/perform_oauth_login.rs`
**Anchor:** `OauthLoginFlow::new`
**Severity:** medium

`McpServerOAuthConfig` (`codex-rs/config/src/mcp_types.rs`) exposes `callback_url` ("Registered callback URL associated with this OAuth client") and `callback_port` ("Fixed callback port that takes precedence over Codex's global OAuth callback port") as independent, user-settable fields — nothing ties them together, and both are threaded through as separate `Option` parameters into `OauthLoginFlow::new`.

In `OauthLoginFlow::new`, the listener socket is always bound using the resolved `callback_port`:
```rust
let bind_addr = SocketAddr::new(bind_ip, callback_port.unwrap_or(0));
let server = Arc::new(Server::http(bind_addr).map_err(|err| anyhow!(err))?);
...
let redirect_uri = resolve_redirect_uri(&server, callback_url)?;
let redirect_uri = if is_enterprise_idp {
    // forcibly overwrite with the actual bound listener port
    ...
} else {
    redirect_uri
};
```
`resolve_redirect_uri` only rewrites the port embedded in `callback_url` when the host is literally `127.0.0.1` **and** the URL has no port at all:
```rust
if parsed.scheme() == "http" && parsed.host_str() == Some("127.0.0.1") && parsed.port().is_none() {
    // insert the real listener port
    ...
}
Ok(callback_url.to_string())
```
So if an operator configures `callback_url = "http://127.0.0.1:9999/callback"` together with a different `callback_port = 8888` (a legitimate, independently documented combination — e.g. to pin both a stable callback path/port for firewall rules), the listener binds to `8888` while the `redirect_uri` sent to the authorization server (and opened in the browser) still says `:9999`. The OAuth callback can never reach the listener; the login simply times out after `DEFAULT_OAUTH_TIMEOUT_SECS` with a generic "timed out waiting for OAuth callback" error, giving no indication that the two settings disagree.

Note that the enterprise-IdP branch of the same function explicitly guards against exactly this by unconditionally overwriting the port in the resolved redirect URI with the real listener port:
```rust
let redirect_uri = if is_enterprise_idp {
    let listener_port = server.server_addr().to_ip()...port();
    let mut redirect = Url::parse(&redirect_uri)?;
    redirect.set_port(Some(listener_port))...
    redirect.to_string()
} else {
    redirect_uri
};
```
This asymmetry indicates the failure mode was already recognized and fixed for one call path but not the other. Fix: either validate at config-resolution time that an explicit `callback_url` port (when present) matches the effective `callback_port`, or apply the same unconditional port-reconciliation used for the enterprise path to the ordinary MCP path as well.

### CR-119: Concurrent tool calls sharing an MRTR input key can silently cross-cancel each other's elicitation prompts
**File:** `codex-rs/rmcp-client/src/tool_input.rs`
**Anchor:** `// Native prompts need distinct UI/cancellation ownership when concurrent tool calls use the same server-assigned input key.`
**Severity:** medium

`call_tool`'s MRTR loop only gives a collision-resistant `RequestId` to native `openai/userVerification` prompts:

```rust
let request_id = if native_verification {
    RequestId::String(format!("tool-input/{id}/{index}").into())
} else {
    RequestId::String(key.clone().into())
};
```

For every other elicitation type (standard MCP `elicitation/create`, `openai/form`, `openai/elicitation/create` form mode), the `RequestId` is just the server-assigned `key` text (e.g. `"confirmation"`), with no per-call disambiguator. That `RequestId` becomes `context.id` inside `ElicitationClientService::create_elicitation` (`codex-rs/rmcp-client/src/elicitation_client_service.rs`), which is the key into a single, per-connection `pending_verifications.pending: HashMap<RequestId, oneshot::Sender<()>>` shared by every concurrent `call_tool` in flight on that connection.

If two concurrent `call_tool` invocations against the same MCP server both reach an MRTR round using the same key (very plausible: `"confirmation"` is the example key used throughout this very test suite, e.g. `mcp_2026_mrtr.rs`'s `elicitation_request`), the second call's `pending.insert(id.clone(), cancel_tx)` silently overwrites the first call's entry. Two concrete failure modes follow:

1. If the first call's round completes normally while the second is still pending, `PendingVerification::drop` removes whatever is *currently* stored under that key — i.e. it deletes the *second* call's `cancel_tx`, not its own. A later legitimate `notifications/cancelled` for the second call's key then finds nothing in `pending` and is filed into the `early` cancellation set instead.
2. Because `early` cancellations are never scoped to a specific call, a *third*, unrelated future elicitation that reuses the same key text will find that (spurious) `early` entry and be auto-cancelled at the top of `create_elicitation` (`cancellations.early.remove(&id)` branch) — without ever invoking `send_elicitation`, i.e. without the user ever seeing the prompt.

This fails safe in the sense that the affected tool call receives `{"action":"cancel"}` rather than a forged acceptance, but it is a real correctness bug: a benign cancellation belonging to one concurrent tool call can cause a wholly unrelated, later confirmation prompt to be silently dropped. The existing test `native_mrtr_concurrent_prompts_have_independent_cancellation` (`codex-rs/rmcp-client/tests/mcp_2026_mrtr/native_verification_tests.rs`) exercises exactly this scenario for the native-verification path and passes only because of the `tool-input/{id}/{index}` disambiguation; there is no equivalent test for two concurrent standard-elicitation MRTR rounds sharing a key, and tracing the code shows they are not protected the same way.

Fix: derive the `RequestId` for all elicitation-carrying `ServerRequest`s from `format!("tool-input/{id}/{index}")` (or otherwise fold in the outer call's `id`), not only for `native_verification`, so `ElicitationClientService`'s per-connection cancellation map can never collide across concurrent tool calls.

### CR-120: Collab resume events leave zero rollout-trace evidence, unlike every other collab lifecycle pair
**File:** `codex-rs/rollout-trace/src/protocol_event.rs`
**Anchor:** `tool_runtime_trace_event`
**Severity:** medium

`tool_runtime_trace_event` turns every other `Collab*Begin`/`Collab*End` pair into a
`ToolRuntimeTraceEvent::Started`/`Ended` runtime observation: `CollabAgentSpawnBegin`/`End`,
`CollabAgentInteractionBegin`/`End`, `CollabWaitingBegin`/`End`, and `CollabCloseBegin`/`End`
are all matched explicitly and keyed by `event.call_id`. `EventMsg::CollabResumeBegin(_)` and
`EventMsg::CollabResumeEnd(_)` are conspicuously absent from those arms and instead fall into
the trailing wildcard `=> None` alongside genuinely non-boundary events (e.g. `TokenCount`,
`AgentMessageContentDelta`).

I confirmed `CollabResumeBeginEvent`/`CollabResumeEndEvent` (`codex-rs/protocol/src/protocol.rs`)
carry the same shape as the other Collab* pairs (`call_id`, `sender_thread_id`,
`receiver_thread_id`, timestamps), so nothing about their shape explains the omission — it
looks like a variant that was missed when the match was extended, not an intentional exclusion.

The same two variants are also absent from `wrapped_protocol_event_type`'s `Some(...)` arms
(they're bucketed into that function's giant `None` list too), so they aren't even preserved as
a generic wrapped protocol event. The net effect: a "resume agent" collab operation produces a
`ToolCall` through the ordinary dispatch-boundary hook (out of this shard), but it will never
get a `ToolCallRuntimeStarted`/`Ended` observation, never receive `raw_runtime_payload_ids`
evidence, and never produce an `InteractionEdge` the way spawn/interaction/waiting/close do
(`reducer/tool/agents.rs`'s `start_agent_interaction_from_runtime` and
`end_agent_interaction_from_runtime` only look at kinds that would come from these runtime
payloads). Anyone using the reduced trace/replay to inspect a multi-agent session that resumes a
closed agent will see the resume as a black hole, in contrast to every structurally identical
sibling event. Fix: add explicit arms for `CollabResumeBegin`/`CollabResumeEnd` in
`tool_runtime_trace_event` (and a matching handler in `reducer/tool/agents.rs` if resume should
produce an interaction edge), mirroring the `CollabClose*` handling.

### CR-121: Directory scan retries forever on a persistent `read_dir` entry error during SQLite backfill

**File:** `codex-rs/rollout/src/metadata.rs`
**Anchor:** `collect_rollout_paths`
**Severity:** medium

`collect_rollout_paths` (used by `backfill_sessions_with_lease` to enumerate every rollout under
`sessions/` and `archived_sessions/` for the SQLite metadata backfill) handles a `next_entry()`
error by logging and `continue`-ing the *inner* loop instead of breaking or propagating:

```rust
loop {
    let next_entry = match read_dir.next_entry().await {
        Ok(next_entry) => next_entry,
        Err(err) => {
            warn!("failed to read directory entry under {}: {err}", dir.display());
            continue;
        }
    };
    ...
}
```

If the underlying error is not a one-off transient glitch but a persistent condition on that
`ReadDir` stream — e.g. `EMFILE`/`ENFILE` (file-descriptor exhaustion, plausible here since the
rollout-compression worker and other fd-heavy operations can run concurrently with backfill), a
permission change mid-scan, or the directory being removed — every subsequent call to
`read_dir.next_entry()` on the same handle returns the same error, and the loop spins
indefinitely calling the same syscall without backoff or an exit condition. This pins a Tokio
worker thread at 100% CPU and the backfill task never completes (never reaches
`mark_backfill_complete`), unlike every other directory-walk in this same shard
(`compression.rs::compress_rollouts_in_root`, `list.rs`'s `collect_dirs_desc`/`collect_files`,
`search.rs`'s `scan_rollout_matches`/`scan_compressed_rollout_matches`,
`rollout_reference_index.rs::scan_paths`), all of which propagate a `next_entry()` error with `?`
or an explicit `return Err(...)` and stop scanning that directory. This is the only place in the
shard using this pattern, which reads as an oversight rather than an intentional retry policy.
Fix: propagate the error (or `break`) instead of looping back to the same failing call.

### CR-122: Rollout writer wedges permanently if a pending item cannot be written twice in a row

**File:** `codex-rs/rollout/src/recorder.rs`
**Anchor:** `write_pending_items_once`, `write_pending_with_recovery`

**Severity:** medium

`write_pending_items_once` walks `pending_items` from the front and only drains the prefix that
was written successfully:

```rust
for item in &self.pending_items {
    match self.ordinal_state.current() {
        Ok(ordinal) => match writer.write_rollout_item(item, ordinal).await {
            Ok(()) => self.ordinal_state.advance(),
            Err(err) => { write_result = Err(err); break; }
        },
        Err(err) => { write_result = Err(err); break; }
    }
    written_count += 1;
}
if written_count > 0 { self.pending_items.drain(..written_count); }
write_result
```

`write_pending_with_recovery` retries this exactly twice (drop-writer-and-reopen once) before
surfacing the error to the caller of `persist`/`flush`/`shutdown`. That retry strategy assumes the
failure is a transient I/O problem that a fresh file handle will fix. It has no way to distinguish
that from an input-dependent, deterministic failure — e.g. `writer.write_rollout_item` calls
`serde_json::to_string(item)` inside `JsonlWriter::write_line`, which errors on a non-finite
(`NaN`/`Infinity`) float anywhere in the item (serde_json rejects these unconditionally); reopening
the file changes nothing about that outcome. Once that happens, the offending item stays
permanently at the head of `pending_items` (nothing ever skips or discards it), so:
- every future `AddItems`/`flush`/`persist`/`shutdown` re-attempts the exact same write and fails
  the same way,
- every item queued after the poison item accumulates in memory forever and is silently never
  persisted to disk for the remainder of the session,
- the caller only learns about this on `persist`/`flush`/`shutdown` calls, not proactively.

I have not found a concrete, currently-reachable value that produces a non-finite float inside a
`RolloutItem` (`SecurityRiskScore`'s `f32` confidence fields are the closest candidate but I did
not trace a producer that could make them non-finite), so I can't hand you a guaranteed repro
input — flag this as a structural gap in the recovery path rather than a proven live bug: the
two-strikes-then-report retry has no "poison item" escape hatch, unlike, say, skipping/quarantining
the bad item and continuing with the rest of the queue.

### CR-123: curl invoked with an unsanitized, attacker/user-influenced URL and no `--` separator
**File:** `codex-rs/skills/src/assets/samples/openai-docs/scripts/fetch-codex-manual.mjs`
**Anchor:** `requestManualWithCurl`
**Severity:** medium

`requestManualWithCurl` builds a curl argv array and finishes with `args.push(url)`, where `url`
is `args.manualUrl` from `parseArgs` — validated only for non-emptiness, never for scheme. `curl`
is exec'd via `execFileAsync` (no shell), so classic shell injection isn't possible, but nothing
stops `url` from being interpreted as a curl **option** instead of the target, because there is no
`--` end-of-options marker before it.

I confirmed this behavior locally: running curl with the same flag set used here
(`--dump-header ... --output ... --user-agent ... --max-time ... --head "-o/tmp/evil.txt"`)
causes curl to consume `-o/tmp/evil.txt` as the short `-o` (`--output`) option rather than as a
URL, changing curl's write target instead of failing as "invalid URL." More dangerous single-token
options exist too (e.g. `-K<file>` / `--config=<file>` to load additional options from a file at
a path the caller can predict, such as the shared `TMPDIR`-based cache dir this same script
resolves).

`requestManual`'s transport-selection logic makes this reachable in the normal control flow, not
just a contrived edge case: when a proxy is configured (`preferCurl`), curl runs first with the
raw `manualUrl`; even when `fetch` is preferred, if `fetch(url, ...)` throws (e.g. because
`manualUrl` is not a well-formed URL), the code falls back to `requestManualWithCurl` with that
same string, still unsanitized, in the very next transport attempt. Any caller or wrapper that
lets an untrusted value reach `--manual-url` (or a future `--url` alias) can therefore inject a
curl flag. Fix by validating `manualUrl` has an `http(s)://` scheme before use, and/or inserting a
literal `"--"` before `args.push(url)` so curl treats everything after it as positional.

### CR-124: Unescaped SQL LIKE wildcards break the documented "substring match" contract for log filters

**File:** `codex-rs/state/src/runtime/logs.rs`
**Anchor:** `fn push_like_filters`
**Severity:** medium

`push_like_filters` builds `module_path LIKE '%' || ? || '%'` (and the same shape for
`file_like`) and binds the caller-supplied filter string directly as the `?`
parameter, without escaping SQLite's `LIKE` metacharacters (`%` and `_`) inside that
value. Because `_` matches "any one character" in SQLite `LIKE`, a filter value that
itself contains an underscore silently becomes a wildcard at that position instead of
a literal character.

I verified this with a standalone SQLite query using the exact pattern this code
builds:

```
sqlite> CREATE TABLE logs (module_path TEXT);
sqlite> INSERT INTO logs VALUES ('codex_core'), ('codexXcore'), ('unrelated');
sqlite> SELECT module_path FROM logs WHERE module_path LIKE '%' || 'codex_core' || '%';
codex_core
codexXcore
```

`codex-rs/cli/src/bin/logs_client.rs` exposes this directly as the `--module` /
`--file` CLI flags, documented as "Substring match on module_path" /
"Substring match on file path" (`struct Args`, fields `module` and `file`). Since
almost every Rust module path in this codebase contains an underscore (`codex_core`,
`codex_tui`, `codex_state`, ...), filtering logs with `--module codex_core` returns
extra, unrelated rows whose module path merely has some other character in the
position of that underscore — a silent violation of the documented substring-match
contract, not just a theoretical edge case. The same unescaped pattern is used for
`file_like`. Fix by escaping `%`, `_`, and the escape character itself in the filter
value before binding (e.g. `LIKE ... ESCAPE '\'` with the value pre-escaped), or by
switching to `INSTR`, which this file already uses correctly for the `search` filter
a few lines below.

### CR-125: Default `code_mode_result` fallback does not redact MCP `_meta` the way the explicit override does
**File:** `codex-rs/tools/src/tool_output.rs`
**Anchor:** `response_input_to_code_mode_result`
**Severity:** medium

`impl ToolOutput for codex_protocol::mcp::CallToolResult` explicitly overrides `code_mode_result` to strip the `_meta` field before handing the value to Code Mode, with the comment "MCP result metadata is private to clients and must not reach Code Mode." That override is reached whenever a `CallToolResult` value itself implements `ToolOutput` directly (its `to_response_item` returns `ResponseInputItem::McpToolCallOutput { output: self.clone(), .. }`).

The default trait method (used by any `ToolOutput` implementer that does not override `code_mode_result`) is:

```rust
fn code_mode_result(&self, payload: &ToolPayload) -> JsonValue {
    response_input_to_code_mode_result(self.to_response_item("", payload))
}
```

and `response_input_to_code_mode_result`'s `McpToolCallOutput` arm does:

```rust
ResponseInputItem::McpToolCallOutput { output, .. } => serde_json::to_value(output)
    .unwrap_or_else(|err| JsonValue::String(format!("failed to serialize mcp result: {err}"))),
```

This path serializes the whole `CallToolResult` — including `_meta` — with no redaction. So the redaction guarantee described in the sibling override's comment is only enforced when a type's `to_response_item` happens to return `McpToolCallOutput` *and* that same type also remembers to override `code_mode_result`. Any current or future `ToolOutput` implementer that relies on the default `code_mode_result` while producing a `ResponseInputItem::McpToolCallOutput` from `to_response_item` would silently leak MCP server metadata (which can contain server-internal identifiers/state not intended for client-visible Code Mode scripts) into the Code Mode result.

I checked every current `impl ToolOutput for ...` in the repo (`grep -rn "impl ToolOutput for" codex-rs`): today only `codex_protocol::mcp::CallToolResult` itself returns `McpToolCallOutput` from `to_response_item`, and it does override `code_mode_result`, so there is no live leak right now — `McpToolOutput` in `codex-rs/core/src/tools/context.rs` also overrides `code_mode_result` and delegates to `self.result.code_mode_result(payload)`, so it is safe too. But this is a real asymmetry in the default trait behavior, not merely a style nit: the type that is *most* likely to be handed to the default path (a bare `CallToolResult`-carrying wrapper) is exactly the type whose metadata the sibling code comment says must never reach Code Mode, and nothing enforces that the redaction travels with the `ResponseInputItem` variant instead of with the trait override. A safer fix is to make `response_input_to_code_mode_result`'s `McpToolCallOutput` arm strip `_meta` itself (mirroring the explicit override), so the guarantee holds regardless of which `ToolOutput` impl produces the response item.

### CR-126: "Cancel task" exit action can silently fail to interrupt the primary thread

**File:** `codex-rs/tui/src/app/event_dispatch.rs`
**Anchor:** `RunningTaskExitAction::CancelTask`
**Severity:** medium

In the "Task is still running" exit popup, choosing **Cancel task** dispatches
`AppEvent::RunningTaskExit { action: RunningTaskExitAction::CancelTask, thread_id }`,
handled as:

```rust
RunningTaskExitAction::CancelTask => {
    if self.chat_widget.thread_id() == Some(thread_id)
        && self.chat_widget.is_agent_turn_running()
        && self.chat_widget.submit_op(AppCommand::interrupt())
    {
```
